Select named review sets with `--review-set <id,...>`, or use `--review-set none` to omit them. Word files contain one word per line and are limited to 8 MiB of valid UTF-8 text.

The summary names observed red flags and separately reports incomplete evidence. No red flags means only “not bad”, never “good”. Use `--detail failures` for bounded samples and `--detail full` for pages of all captured cases. Select a section with `--section`, and use its continuation cursor to read another page. With `--case`, choose the `readings`, `expectations`, `memberships` or `sources` section to page that case’s details; `--side` selects before or after readings. `--word-results` is an alias for the first full word page.

Use `--job` or `--report` to select a particular Trial or saved report. `--refresh-report` explicitly produces a new report from retained evidence; a normal read does not rerun the parser. A report can have limitations when the original Trial did not retain a comparable check, set or other evidence.

For one exact case, use `--case <caseKey> --trace --side before` or `--side after`. Tracing may run a diagnostic against the report’s recorded grammar, parser and settings; a missing input requires a new Trial. A diagnostic can differ from the saved batch evidence and does not change the report.

After Motif's own Apply, the next Trial captures a new Baseline. After a save made outside Motif, measuring pending changes is refused with `change.refresh-required` until you capture a new Baseline with `motif baseline capture`.

entries.title: Read Trial progress
entries.description: Waits for a Trial job and reads its state. Read the stored review report after the Trial completes.
entries.helpPage:
# Read Trial progress

Waits for a Trial job and reads its state. Once the Trial has finished, read its saved report to examine the evidence and its limitations.

entries.title: Read grammar warnings
entries.description: Reads stored grammar findings and allomorph refusals from parsing, with filters by code or warning level. Confirmed uses of Selection words stay separate from spelling and membership matches.
entries.helpPage:
# Read grammar warnings

`warnings` reads grammar-check findings and allomorph refusals already recorded by parsing for a project. It can filter by diagnostic code or show only findings at warning level. Add `--proposal <id>` to read the check stored with that Proposal's latest Trial. When the current Baseline has not been checked, `warnings` refuses and tells you to run `grammar check`; it does not return an empty findings list.

PanGloss reports an unreadable phonological environment as a warning. Roots ignore that restriction but keep valid ones; ordinary affixes add an unrestricted pass beside valid passes; an infix with no valid position is skipped.

## When to use it

Use it after [Check a grammar](cmd:grammar%20check) when you want to inspect reported findings. Combine `--kind` and `--left-out` to narrow a large result without rerunning the check.

## Example

```powershell
motif warnings --project "C:\FieldWorks\Projects\Koro\Koro.fwdata" --left-out --json
```

## What it prints

The response includes separate error, warning, and information counts, plus findings with PanGloss-owned titles, explanations, guidance, optional background, verified FieldWorks places, subjects, and links where available. Information can identify a stored analysis that PanGloss no longer reproduces, name the rule that changed its surface, or explain why the loss could not be attributed. Each finding retains the report locale. Missing references and project settings have explicit statuses and unavailable-link reasons. `--left-out` keeps warning-level findings only. Without a Baseline, the command refuses and tells you to run `motif baseline capture --project <fwdata>`. When a Baseline has no stored check, it refuses and tells you to run `motif grammar check --project <fwdata>`.

The response includes the Baseline's lexical entry and rule counts when that inventory is available. Motif advisories are listed separately from parser findings.

Motif findings include `grammar.required-slot-empty` when a required inflectional slot in a template has no affixes. Each finding names the template, part of speech, slot and canonical slot ID. The slot is marked required, but FieldWorks and PanGloss currently treat an empty required slot as optional.

Motif findings also include `grammar.negated-feature-value` for a stored negated feature value, which FieldWorks' parser loader cannot read. Each finding names the feature, the value and the object that holds it, and, for a stem or inflectional affix, points to [removing the feature value](cmd:compose-remove-feature-value); for other objects it says Motif has no command for it.

Motif findings also include `grammar.derived-stem-keeps-from-class` for a derivational affix with a From Inflection Class and no To Inflection Class. Each finding names the affix and the class its derived stems keep, and says to set a To Inflection Class when they belong to another class.

Motif findings also include `grammar.template-has-no-slots` for an affix template with no slot, which the parser cannot use. Each finding names the template and its part of speech and says to add a slot.

Motif findings also include `grammar.phoneme-case-alias-missing` when a featured lowercase phoneme lacks titlecase or uppercase spellings on the same phoneme. It names the missing aliases and points to [Edit a phoneme](cmd:compose-edit-phoneme), so implicit featureless capitals do not admit unintended analyses.

Motif findings also include `grammar.phoneme-spelling-ambiguous` for a phoneme whose spelling is other phonemes' spellings joined (`ng` beside `n` and `g`), which the parser always reads as the longest spelling, and `grammar.allomorph-environment-ignored-by-parser` for a form whose environment the parser cannot read and so drops, leaving the form unrestricted by it. Each finding names the phoneme or form and says what to change.

Motif findings also include `grammar.allomorph-repeats-environment-material` for a form that already spells the material its environment asks of its neighbour (`batan-ung` before `ng`); it is a second look, not a refusal.

Motif findings also include three lexicon hygiene warnings: `lexicon.stem-typed-as-content-word` for a Noun, Verb or Adjective stem that is a single letter, a cross-reference stub or a function word by its gloss, `lexicon.duplicate-entry` for entries with the same form and first gloss, and `lexicon.affix-hyphen-on-wrong-side` for a prefix written `-i` or a suffix written `i-`. They report only; see [`grammar-check`](cmd:grammar%20check) for what each looks for and how to fix many at once.

When a stored Assessment matches the Baseline and Selection, all recorded allomorph segmentation refusals are included under `parse.allomorph.unsegmentable`, labelled **Parse all words**. Their descriptions preserve the parser's reason, without truncating the allomorph list or inventing guidance. These findings can differ from the whole-grammar check's findings.

## Your words

When a stored Assessment from [Measure a Selection](cmd:assess) matches the current Baseline and Selection, each finding lists the words in the Selection reached by its subjects, with their meanings, such as Lost or Kept. The headline counts exact uses only, once per word, and says how many of those don't parse. Membership and spelling candidates have separate counts and never enter that headline. Each kind of finding gets the same separate counts.

Motif finds the words from the object the finding names, by its FieldWorks identity:

- an allomorph or grammatical info: the FieldWorks or parser analyses that use it;
- an entry or an environment: the FieldWorks or parser analyses that use its allomorphs;
- a sense: the FieldWorks or parser analyses that use its grammatical info;
- a natural class: the allomorphs its environments condition, and the words the phonological rules that name it ran in;
- a rule: the words its stored per-word timings say it ran in.
- a feature definition, value or specification: the allomorphs, grammatical infos and rules whose feature specifications name it;
- a stem name or inflection class: the allomorphs or grammatical infos that refer to it;
- a boundary: the allomorphs and rules whose contexts name it.

Templates and slots reach words using their affixes as **membership candidates**. Inflection types, ad hoc prohibitions, phoneme sets and feature systems also reach members as candidates: using a member does not prove a parse selected the named resource.

Letters and phonemes reach **spelling candidates; not confirmed uses of the phoneme**. Spelling uses case-insensitive, canonically decomposed substring matching, which cannot establish phoneme identity. A feature owned by a phoneme keeps that same limit, including when reached through its feature system. A phoneme set follows its members' grammar references and omits spelling candidates.

For a word with no analysis, an allomorph or entry also reaches spelling candidates through the vernacular forms recorded for the Baseline. This includes typed words the parser refused. The window calls these **spelling matches**, lists the words, and never presents the spelling alone as an exact use.

For each finding, exact uses take precedence over membership candidates, then spelling candidates. The lists never share a word. The overall counts apply that precedence across all findings, too. The words show use, not cause: a word that uses what a warning names may fail for some other reason.

Every finding has an attribution state. A supported route with no matching word says **none in this Selection**. A project resource without word attribution says **project-wide**. A **missing object** distinguishes a GUID absent from the checked Baseline from one belonging to a different FieldWorks class. **Unresolved identity** distinguishes no subject, a named subject without a project GUID, and a class with no supported route.

Features also follow shared references to their enclosing complex specifications. If some feature owners have no supported route or no word attribution, the finding retains those attribution limits alongside any exact uses or candidates. When no owner has a supported route, the finding reports the limit rather than claiming there are no words in the Selection.

Without a matching Assessment, supported routes say **evidence unavailable**; their counts are absent rather than zero. Missing and unresolved subjects retain their specific reasons. Motif refuses stores with an older shape and asks the developer to delete the database so it can recreate it.

## Related commands

- [Check a grammar](cmd:grammar%20check) records fresh findings.
- [Read the project Overview](cmd:overview) includes the warning count with other stored evidence.

entries.title: Withdraw a Proposal
entries.description: Takes back an open Proposal and keeps its history. A person can reopen it later as a Draft.
entries.helpPage:
# Withdraw a Proposal

`motif withdraw --proposal <id>` takes back an open Proposal and marks it withdrawn. The Proposal and its Trials stay in the project's closed list; the changes are not applied.

## When to use it

Use it when an author no longer wants an open Proposal to go forward. Motif finalizes a Draft before withdrawing it, so its content remains available if someone reopens it. This command does not withdraw your own pending changes; undo those on **Review Changes** instead.

Assistants need Advanced AI mode to use the MCP tool. Turn it on in **AI Assistants** or run `motif settings advanced-ai on`. In a sandbox, set `MOTIF_ADVANCED_AI_MODE_PATH` to a writable preference file.

## Example

```text
motif withdraw --proposal <id> --project <project> --json
```

## What it prints

The Proposal's id and new status, `withdrawn`. A person can reopen a withdrawn Proposal as a Draft under the same id, with its history kept.

## Related commands

- [List Proposals](cmd:proposals) shows withdrawn Proposals with `--include-set-aside`.
- [Reopen a Proposal](cmd:reopen%20--proposal) opens a withdrawn Proposal as a Draft.
- [Delete a closed Proposal](cmd:delete%20--proposal) removes a withdrawn Proposal that never applied.

entries.title: Read one word's context
entries.description: Reads a word's captured FieldWorks presence and every stored analysis with its individual Opinion. Uses the current Baseline without requiring a Selection or an Assessment, and reports whether FieldWorks has saved since.
entries.helpPage:
# Read one word's context

`word-context` reads one word's captured FieldWorks presence and all of its stored analyses, including Approved, Disapproved and Unknown opinions. It uses the same query as Try a Word and does not require an Assessment or membership in a Selection.

## Example

```text
motif word-context --project Koro.fwdata --word dogs --json
```

## What it prints

The response includes the exact Baseline identity, its source-save and publication times, word membership, each stored analysis with its identity and individual opinion, and an exact Word Analyses link when available. `isStale` says whether the saved FieldWorks project is newer than the Baseline's source save. A later save does not replace the captured analyses.

Before a Baseline exists, membership is unknown and no analysis context is supplied; this does not mean the word is absent. A missing Baseline file is refused. When several wordforms have the same form, their stored analyses retain their own identities and no unique navigation target is invented.

## Related commands

- [Capture a Baseline](cmd:baseline%20capture) records the saved project state.
- [Inspect approved analyses](cmd:analyses) reads the approved-analysis aggregate.
- [Trace a word](cmd:trace) records the parser's search.

entries.title: Show writing systems
entries.description: Reads fonts, features, direction and style sizes from the current Baseline, in FieldWorks writing-system order. Change these settings in FieldWorks, then capture a new Baseline to read them here.
entries.helpPage:
# Show writing systems

`motif writing-systems --project <fwdata> [--json]` reads the current [Baseline](term:baseline)'s writing systems without opening the FieldWorks project. Before the first capture, it reports that no Baseline exists.

Each current vernacular and analysis list keeps FieldWorks' order and default. The response includes the id, name, abbreviation, requested default font family, verbatim feature string, direction, and each style's effective font, features and point size. A writing system in both lists appears once per membership; positions in JSON count from zero.

The command includes every project style; a missing style uses that writing system's effective Normal settings. Normal without a size uses FieldWorks' 10-point default. Sizes contain no window units or zoom.

For which FieldWorks style each part of the window uses and where to change its writing-system settings, see [Writing systems in the window](guide:writing-systems).

The font name is the project's request. The command reports saved settings and does not inspect installed fonts.

entries.title: A recorded measurement
entries.description: An Assessment is one immutable measurement of one kind, made by an Assessor. A PanGloss run may produce several Assessments, such as parse timing and correctness for a Selection.

entries.title: A saved project starting point
entries.description: A Baseline is a saved, minimal, file-backed copy of a project from which Motif can make independent Dry Run copies. When captured from a project FieldWorks holds open, it reflects FieldWorks' last save.

entries.title: Where a change came from
entries.description: A citation records the work a change was taken from, such as a grammar section or a dictionary entry, with an optional page or section. It is shown beside the change and never changes what the Proposal does.

entries.title: Words measured by default
entries.description: A project's Default Selection is the chosen Texts plus any added words Motif measures when no other Selection is named. Motif resolves it to an exact word list for each run.

entries.title: A durable choice about a recommendation
entries.description: A Disposition records fix, keep, ask, or defer for one Parsimony recommendation and its relevant evidence. It belongs to durable FieldWorks project data; its storage shape is defined separately.
entries.helpPage:
# Disposition

A Disposition records what a person wants to do with one [Parsimony recommendation](term:parsimony-recommendation): fix it, keep it (with an optional reason), ask a question, or defer it. An applied keep or defer moves the recommendation to the Suppressed set, where you can list it again with its reason and history. It stays tied to the exact evidence considered; relevant new evidence returns it to Active with the previous decision and reason. Fix and ask remain Active. A pending choice stays Active until Apply.

entries.title: Evidence no longer matches
entries.description: Drift means a Dry Run or an individual change no longer matches the project state it was made against. In the window, a change with missing or changed inputs is shown as ‘no longer fits’.

entries.title: Effects measured on a copy
entries.description: A Dry Run applies a Proposal to a throwaway project copy and reads back the effects. It leaves the live model unchanged.

entries.title: Motif's project workflow records
entries.description: The Motif store keeps project workflow records and frozen Report bindings in the project's paired database. Parsimony judgments remain durable FieldWorks project data, while analysis artifacts are disposable files.
entries.helpPage:
# Motif store

The Motif store keeps a project's Proposals, jobs, Assessments, Reports, Receipts, and other workflow records. Parsimony judgments belong with the FieldWorks project; the files used to analyse a grammar can be rebuilt.

entries.title: The latest stored evidence
entries.description: The Overview presents project counts and measurements already recorded by Motif. Reading it does not start a Refresh or a parse.

entries.title: Parse every chosen word
entries.description: Parse all words asks PanGloss to parse the words you chose and saves the result against the Baseline. A search stopped at a limit is saved as not finished, never as a word that cannot parse.

entries.title: Fewer repeated grammar statements
entries.description: Parsimony is the axis that favors fewer or less-duplicated grammar statements while preserving known valid readings. It is distinct from restrictiveness, which asks how narrowly a statement licenses forms.
entries.helpPage:
# Parsimony

Parsimony favors fewer or less-duplicated grammar statements while preserving known valid readings. It is one of the two axes in a [Parsimony review](term:parsimony-review), alongside [restrictiveness](term:restrictiveness).

entries.title: A specific grammar recommendation
entries.description: A Parsimony recommendation names one grammar object or group, its evidence, and a recipe or limitation. Its stable finding identity is separate from the digest of evidence supporting it.
entries.helpPage:
# Parsimony recommendation

A Parsimony recommendation identifies one grammar object or group worth examining, shows the evidence for it, and gives a recipe or explains what information is missing. Its evidence remains attached to the exact item it concerns.

entries.title: Advice about grammar statements
entries.description: A Parsimony review offers specific grammar recommendations along the parsimony and restrictiveness axes. It records evidence and limitations, and never decides whether to Apply a change.
entries.helpPage:
# Parsimony review

A Parsimony review gives specific, advisory recommendations about a grammar's parsimony and restrictiveness. Each finding shows whether it comes from grammar structure, Text evidence, or a parser Assessment, and states what that evidence cannot establish.

entries.title: Phonology Example Set
entries.description: A Phonology Example Set is a saved list of underlying forms with the surface forms an author expects, kept as advisory evidence that never changes Readiness or Apply. Its subcommands are phonology-examples save, list, show, check and results.
entries.helpPage:
# Phonology Example Set

A Phonology Example Set is a list you write down of what a form should become: an underlying form such as `n+baya`, the surface form you expect, such as `mbaya`, and the lexical entry that supplies the context. Each example can carry a citation to its source. Motif keeps each saved version unchanged, so a later edit is a new revision and the earlier one can still be read.

A set is advisory evidence. A [Phonology Check](cmd:phonology-examples%20results) can measure the current grammar against it and report, for every example, whether the expected surface form was produced (agree), the search finished without it (disagree), or the question could not be answered (unavailable). None of that changes Readiness, and Apply ignores it.

## Commands

- `phonology-examples save` records a new revision of a set. Assistants need Advanced AI mode to use it as an MCP tool.
- [List phonology examples](cmd:phonology-examples%20list) shows the current revision of each saved set.
- [Show phonology examples](cmd:phonology-examples%20show) reads the examples of one saved revision, a page at a time.
- `phonology-examples check` queues a check of a saved revision against the current Baseline. It is an advanced AI command and needs a captured Baseline.
- [Read phonology check results](cmd:phonology-examples%20results) reads a finished check as summary pages or one complete example.

entries.title: The final fit check
entries.description: The CLI's preflight command checks changes against the live model before Apply. A change whose required inputs changed or disappeared no longer fits.

entries.title: A reviewable set of changes
entries.description: A Proposal groups related Motif operations so a person can inspect, measure, and apply them as one unit.

entries.title: A finding from frozen evidence
entries.description: A Report presents statistics and findings from stored evidence. A Parsimony Report may use a frozen evidence bundle without an Assessment and is always advisory; other Report kinds retain their configured regression behavior.
entries.helpPage:
# Report

A Report presents findings from stored evidence. A Parsimony Report can describe frozen grammar and Text evidence without an Assessment, and its advice never decides whether a person may Apply a change.

entries.title: The narrowest statement that still fits
entries.description: Restrictiveness favors the narrowest grammar statement that covers known valid forms and excludes explicitly forbidden readings. An unattested form is not a negative without suitable evidence.
entries.helpPage:
# Restrictiveness

Restrictiveness favors the narrowest grammar statement that still covers known valid forms and excludes readings people have explicitly forbidden. A form missing from the chosen Texts is unobserved; that absence alone does not make it bad.

entries.title: A human-confirmed forbidden form or reading
entries.description: A reviewed negative is a human-confirmed form or reading the grammar must not accept. A FieldWorks Disapproved analysis is negative for that reading only, not for the whole word.
entries.helpPage:
# Reviewed negative

A reviewed negative is a form or reading that a person has explicitly confirmed the grammar must not accept. A FieldWorks Disapproved analysis rejects that reading only; it does not reject every analysis of the word.

entries.title: Share of your text that parses
entries.description: Text Coverage is the share of the Default Selection's words, and of their occurrences in the chosen Texts, that parse. The same share measured over a Corpus is called grammar coverage.

entries.title: A Proposal tried on a copy
entries.description: A Trial applies a Proposal to a throwaway copy of the project and parses words again, so its numbers can sit beside today's. A Trial is out of date once the project or the Proposal changes; the window then says it needs another try.
entries.helpPage:
# Trial

A Trial applies a [Proposal](term:proposal) to a throwaway copy of the project and parses words again, so its numbers can be read beside today's. It never changes the real project.

A Trial goes out of date when the project is refreshed or the Proposal changes. The window then says the Proposal needs another try; nothing re-runs until you ask.

entries.title: A tested window guide
entries.description: A Walkthrough is a script that tests the real Motif window using fixed data and produces screenshots at marked steps. It can also render a short, silent clip.

entries.title: Reading a Handoff
entries.description: Start with handoff.md for the included files and reading examples; use the separate pastedHeader text for the prepared chat prompt.
entries.helpPage:
# Reading a Handoff

Start with `handoff.md` for the included files and reading examples; use the separate `pastedHeader` text for the prepared chat prompt.

An assessed Handoff lists files alphabetically: `grammar.json`, `handoff.md`, `parse-results.json`, `read_results.py`, then `texts.json`. A Baseline-only Handoff omits `parse-results.json`. The App's one-word Handoff contains `grammar.json`, `handoff.md`, `read_results.py`, `texts.json`, then `traces/<word>.trace.json`; it carries the raw diagnostic and omits batch parse results.

| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `grammar.json` | The grammar Motif exports for PanGloss to parse. |
| `handoff.md` | Explains the included material and gives reading examples. |
| `parse-results.json` | One result for each selected word, including its parser outcome and timing. |
| `read_results.py` | Queries the Handoff's JSON files from a terminal. |
| `texts.json` | The selected Texts with the analyses the project stores. |
| `traces/<word>.trace.json` | The raw diagnostic for the selected word, including parser fields Motif does not interpret. |

Read the files as linguistic project data; they may contain real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and text.

Use the helper’s own help to see its commands, then ask focused questions against the supplied files:

```powershell
python read_results.py --help
python read_results.py word --help
```

For an assessed folder, the current CLI exports a retained Assessment invocation rather than silently running a fresh one. To create one, first run [assess](cmd:assess) with `--json`, read `invocationId` from its response, then pass that value to [handoff](cmd:handoff):

```powershell
motif handoff "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --out "C:\handoffs\Sena" --invocation <invocationId> --json
```

The successful JSON response reports `outputDirectory`, `baseline`, `selection`, `files`, `assessmentIds`, optional `invocationId`, `pastedHeader`, and `handoffMarkdown`. Use `--no-assess` for a folder without `parse-results.json`; `--texts <guid,guid>` is accepted only with that option, to select texts.

Treat every file as potentially sensitive and share it only with a service approved for that project.

entries.title: Measuring a grammar
entries.description: These commands answer different questions. grammar check asks PanGloss to inspect the whole grammar and stores findings for the current Baseline. It does not parse selected words. assess parses a Selection and records one or more Assessments. overview reads stored summaries; stats queries statistics from a stored run.
entries.helpPage:
# Measuring a grammar

These commands answer different questions. `grammar check` asks PanGloss to inspect the whole grammar and stores findings for the current [Baseline](term:baseline). It does not parse selected words. `assess` parses a Selection and records one or more [Assessments](term:assessment). `overview` reads stored summaries; `stats` queries statistics from a stored run.

Capture a Baseline explicitly with [baseline capture](cmd:baseline%20capture) when you want to name that step:

```powershell
motif baseline capture --project "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --json
```

Then use [assess](cmd:assess) to measure the saved Default Selection, or name a source such as all wordforms. Read stored summaries with [overview](cmd:overview) and query statistics by replaying the retained parser evidence and cache for a stored Assessment with [stats](cmd:stats):

```powershell
motif assess "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --all-wordforms --json
motif overview --project "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --json
motif stats "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --json
```

`assess` is synchronous in the current CLI. If you give no Selection flags, it uses the saved Default Selection. Other supported sources include `--texts <guid,guid>`, `--words <file>`, and retry options such as `--retry-failed --retry-source-assessment <id>`. The command ensures a Baseline exists if needed.

The successful `assess --json` response includes the invocation identifier and the Assessment records produced. For example, its relevant fields have this shape:

```json
{
  "invocationId": "<invocation-id>",
  "assessmentIds": ["<assessment-id>"],
  "measurements": [
    {
      "assessmentId": "<assessment-id>",
      "kind": "ObjectTiming",
      "invocationId": "<invocation-id>"
    }
  ]
}
```

Use `invocationId` when you need to create a [Handoff](cmd:handoff) for this exact retained run. The number and kinds of `measurements` can vary with the Assessor’s supported kinds; do not assume a fixed Assessment count.

Use [grammar check](cmd:grammar%20check) to check the whole grammar. [warnings](cmd:warnings) reads findings that have already been stored:

```powershell
motif grammar check --project "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --json
motif warnings --project "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --json
```

`warnings` reads findings already stored for that Baseline; it does not rerun the check. Without a Baseline, `grammar check` refuses and tells you to run `motif baseline capture --project <fwdata>`. Use **Working with jobs** for commands that enqueue background work.

entries.title: Output and exit codes
entries.description: Use the process exit code as the success signal. Successful text output goes to stdout; handled failures go to stderr. With --json, successful responses are usually the command’s JSON object itself, using camelCase fields, not a common success wrapper. Some enqueue-only commands return a bare job ID even with --json.
entries.helpPage:
# Output and exit codes

Use the process exit code as the success signal. Successful text output goes to stdout; handled failures go to stderr. With `--json`, successful responses are usually the command’s JSON object itself, using camelCase fields, not a common success wrapper. Some enqueue-only commands return a bare job ID even with `--json`.

Handled failures requested with `--json` write a failure object to stderr and nothing to stdout. Its shape is:

```json
{
  "ok": false,
  "reason": "Busy",
  "message": "<human-readable reason>",
  "detail": { "project": "<project path>" }
}
```

`code` and `detail` are optional. The `reason` is a stable failure class; `message` is for a person. Exit codes are `1` for an invalid invocation, `2` for a refusal, missing item, or cancellation, `3` when the request cannot be attempted now (such as a busy project), `4` for an inconsistent store or unexpected failure, and `5` when an Assessment stops at its whole-run time limit. Retry a `3` later; do not retry a refusal unchanged.

The `help` command has its own plain stderr errors and exits `2` for invalid help syntax or an unknown entry; it does not use the failure object. An unexpected exception escaping the top-level command handler exits `4`; with `--json` it writes the failure object with code `cli.unexpected`, and without it a plain `error: ...` line. A command stopped by Ctrl+C exits `2` with code `cli.cancelled`, as a failure object with `--json` or a plain `cli.cancelled: ...` line without it. Treat any nonzero exit as failure and keep stdout and stderr separate.

entries.title: Using Motif from an agent
entries.description: Call Motif as motif <verb> .... Each process handles one command; durable project state is stored between calls, so commands do not depend on a setup command in the same process. Use an explicit project path with commands that accept --project or take the .fwdata path as a positional argument.
entries.helpPage:
# Using Motif from an agent

Call Motif as `motif <verb> ...`. Each process handles one command; durable project state is stored between calls, so commands do not depend on a setup command in the same process. Use an explicit project path with commands that accept `--project` or take the `.fwdata` path as a positional argument.

Prefer `--json` when the command’s usage line supports it, and read the response from stdout. Do not parse the human text rendering. For example:

```powershell
motif overview --project "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --json
motif assess "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --all-wordforms --json
motif jobs list --json
```

To list help entries in one call, run `motif help --all --json`. The JSON has a `locale`, a `siteRoot`, and `entries` for available CLI commands, glossary terms and Guide pages. Each entry has a kind, code, slug, title, description, a `helpPage` field containing the full Help page Markdown when a page exists, and a URL; command entries also include usage lines and a surface. For one entry, `motif help <code>` prints its title, description, URL, and (for a command) usage. Add `--full` to print the expanded page, or `--json` to get that entry's metadata, including its full Help page when available. The documentation website also publishes `llms.txt`, a plain-text index of every page. With no arguments, `motif` prints the usage catalog to stderr and exits with code 1.

Assistants need Advanced AI mode to use MCP tools. In the window, open **AI Assistants**, select **Let Assistants Use Motif's Tools**, then choose which assistants to connect. The **AI Assistants** Guide page explains the client steps. A person can also enable it with `motif settings advanced-ai on`. The MCP server starts with `motif mcp`; each project tool takes a Known project name or recorded path in its `project` argument. Use the workflow resource to draft, Dry Run, Trial, revise and Finalize for a person to review and Apply. Most commands run synchronously, but `baseline-refresh`, `dry-run`, and `trial` enqueue jobs. See **Working with jobs**. For errors and retry decisions, see **Output and exit codes**.

Before composing rules, read the encoding guide for the phenomenon: `motif help` lists the guides, and `motif help guide:encoding/workflow --full` shows the working order. Over MCP the same text is the `motif_guide` tool.

A completed Trial has a saved report. Read its summary and limitations, then use failures or full detail to page through the cases needed for review. In MCP, `motif_trial` reads and refreshes reports explicitly, and `motif_difference` reads a particular report or its cases; a trace is an explicit diagnostic. No red flags means only not bad, never good.

entries.title: Working with jobs
entries.description: The Motif job runner handles durable work that outlives the command that queued it. baseline-refresh, dry-run and trial enqueue jobs. A synchronous assess command is not a job.
entries.helpPage:
# Working with jobs

The Motif job runner handles durable work that outlives the command that queued it. [baseline-refresh](cmd:baseline-refresh), `dry-run` and `trial` enqueue jobs. A synchronous [assess](cmd:assess) command is not a job.

```powershell
motif jobs list --json
motif jobs show <jobId> --project "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --json
motif jobs assessments <jobId> --project "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --json
motif jobs cancel <jobId> --project "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --json
motif jobs requeue <jobId> --project "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --json
motif jobs move <jobId> --project "C:\Projects\Sena.fwdata" --to-top --json
```

[`jobs list`](cmd:jobs%20list) spans every Known project and reports active work in queue order; it is the jobs command that does not take `--project`. [`jobs show`](cmd:jobs%20show) returns the job’s status, attempt, update time, cancellation request, failure category, version, and queue position when available. Status values are lower-case hyphenated strings such as `waiting-for-project-host`. A status response has fields like:

```json
{
  "jobId": "<job-id>",
  "projectKey": "<project-key>",
  "found": true,
  "kind": "trial",
  "status": "waiting-for-project-host",
  "attempt": 1,
  "updatedUtc": "<UTC timestamp>",
  "cancellationRequested": false,
  "failureCategory": null,
  "version": 1,
  "queueOrder": 1
}
```

A job whose claiming runner stopped adds `"claimLost": true` and a `warnings` array to the status response; each warning has a `code` and a `message`, and the code for this case is `job.claim-lost`. If the job was parked waiting for something that now exists, `status` is `queued`, the status the next runner gives it. A job parked on purpose, such as `waiting-for-project-host`, has released its claim, so it shows that status with no warning. `claimLost` and `warnings` are left out otherwise. The CLI starts a runner when `jobs show` or `--wait` sees a queued or claim-lost job; the MCP `motif_job` tool only reports, so run any command that queues work, or start `SIL.Motif.Worker`, to restart a runner.

The queue-list response is `{ "jobs": [...] }`. Each entry includes `jobId`, `projectKey`, `projectPath`, `kind`, `status`, `attempt`, `updatedUtc`, and `queueOrder`. `jobs assessments` returns `jobId` and an `assessments` array whose entries contain `assessmentId`, `assessor`, `kind`, and `savedUtc`.

[`jobs cancel`](cmd:jobs%20cancel) on a queued or parked job moves it to cancelled. Cancelling a running job requests cancellation; the runner completes it. [`jobs requeue`](cmd:jobs%20requeue) is for a terminal job and creates a fresh attempt with a new job ID. Use [`jobs assessments`](cmd:jobs%20assessments) to read the Assessment IDs produced by a completed job.

Without `--wait`, enqueueing `dry-run` or `trial` returns a bare job ID, including under `--json`. With `--wait`, the CLI waits up to two minutes by default; `--wait-timeout-ms <ms>` changes the bound. See **Output and exit codes** for the failure shape and exit mapping.

entries.title: Connect an assistant
entries.description: Advanced AI mode lets selected assistants use Motif's project tools. The assistant still cannot Apply a Proposal; a person reviews and Applies it in Motif.
entries.helpPage:
# Connect an assistant

Advanced AI mode lets selected assistants use Motif's project tools. The assistant still cannot Apply a Proposal; a person reviews and Applies it in Motif.

Open **AI Assistants** in the window and select **Let Assistants Use Motif's Tools**. Motif lists the supported assistants it finds (Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Codex); if it finds none, the page says so. Check the ones to connect, then choose **Connect Selected Assistants**.

Changing Advanced AI mode affects new Motif sessions. Restart an assistant session to apply the setting to a session that is already open.

For Claude Desktop, Motif adds `motif mcp` to Claude's MCP configuration. Choose **Open Plugin Folder**, then **Open Claude Plugins**, upload `motif-plugin.zip` in **Customize → Plugins**, and restart Claude Desktop. Upload the latest ZIP again after a Motif update to refresh the skills saved to your Claude account.

For Claude Code and Codex, Motif installs the plugin from its local marketplace with the assistant's CLI. Start a new assistant session so it loads the plugin and its tools.

If the bundled skills and server have different versions, Motif shows a warning on this page. Restart Motif after an update so its local marketplace copy is refreshed before connecting again. Claude Desktop keeps uploaded plugins in your account, so Motif cannot check whether that account copy needs an update.

entries.title: AI Handoff
entries.description: AI Handoff writes a folder you can share with a chat model. It includes project context for the words you parsed and a starter question. The page shows what it plans to write and a data-sensitivity notice before you start; the folder can include real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and sentences from the selected Texts.
entries.helpPage:
# AI Handoff

**AI Handoff** writes a folder you can share with a chat model. It includes project context for the words you parsed and a starter question. The page shows what it plans to write and a data-sensitivity notice before you start; the folder can include real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and sentences from the selected Texts.

Only one parse can run for a project at a time. A Handoff that needs a fresh parse runs it before writing. Motif refuses another parse request for the project until the Handoff finishes.

From Try a Word, **AI Handoff for this word** keeps the displayed trace and the Baseline captured with it. Motif does not parse the word again or make a replacement trace; this Handoff includes the raw diagnostic and leaves out measured results from a separate parse.

1. Read the notice. If it says the files will include only words chosen on the Texts page, choose **Hand off every parsed word instead** to use every word from the last parse.
2. Choose **Write the AI Handoff**. If you have already written one, the button says **Write the AI Handoff again**.
3. Choose an output folder when prompted and wait for Motif to finish writing.
4. Review the files, then drag the files into your chat or use the page’s copy actions for the prompt and paths.

The page shows when the files were last written and marks them out of date when a newer parse finishes. Times use your local clock; a timestamp from another day includes its weekday and date. The `read_results.py` reader works over `parse-results.json` and `texts.json`. Write the Handoff again when you want the chat model to receive newer results. Only share the files if you are comfortable sending their linguistic data to that service.

![AI Handoff files ready to share](shot:handoff-cancel-retry/completed-files)

A Handoff from a parse records refused words with a refusal code and reason in `parse-results.json`. Word forms use composed Unicode for reading and searching. `texts.json` is an empty array when no Texts were chosen; added words can still have measured parse results.

entries.title: Applying changes
entries.description: Apply writes the pending analysis changes to the FieldWorks project as one operation. Before starting, save your work in FieldWorks and close the project there; Motif blocks Apply while FieldWorks is holding it open.
entries.helpPage:
# Applying changes

Apply writes the pending analysis changes to the FieldWorks project as one operation. Before starting, save your work in FieldWorks and close the project there; Motif blocks Apply while FieldWorks is holding it open.

1. Open **Review Changes** and read every listed change.
2. Choose **Check these changes** and wait for the measurement to finish. Read the summary of what applying does to the numbers on the Apply area.
3. Confirm that each change still fits, the evidence is complete and current, and no approved analysis would be lost.
4. Choose **Apply to FieldWorks project**. Motif shows a receipt when it succeeds.

If Apply is unavailable, read the reason beside the button. A stale result needs **Refresh**; incomplete evidence needs another successful check; a change that says **No longer fits** must be removed or checked against a refreshed project. The window does not offer a way to force a change that no longer fits.

![Receipt after changes are applied to the FieldWorks project](shot:review-apply-refresh-parse/applied)

entries.title: Parse all words
entries.description: Parse all words asks PanGloss to parse the words you chose and keeps the result with the version of the project and the words it measured.
entries.helpPage:
# Parse all words

**Parse all words** asks PanGloss to parse the words you chose and keeps the result with the version of the project and the words it measured.

While it runs, the progress panel stays visible at the top of the window. It shows how many words are done, the word currently being parsed, elapsed time and an estimate of the time left. It also shows the slowest word so far, with its parser work, and lists words that stopped at the work limit or the time safety net, each with its parser work. If no word finishes for a long time, the panel explains that the parser may have stalled and offers **Cancel** and **Report a problem**.

The result tells you which words parsed, which approved analyses PanGloss built again, and the time on this computer. Parser work gives a more stable measure for comparing grammar changes. A search that was interrupted or stopped at a limit is saved as not finished; it should not be read as a completed “no parse.” The **Overview** and **Texts** pages read the saved result. Opening either page does not run PanGloss.

After saving in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh** (the ⟳ beside the project name in the top bar) to read the saved project, then **Parse all words** in the project card to parse your [Default Selection](term:default-selection) again. A parse is evidence about one run, not a verdict that the grammar is good or bad.

Motif allows only one Parse all words run for a project at a time, even across windows and processes. If another window is already parsing that project, a second request is refused; use the running window to follow progress or cancel the run.

entries.title: Baseline
entries.description: A Baseline is Motif’s saved reference copy of a FieldWorks project. Motif uses it to reproduce parser behavior and to compare later results with the project state it measured. It reads the .fwdata file on disk, so the Baseline reflects FieldWorks’ last save, not edits still open and unsaved there.
entries.helpPage:
# Baseline

A [Baseline](term:baseline) is Motif’s saved reference copy of a FieldWorks project. Motif uses it to reproduce parser behavior and to compare later results with the project state it measured. It reads the `.fwdata` file on disk, so the Baseline reflects FieldWorks’ last save, not edits still open and unsaved there.

The Baseline is not a backup of linked media, and it is not a live view of FieldWorks. It stays in place until you capture another one. When a project has no Baseline, Motif captures one the first time you open it, then asks what to measure. Later, **Refresh** captures a new Baseline; **Parse all words** measures your chosen words against it. Opening a project with a Baseline reads it and the results already stored.

If the project has changed since the Baseline, Motif can mark its stored numbers as stale. A stale parse and a change that says **No longer fits** are related to different things: one is old measurement evidence; the other is a particular pending choice that no longer matches the project. See [Drift](term:drift).

entries.title: Building a grammar: a suggested order
entries.description: This page describes the order in which linguists usually build a morphological grammar for FieldWorks, and the reason for each step. It is advice, not a rule. entries.helpPage:
# Building a grammar: a suggested order

This page describes the order in which linguists usually build a morphological grammar for FieldWorks, and the reason for each step. It is advice, not a rule. Motif does not check, enforce or remember where you are in it, and nothing in the window is greyed out or reordered by it. Motif has no setting for the type of language, and FieldWorks has none either. Work in whatever order your language and your data suggest, and go back to any part when a test shows a gap.

The method follows H. Andrew Black, *A Conceptual Introduction to Morphological Parsing for FieldWorks Language Explorer* (SIL, 3 July 2025), which ships in the FieldWorks 9 Help. Black organises his guide by mechanism, not as a numbered procedure. The order below is our reading of his tips and worked examples, so where it says "Black §2.1.1" it names the section that supports one step, not a sequence he sets out himself. Lessons from our own grammar builds are labelled **In our experience**; they are not from Black or from any textbook.

Black states the goal this way: "The idea is to use the morphotactic mechanisms to correctly describe the facts of the language and thereby not only provide correct parses, but also rule out false parses" (§2, opening). So the aim is a grammar that parses what is a word and does not parse what is not. Neither Black nor Motif sets a percentage to reach.

You make grammar and lexicon changes in FieldWorks. Motif shows what the parser did with them: save in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh**, then [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to measure again.

## Texts and words to test on

**What to do.** Choose some Texts you have interlinearized, and add any extra words you care about. This is your [Default Selection](term:default-selection), the words Motif measures every time. Mark spellings you know are not words as Incorrect spelling.

**Why.** Texts give you real words to test every later step against, and measuring the same words each time lets you compare one run with the next. Fieldwork textbooks place connected texts alongside the rest of the work: Claire Bowern, *Linguistic Fieldwork* (2nd ed., 2015), has a chapter titled "Discourse, Pragmatics, and Narrative Data" (chapter 9).

Our own suggestion, which has no source: Motif measures only the Default Selection, so you can leave one Text out of it and add it later to see how the grammar does on words you did not tune it to.

**In Motif.** Setup asks you to choose texts or add words in **What Should Motif Measure Every Time?**; choose **Configure…** from the project menu to change it later (see [Choosing what to measure](guide:first-run-setup)). In **Analyze texts**, **Word list** or **Lists**, choose **Incorrect spelling** on a word, or press **S** in Analyze texts; the change stays pending until you review and apply it (see [Texts](guide:texts) and [Keyboard shortcuts](guide:keyboard-shortcuts)).

## Sounds

**What to do.** Define the phonemes and natural classes before anything refers to them. If you will use phonological rules, give the phonemes features too; Black's worked example creates the features, makes sure every phoneme is defined, assigns the features, then writes the rules.

**Why.** Black §3.1.3 says environments for allomorphs are defined "once the set of phonemes and natural classes are defined", and §3.1.1 says you need a list of all the phonemes to use environments or natural classes. For the rule-based parser, §6.2.1 says every phoneme used in the orthography must be defined, and a word with even one undefined phoneme is "guaranteed to not give an analysis"; §6.2.2 says features must give each phoneme a distinct set of values; §6.2.3 and §6.2.4 say to be as specific as practical. Black's worked example in §6.1.2.1.4.1 (Figure 51) runs: create the features, make sure every phoneme is defined, assign the features, then write ordered rules. The fieldwork textbooks also take sounds first: Bowern's chapter 5 is titled "Fieldwork on Phonetics and Phonology", before chapters 6 and 7 on morphology and syntax.

**In Motif.** A word PanGloss cannot read shows **PanGloss can’t read it** with its recorded reason. If the reason names the project’s phonemes, inspect the phoneme inventory before parsing again (see [Texts](guide:texts)). **Try a Word** accepts any word, even one that is not in a Text (see [Try a Word](guide:try-a-word)).

## Words and their parts

**What to do.** Work out the morphemes by comparing forms, for example, forms that share a part with the same meaning. Enter roots, stems and affixes as lexical entries, each with the right morpheme type. When you know whether an affix is inflectional or derivational, say so.

**Why.** Black §1.2 lists what a parser must know: the forms and glosses of prefixes, infixes, roots and suffixes, which affixes go with which roots, their relative order, and when a shape is legitimate. For a word made of one morpheme, §2 says to add a lexical entry and set the morpheme type of its allomorph to a root or stem type; §4.2 lists the morpheme types the parser keys on. On classification, §2.1.1 says an unclassified affix "is relatively unconstrained as to where it can appear", so the parser may return incorrect parses, and "the best solution, of course, is to classify the affix as being either inflectional or derivational". §2.1.5 gives criteria for deciding (Bickford's table) and adds that they "are not hard and fast rules". Label an affix unclassified when you do not know yet, and change it when you do.

**In Motif.** Parse your Selection and open the Overview. [Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) says how many of your chosen words parse. Read it as one measure among several: it is not a score for the grammar (see [Reading the Overview](guide:reading-the-overview)).

## Where affixes go

**What to do.** Give each category its templates and slots, so affixes appear only in the positions they can occupy.

**Why.** Black §2.1.2.1 to §2.1.2.5 cover templates, optional slots, multiple templates, discontinuous morphemes and the interaction with categories. Black's Morphotactics section (§2) opens by saying morphotactics controls the order of morphemes and which can co-occur.

**In Motif.** After a change in FieldWorks, parse again and use **Try a Word** on a word that should contain the affix. It shows what the parser built and where it stopped.

## Allomorphs

**What to do.** When one morpheme has several shapes, decide what chooses between them. If a sound environment does, use a phonological environment. If it is a lexical property of the stem, use an inflection class. If it tracks something the word agrees with, use a feature.

**Why.** Black §3.1.3 and §3.1.4 cover environments and allomorph ordering; §2.1.2.6 inflection classes; §2.1.2.7 agreement and other inflection features; and §2.1.2.8, Table 9, offers guidelines for choosing between a class and a feature. Order here is ours: Black explains environments in his morphophonemics section and classes and features in the morphotactics section.

**In our experience.** Give each stem its class as you add it. In a Tamil build, a restriction that limited a past-tense suffix to one inflection class made nine types that had parsed stop parsing, because two verb stems had no class yet. Eight parsed again once those two stems were given the class (Tamil checkpoint report).

**In Motif.** The **Lost** outcome in the **Matrix** marks a word FieldWorks holds an Approved analysis for that the grammar no longer builds (see [Texts](guide:texts)).

## Agreement

**What to do.** Put the features on the words that are agreed with, and then on the affixes that agree with them. The order is ours; Black §2.1.2.7 shows the mechanism, not a sequence.

**Why.** Black §2.1.2.7 uses Spanish gender to show how inflection features rule out incorrect parses, and Table 8 lists situations where features can do the same.

**In our experience.** In a Swahili build, adjective concord was entered with noun-class features required on the affixes (proposal 0133) before nouns carried the feature (proposal 0134). The build log records that a mismatched noun and adjective could not be shown to fail until the nouns had it (Swahili build report). Later, of the 523 tokens in an annotated sample that a reference marked as real words but the grammar did not parse, 174 needed concord series for function words, the second-largest group after missing lexemes (206). The reference was drafted with AI help and has not been reviewed by a native speaker (Swahili gap report).

## Stem alternations and exceptions

**What to do.** For stems or affixes whose shape changes in ways sound environments do not explain, condition the allomorphs on morphosyntactic features. For single combinations that are simply wrong, mark the exception.

**Why.** Black §3.7 covers non-phonologically conditioned allomorphy, with stem allomorphs and affix allomorphs conditioned by features; §3.8 covers irregularly inflected forms; §2.1.6 covers exception "features", for stems and affixes that combine incorrectly "due to historical or some other seemingly arbitrary reasons".

## Derivation, compounds and clitics

**What to do.** Add derivational affixes, compound rules and clitics once the inflection beneath them is working.

**Why.** Black covers derivational affixes in §2.1.3, stem compounding in §2.2 and clitics in §2.3. The ordering is ours; Black does not say to do these after inflection.

## Ordered phonological rules

**What to do.** Write phonological rules once you have stems and affixes to test them on.

**Why.** Black §6.1.2 notes that these rules are ordered, so that the output of one is the input to the next, and §6.2 lists the checks that make the rule-based parser work. The sequence "once there are stems and affixes to test them on" is ours.

**In Motif.** **Try a Word** lists the **Phonological rules applied** in a trace, and says that **Tried** does not mean **Applied** (see [Try a Word](guide:try-a-word)).

## Ad hoc rules, last

**What to do.** Use an ad hoc rule only when a wrong parse persists after you have used the other mechanisms.

**Why.** Black §2.4 says to use them "when one has used all the mechanisms provided by the parser to the best of one's ability and such incorrect parses continue to surface"; §3.10 says the same for allomorph-oriented rules.

## Keep null morphemes few

Black §4.1.1 says one "wants to avoid having null allomorphs if for no other reason than that they can make the parser run rather slowly". If a null allomorph is the best analysis, keep it. The **Timing** page shows which words are slow.

## How this varies by type of language

Motif has no typology setting, and FieldWorks has none either. A language's type shows in its grammar, in what you end up needing: templates and slots for rich affixation, affix processes for reduplication or infixation, compound rules, inflection classes and features for agreement systems, and phonological rules where sounds change at morpheme boundaries. A language with little inflection may never need most of these steps; a language with heavy agreement will spend most of its time in the Agreement section. Black's guide has sections for reduplication (§3.2), infixation (§3.3), epenthesis (§3.4), metathesis (§3.5) and incorporation (§2.2.3).

## Optional checks

You may also list a whole closed class, such as all the demonstratives or all the pronouns, and check that each parses. You may also lay out a paradigm table for one stem and look for empty cells. Motif does not measure either one; the checks are yours to run with **Try a Word**.

## Going back

The order loops. Testing shows gaps in earlier work, and Black says as much about affix classification: "as you study the language more, you should eventually figure out whether such affixes are inflectional or derivational" (§2.1). Return to any part when a Parse all words shows a gap. The same holds for false parses: when a word you know is not a word parses, go back to the part that lets it through.

## Further reading

- H. Andrew Black, *A Conceptual Introduction to Morphological Parsing for FieldWorks Language Explorer* (SIL, 2025), in the FieldWorks 9 Help.
- Claire Bowern, *Linguistic Fieldwork: A Practical Guide* (2nd ed., 2015), chapters 5 to 9 and Appendix B, "Suggested Fieldwork Programme for an Undescribed Language".
- Eugene A. Nida, *Morphology: The Descriptive Analysis of Words* (1949).
- The Rapid Word Collection method (rapidwords.net), for gathering vocabulary by semantic domain.

entries.title: Cancelling a run
entries.description: During Parse all words, choose Cancel in the progress panel at the top of the window. The panel stays visible while you move between pages. If no word has finished for a long time, it shows a stalled-search notice; cancel there if you do not want to keep waiting. A second Parse all words request for the same project is refused while the first run is active. Use the window that owns the run to see its progress or cancel it.
entries.helpPage:
# Cancelling a run

During **Parse all words**, choose **Cancel** in the progress panel at the top of the window. The panel stays visible while you move between pages. If no word has finished for a long time, it shows a stalled-search notice; cancel there if you do not want to keep waiting. A second Parse all words request for the same project is refused while the first run is active. Use the window that owns the run to see its progress or cancel it.

Cancel keeps the results from the previous completed parse. The unfinished parse is not saved, and Motif does not change the FieldWorks project. For other long actions, use the **Cancel** control beside the running action: on **Try a Word**, **AI Handoff**, or beside **Re-run chosen words** in **Timing**. The global progress panel also has **Cancel** while **Parse all words** runs.

![Parse all words progress and its Cancel control](shot:first-run-setup-parse/cancelling)

entries.title: Changing an analysis
entries.description: In Texts, open the word in Analyze texts, then choose the analysis and the opinion you want for it: approve or disapprove it, or make it Unknown. Opinions change one analysis at a time, in the text. For several words at once, the Matrix and Analyze texts can add parser readings as Unknown or mark a spelling Incorrect. The available action may vary with the word’s current state and the reading you select.
entries.helpPage:
# Changing an analysis

In **Texts**, open the word in **Analyze texts**, then choose the analysis and the opinion you want for it: approve or disapprove it, or make it Unknown. Opinions change one analysis at a time, in the text. For several words at once, the Matrix and **Analyze texts** can add parser readings as Unknown or mark a spelling Incorrect. The available action may vary with the word’s current state and the reading you select.

Each word has two buttons. The first is its opinion mark: **A**, **U**, **D**, or a dashed mark when FieldWorks holds no analysis. Choose **Set analysis** to see each stored analysis and choose **Set analysis: Approved**, **Set analysis: Unknown**, **Set analysis: Disapproved** or **Set analysis: Remove**, or to mark the spelling Incorrect. The current Opinion is shown without staging it again. Once you stage a change, the mark turns solid. The second button, **+** and a number, appears when PanGloss found analyses FieldWorks does not hold; choose **Add analysis from PanGloss** to add one as Approved or Unknown, or to add them all as Unknown. A chosen analysis shows **✓** and its number. Ctrl+Z (⌘+Z on macOS) undoes the last staged choice.

The change is kept as pending work for this project. It applies to the word form everywhere, not only the occurrence you were looking at. Look for the count of changes not applied yet, then open **Review Changes** to inspect it. Nothing is written to FieldWorks while you are choosing or reviewing.

To measure the effect before applying, choose **Check these changes** in Review Changes. When you are ready, close FieldWorks and choose **Apply to FieldWorks project**. See **Review Changes** for the conditions that must be met first.

## Inside a Proposal

When a Proposal is open, a word card adds a block called **In PanGloss · with this Proposal**. It shows the analyses PanGloss built for the word when the Proposal was last tried, and for each one the changes in the Proposal that built it. If the Proposal has not been tried yet the block says **Not tried yet**, while it is being tried it says **Trying…**, and if the project or the Proposal changed since, it says **Needs another try**. Nothing is tried again on its own.

Choose **Set analysis** to stage a change into the open Proposal instead of your pending word changes. **Approve … in** the Proposal's name approves an analysis FieldWorks already holds as Unknown that the Proposal now builds. **Add an expected parse to** the Proposal's name adds an analysis FieldWorks does not hold, as Approved, and Review Changes shows it as **Will add as Approved**. Either way the change is checked against the Proposal's own copy of the project, and it is applied together with the Proposal's other changes. If that copy has been cleaned up, the change is marked as needing another check; choose **Try again** on the Proposal bar.

Outside a Proposal nothing changes: your choices go to the pending word changes as before.

![A pending choice shown on its word card](shot:explained-word-card/unknown-staged)

entries.title: Default Selection
entries.description: The Default Selection is the set of Texts and added words Motif measures when you run the project without choosing another Selection. Motif saves it with the project. Each parse keeps the exact word list it measured, so changing the Default Selection does not rewrite earlier results.
entries.helpPage:
# Default Selection

The [Default Selection](term:default-selection) is the set of Texts and added words Motif measures when you run the project without choosing another Selection. Motif saves it with the project. Each [parse](term:parse-all-words) keeps the exact word list it measured, so changing the Default Selection does not rewrite earlier results.

The first time you set up a project, choose texts and add any extra words in **What Should Motif Measure Every Time?** Choose **Configure…** from the project menu to edit that choice later. The Selection needs at least one text or added word before Motif can parse. Setup, Settings, and **Analysis options** edit the same saved parsing policy; see [Settings](guide:settings) for its time-limit choices.

The Default Selection is not a search query that changes behind your back. Motif resolves the chosen material for each run and records what it measured. After saving in FieldWorks, press **Refresh** to read the saved project, then choose **Parse all words** to measure the current Default Selection again.

entries.title: Stale numbers and changes
entries.description: In the window, Motif marks a pending change as No longer fits when the FieldWorks project has changed something that choice depended on, such as the word form or an analysis. This means the pending choice cannot safely be applied as written. It is different from stale numbers, which mean stored measurement evidence describes an earlier project state.
entries.helpPage:
# Stale numbers and changes

In the window, Motif marks a pending change as [**No longer fits**](term:drift) when the FieldWorks project has changed something that choice depended on, such as the word form or an analysis. This means the pending choice cannot safely be applied as written. It is different from stale numbers, which mean stored measurement evidence describes an earlier project state.

For steps to check or remove a change, see **When a change no longer fits**.

entries.title: Archiphonemes and the glottal stop
entries.description: An archiphoneme is a sound that an underlying form carries and a rule changes. The nasal of a prefix such as paN- is one example: it is m, n or ng by the sound after it, and never N. LibLCM has no archiphoneme flag, and neither HermitCrab nor PanGloss treats one specially. It is a plain phoneme, so Motif authors it with Author a phoneme like any other.
entries.helpPage:
# Archiphonemes and the glottal stop

An archiphoneme is a sound that an underlying form carries and a rule changes. The nasal of a prefix such as `paN-` is one example: it is `m`, `n` or `ng` by the sound after it, and never `N`. LibLCM has no archiphoneme flag, and neither HermitCrab nor PanGloss treats one specially. It is a plain phoneme, so Motif authors it with [Author a phoneme](cmd:compose-author-phoneme) like any other.

## Encode the pattern

1. Choose a letter or symbol that the written language never uses for another sound, and author it as a phoneme (`compose-author-phoneme`). If the symbol is not a letter of the writing system, make it a word-forming character of the vernacular writing system first, or the form that holds it cannot be split into phonemes.
2. Give the phonemes of the surface sounds their features: define the features with `compose-author-phonological-feature`, then set them with `compose-edit-phoneme-features`. A natural class by features (`compose-author-natural-class`, `compose-edit-natural-class-features`) then picks out the conditioning sounds.
3. Write the underlying form of the affix or stem with the archiphoneme (`compose-author-lexical-entry`, `compose-author-alternate-form`), and add the rule that changes it (`compose-author-phonological-rule`).
4. Run a Trial with a word for each surface sound and with words that must not parse.

A rule that only changes the archiphoneme near some sounds leaves it in place elsewhere. If it must always change, add a rule for the elsewhere case.

## What Motif checks

Motif reports, with code `grammar.phoneme-never-used` at level information, a phoneme that no form, wordform, rule, natural class or environment uses. An archiphoneme without an underlying form, or one whose rule was never written, is reported until it is used. An inventory authored ahead of the lexicon is also reported; nothing needs changing then.

## The glottal stop

The glottal stop is an ordinary phoneme too. Two choices decide how it shows in a word:

- The orthography writes it, with a hyphen or an apostrophe or a letter. Author the phoneme with that representation. A hyphen or an apostrophe is a word-forming character only if the writing system says so.
- The orthography leaves it out where it is predictable, for example at the end of a word. Author the phoneme with a symbol that never appears in text, and let a rule delete or realise it, as for an archiphoneme.

Decide from the attested spellings, and ask the linguist when they do not decide it (guide ask-the-linguist).

## Pitfalls

- Do not author a second phoneme for a surface variant that a rule can derive.
- Do not remove an unused archiphoneme while a rule that will use it is still planned.
- Segment classes in a rewrite rule behave the same in a featureless project and in one with features (guide nasal-assimilation).

entries.title: Ask the linguist when evidence runs out
entries.description: Ask when two analyses fit the evidence and choosing between them changes the Proposal. A useful question lets the linguist distinguish those analyses using forms already in the project and one concrete prediction.
entries.helpPage:
# Ask the linguist when evidence runs out

Ask when two analyses fit the evidence and choosing between them changes the Proposal. A useful question lets the linguist distinguish those analyses using forms already in the project and one concrete prediction.

## Guess, ask or defer

- **Guess** only a low-impact, reversible choice that the existing evidence supports; keep it in a Draft and check it with a Dry Run and Trial.
- **Ask** when the linguist can answer a concrete contrast. Ask one question at a time and show the evidence plus the competing predictions.
- **Defer** when the project lacks the forms or the linguist cannot yet distinguish the choices. State what evidence would resolve the choice, and do not invent a Proposal.
- **Say the tool is missing** when Motif cannot create a required FieldWorks object. Explain the needed encoding and wait for a composer; do not imitate it with a different object.

When the project has no evidence for requested forms, do not suggest an affix shape, allomorph or example word, even as a prediction or an unapplied draft. Say what attested forms and contexts would resolve the question, then ask for them.

For example: “I can’t determine this pattern from the project. Could you share attested forms in the relevant contexts, including a contrasting form if available?”

## Build the question from evidence

Read forms with `motif_lexicon`, `motif_word` or `motif_texts`. Use the actual spellings and contexts returned for this project. Do not present guessed forms as attested; when requested forms are absent, ask for attested forms instead of predicting spellings.

Use this frame and replace every bracketed item with project evidence:

> “I found `<attested form A>` in `<observed context A>` and `<attested form B>` in `<observed context B>`. The two analyses predict `<predicted form A>` versus `<predicted form B>` for `<unobserved or contrasting context>`. Which form would a speaker use there?”

Ask for the missing fact only. Do not bundle a request to choose the analysis, name a rule, provide more examples and approve a Proposal into one question.

## Common wrong choices

- Guessing a high-impact choice the evidence does not support.
- Asking several questions at once, or with forms that are not attested in the project.

entries.title: Phonologically conditioned allomorphs
entries.description: A linguist sees one morpheme with different spoken or written forms in different sound contexts. FieldWorks can keep those forms together and condition each one on its surrounding sounds.
entries.helpPage:
# Phonologically conditioned allomorphs

A linguist sees one morpheme with different spoken or written forms in different sound contexts. FieldWorks can keep those forms together and condition each one on its surrounding sounds.

## Encode the pattern

- Keep the variants under one lexical entry when the evidence supports one morpheme.
- Give each variant the sound environment where it occurs. Use a natural class when several sounds share the relevant property.
- Put the narrowest conditioned forms before a less restricted or elsewhere form.
- Do not duplicate the same unrestricted form for every stem. Do not use an environment broader than the evidence, such as “after any consonant” when only one class is supported.
- Check whether the forms are truly one morpheme before treating their difference as phonological conditioning.

Existing ordinary alternate text can be edited in place with [Edit an allomorph form](cmd:compose-edit-allomorph-form) (`motif_edit_allomorph_form`), naming its expected owner, writing system and current text. This keeps conditions and references on the same form ID. Lexeme forms use [Rewrite lexeme forms](cmd:compose-rewrite-lexeme-form) with explicit `newForm` and `foldStressMarks=false` when underlying distinctions condition the grammar. [Edit a citation form](cmd:compose-edit-citation-form) (`motif_edit_citation_form`) retains a selected marked source headword separately from parser forms.

## Motif support

`motif_lexicon` with detailed results can read existing allomorphs and their environments. `motif_grammar` can read natural classes and environments. `motif_add_phoneme`, `motif_add_natural_class` and `motif_add_environment` create the sound inventory and context. `motif_add_lexeme_form` changes an existing lexeme form. `motif_add_alternate_form` creates a stem or affix alternate under an existing entry. It accepts optional sound `environments` and, for affix forms, optional `inflectionClasses`. When alternates already exist, supply an exact `placement` gap. `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph` adds a pattern-based form (an affix process with its own input and output) to an affix entry whose other forms may be plain allomorphs or processes; it takes no environments and applies to all of the entry's grammatical info. `motif_add_alternate_form` likewise adds a plain affix allomorph beside process forms. Both take `inflectionClasses` for inflectional grammatical info; the parser ignores them for a derivational analysis (the stem features an allomorph requires, `MsEnvFeatures` in LibLCM, are read for a derivational affix too, but Motif has no composer for them yet), so a mixed entry can use them for its inflectional analysis while restricting the derivational analysis through the `motif_edit_derivational_affix_restriction` MCP tool or `compose-edit-derivational-affix-restriction` CLI verb (guide suffix-prefix-slots). When the entry has no inflectional grammatical info, Motif refuses `inflectionClasses` and points to that composer. `motif_edit_allomorph_condition`, when selected by the profile, can link an environment to an existing allomorph.

## What an allomorph can and cannot carry

FieldWorks holds the meaning of a morpheme on the entry, not on its forms. So one form cannot have its own tense, gloss or slot.

| An allomorph can carry | An allomorph cannot carry |
|---|---|
| Sound environments the form occurs in (`environments`) | Its own gloss, tense or other label |
| Inflection classes of the stems it attaches to, for an inflectional analysis (`inflectionClasses`) | Its own grammatical info or slot |
| For an affix, the stem features and category it needs (conditions on the stem it attaches to) | A different category or meaning from the entry's other forms |
| For a stem, a stem name tied to inflection features | A rule to apply or skip (use exception features on the analysis) |
| Its place in the order of the entry's forms | Anything that changes which senses it serves |
| Being abstract (a form no word shows) | |

When the form needs a different label, as a past form beside a future one, make it its own entry with its own grammatical info, slot and sense. Two analyses on one entry do not help: the parser gives every form of the entry to every analysis, so both labels would apply to both forms.

## Two forms that must not block each other (free variation)

An earlier form with an environment blocks every later form of the same entry wherever it matches, the lexeme form (always last) included. HermitCrab's one exception is free fluctuation: neighbouring forms whose environment sets are exactly equal are not disjunctive, so both parse and neither blocks the other. For an affix this is the only encoding; an affix variant entry is not read by the parser. A stem can also be a variant entry with no sense of its own, which the parser loads as a separate stem, but that is a different morpheme, not a form of this one.

- To let the plain suffix `an` and a variant that starts with a hyphen character, `-an`, both parse after any sound, give the entry two forms with no environment. `motif_add_alternate_form` with no `environments` does this; leave the new form last, beside the unrestricted lexeme form. A real-parser test (`AuthorFreeVariationParserTests`) shows two spellings (`an` and `ang`) both parse after `o` and after `a`.
- Two alternates that carry the same environments are free variation with each other (the same test file shows both parse where the environment matches, and the plain lexeme form is blocked there). A form whose environments differ from its neighbour's is not free variation. An alternate restricted to "after a consonant" blocks the lexeme form after every consonant, so the plain spelling stops parsing there. The parser has no way to say "this form where the environment matches, and the plain form everywhere as well".
- Best workaround when the variant should occur only in one context but the plain form must stay possible there too: make the variant unrestricted (free variation) and accept that it also licenses the variant in other contexts, such as a hyphen after a vowel; measure that over-generation with a Trial.

## A hyphenated spelling of an affix process
