An affix process cannot carry a written alternate form: it has no spelling of its own, only an input and an output. When the text writes a hyphen between the affix and the stem (Cebuano `l`-forms and `X-X` reduplication), make the hyphen part of the output. Add a second process to the same entry with `compose-author-affix-process-allomorph` (`motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`) whose output inserts the hyphen phoneme where the text writes it, for example `{"insert":["<i>","<k>","<a>","<hyphen>"]},{"copy":"rest"}` beside the process that inserts the same sounds without the hyphen. The hyphen must be a phoneme (`compose-author-phoneme`). LibLCM holds the entry's processes as ordered alternate forms of one entry, so both spellings share its gloss and grammatical info and the real parser reads either; for full reduplication a single process that copies the stem, inserts the hyphen and copies it again already gives the hyphenated spelling, so no second process is needed. A plain written alternate (`compose-author-alternate-form`) may share the entry with processes when it expresses a written realization rather than a pattern change.

Do not add a shape-restricted solid form to the entry of an unrestricted hyphen form. A form earlier in the order blocks every later form of the entry for the stems it matches, so a solid form restricted to, say, three-sound stems stops the hyphen spelling of exactly those stems (`RealParserReduplicationBlockingTests` shows `pul-pul` lost while `kaun-kaun` still parses). That is the loss an earlier round saw when it put shape forms on the hyphen entry. Give the restricted solid form its own entry: both spellings then parse, each by its own entry.

## Replace a process with a plain archiphoneme form

Keep the entry, its senses and grammatical analyses. In one Draft, author a plain alternate with `compose-author-alternate-form`, then move each prohibition occurrence to that form with [Retarget a prohibition](cmd:compose-edit-adhoc-prohibition-references). Use [Delete a prohibition](cmd:compose-delete-adhoc-prohibition) for restrictions that should disappear. Supply the complete expected state, including Disabled and legacy allomorph references. Morpheme prohibitions can keep their grammatical-analysis references when the entry and analyses stay the same.

Finally use [Delete an affix process](cmd:compose-delete-affix-process) with `entry`, the process `form` and the plain form as `replacement`. A lexeme process is replaced by promoting the plain alternate; an alternate process is removed while the plain form stays. The command refuses until every reference into the process graph has moved or gone, naming each remaining occurrence and its remedy. These steps can be one `compose` request, with an earlier step's created form referenced by its label. MCP stages only; a person reviews the Dry Run and Trial and Applies.

An archiphoneme is an ordinary phoneme whose spelling the plain form carries. Author its sound rule separately. Trial the unaffected forms and the forms the prohibitions exclude, as well as forms changed by the rule; a structural replacement alone does not prove parse preservation.

## One form blocked after one form of another affix

Sometimes one form of an affix is wrong only after one particular form of an earlier affix: a stative `-lik` fits after an applicative `-o` but not after `-e`, while `-k` fits after both. Create an allomorph prohibition with the CLI verb `compose-author-adhoc-prohibition`, which MCP offers as `motif_author_adhoc_prohibition` (kind `allomorph`; the later form as `first`, the earlier form as `rest`, adjacency `adjacent-to-right`). The parser drops only that pair of forms. Use it between forms of different entries: in an inflectional template an entry fills one slot, so a rule between two forms of the same entry would never fire there. To choose between forms of one entry, give each its own environment, or put the narrowest first and the general form last.

## Every sound except some, and a zero form chosen by class

A natural class is a fixed list of sounds (or of feature values), and FieldWorks has no complement or negated class. A project file can hold a negated feature value (LibLCM stores one), but FieldWorks' parser loader cannot read it and FieldWorks offers no way to make one, so do not rely on it; the grammar check warns (`grammar.negated-feature-value`) when a project holds one. For "every consonant except `<sound>`", list the sounds wanted (author the class with `motif_add_natural_class`) and add a sound to it when the inventory grows. A zero affix that should depend on the stem's class, not on the sounds around it, takes `inflectionClasses` (`motif_add_lexical_entry`, or `motif_add_alternate_form` for a form of an existing entry) and no environment; a stem of any other class gets no reading from it.

## Circumfix parts

Each part of a circumfix keeps its own environment on the real parser (a real-parser test, `RealParserCircumfixEnvironmentTests`, authors `ma-` with `-ang` after a consonant and `-x` after a vowel as two circumfix entries, each part with its own environment, and the parser chooses by the stem's last sound; the prefix part's environment is tested at the stem start and the suffix part's at the stem end). A part whose environment names the other part's side can never hold, so give each part a context on its own side of the stem. Run a Trial with the words each way: a missing half, the wrong linker and a stem the prefix environment excludes all stay unparsed.

## Check with a Trial

After a composer can express the change, include attested words from each sound context and words just outside those contexts. Confirm each variant appears where expected and that the unrestricted form does not win before a narrower variant. Include words that should remain unchanged.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the evidence does not show whether the variants share a morpheme or what sound defines the environment. Use real project forms: “I found `<attested form A>` before `<observed sound class A>` and `<attested form B>` before `<observed sound class B>`. Does `<variant>` also occur before `<attested sound C>`, or is that a separate morpheme?” Replace bracketed items with forms read from this project; label any unobserved form as a prediction.

## Common wrong choices

- A separate entry for each variant of one morpheme.
- An environment broader than the evidence, or an unrestricted form placed before narrower ones.
- Listing variants for a regular sound change across many forms; a phonological rule fits that better.
- A new entry for each pattern-based form of one affix, or a plain alternate form for a pattern change; use `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`.

entries.title: Feature-conditioned template slots
entries.description: A linguist sees an affix change with a grammatical value such as person, number or noun class. FieldWorks records those values on grammatical analyses and uses them to restrict which affix can fill a template slot.
entries.helpPage:
# Feature-conditioned template slots

A linguist sees an affix change with a grammatical value such as person, number or noun class. FieldWorks records those values on grammatical analyses and uses them to restrict which affix can fill a template slot.

## Encode the pattern

- Declare a feature and its values when the distinction has grammatical meaning the rest of the analysis needs to see.
- Put a noun's gender pair (for example 7/8) on the stem's grammatical analysis and its number on the class prefix's required features: each reading shows the prefix's number, the stem's gender filters which prefixes fit, and a number requirement never filters a stem that lacks one.
- Make two affixes in different slots agree (a subject marker and a relative marker, say) by giving both the same feature value in their required features: the parser keeps each affix's requirement on the word, so a pair that disagrees has no analysis. Use one feature whose values are the agreement groups, and give an affix that serves two groups one entry per group. Do not use this where the second affix agrees with something else, such as a suffix relative that agrees with the object.
- Put the supported value on the stem's grammatical analysis. Restrict an inflectional affix to its required feature values, then link it to the appropriate slot.
- Keep the template for the shared order of positions. Use separate templates only when forms have different required positions; use an optional slot only when that position may truly be absent.
- A template cannot be limited to a stem inflection class: FieldWorks ties a template to a category and the parser reads no class on it. To give one class its own affixes, restrict each affix in that template's slots to the class (`inflectionClasses` on `motif_add_lexical_entry` or `motif_add_alternate_form`, or `compose-edit-affix-inflection-classes`) or require a feature value on the affix. A stem of another class then finds no complete template; an optional slot lets it pass without the affix.
- Do not use an arbitrary inflection class for a value that must participate in agreement. Do not let every affix compete in the slot without the feature restrictions the data supports.

## Motif support

`motif_grammar` can read features, feature values, inflection classes and templates. `motif_add_inflection_feature` declares a closed morphosyntactic feature with its named values, and `motif_add_inflection_class` creates a category-owned class that can be assigned to a stem MSA through `motif_add_lexical_entry`. `motif_add_affix_slot` and `motif_add_affix_template` create the category-owned positions and their order. `motif_add_feature_structure` creates an empty feature structure on an existing or earlier-staged stem, inflectional affix or derivational affix MSA (a derivational affix takes side from or to), refusing an occupied slot. Use its returned exact structure identity with `motif_add_feature_value` to require a closed-feature specification, optionally selecting an existing value belonging to that exact feature. Inflectional affix selections are requirements on the word, not output features; their definitions must belong to the current morphosyntactic feature system and any declared structure type. A stem's values remain separate from the affix's requirements. `motif_remove_feature_value` removes one feature's specification from a stem or affix structure, including a derivational affix's From or To structure.

## Check with a Trial

Try words with each attested value and a contrasting value. Confirm the right affix appears for each value, the wrong affix does not, and a word with missing or incompatible information does not acquire an unsupported analysis. Include negative words and any known exceptions.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when it is unclear whether a contrast is grammatical agreement or arbitrary lexical grouping, or which value belongs to a form. Use attested forms: “`<attested form A>` takes `<affix A>` and is marked `<observed value A>`; `<attested form B>` takes `<affix B>`. Does `<attested form C>` have value `<value A>` or `<value B>`?” Replace bracketed items with project evidence and ask only the question that distinguishes the encodings.

## Common wrong choices

- An arbitrary inflection class for a value that must agree with other words.
- Letting every affix compete for a slot without feature restrictions the data supports.
- A separate affix or slot per feature value.

entries.title: Feature changes and alpha variables
entries.description: A feature change sets named features on the segment matched by the Input and preserves its other features. Use it for a regular alternation such as voicing, nasalisation or place assimilation. Follow Andy Black's section 6.3.2: an archiphoneme N takes its place from the following consonant across a morpheme boundary, N → [α place] /  + [α place].
entries.helpPage:
# Feature changes and alpha variables

A feature change sets named features on the segment matched by the Input and preserves its other features. Use it for a regular alternation such as voicing, nasalisation or place assimilation. Follow Andy Black's section 6.3.2: an archiphoneme N takes its place from the following consonant across a morpheme boundary, `N → [α place] / _ + [α place]`.

First define the phonological features and their values with [Author a phonological feature](cmd:compose-author-phonological-feature), give the phonemes their features with [Edit a phoneme's features](cmd:compose-edit-phoneme-features), and create the feature natural classes with [Author a natural class](cmd:compose-author-natural-class). Each surface phoneme needs enough features to distinguish it from the others (Black section 6.2). An underlying archiphoneme may leave place unspecified. A separate feature can distinguish underlying N from surface nasals; the Output then sets that feature to its surface value as well as copying place.

## Feature change

An Output item uses `change`, an array of `{ "feature": "<feature-id>", "value": "<value-id>" }` pairs. These are feature and value identities from this project's phonological feature system. A plus or minus feature value is an ordinary value identity, distinct from the polarity of an alpha reference. For example:

```json
{
  "name": "voice the matched consonant",
  "direction": "simultaneous",
  "input": [{ "naturalClass": "<voiceless-consonant-class-id>" }],
  "output": [{ "change": [{ "feature": "<voice-id>", "value": "<plus-id>" }] }]
}
```

The Output changes voice and keeps place and manner. Motif creates a feature natural class (`PhNCFeatures`) for this partial description, as FieldWorks does. Input and Output must have the same number of items when an Output item uses `change`, so each change has a matched segment. A rule whose Output is a multi-member segment class does not choose a member. It applies only the features the members share, so the input segment keeps its own value for every feature the members differ on. An *l* stays *l* under {l,w}, and a [-lat] *d* becomes *r* under {r,l}. Only an input with no value for those features matches every member (fieldworks-parser-conformance#38). To change named features, use a feature natural class at an aligned Output position; for free variation, use alternate forms of the stem.

## Alpha agreement and disagreement

A `variables` array adds alpha references to a feature natural class in Input or either context, or to an Output `change`. Each reference contains a `variable` name, a closed phonological `feature` identity, and `polarity` (`+` by default). Use the same variable name for the same feature everywhere in that rule. Plus requires agreement with the variable; minus requires disagreement. Either polarity can bind a variable, and a variable may have a single reference. A minus is not a fixed minus feature value. FieldWorks' loader can name at most 24 distinct alpha variables across the whole rule, including all right-hand sides; Motif refuses a larger rule before staging it.

Here is the Black section 6.3.2 shape. The archiphoneme class matches N, the following-consonant class supplies place, and the Output makes a surface nasal with that place:

```json
{
  "name": "nasal place assimilation",
  "direction": "simultaneous",
  "input": [{ "naturalClass": "<archiphoneme-class-id>" }],
  "output": [{
    "change": [{ "feature": "<archiphoneme-feature-id>", "value": "<surface-value-id>" }],
    "variables": [{ "variable": "alpha", "feature": "<place-id>", "polarity": "+" }]
  }],
  "right": [
    { "boundary": "morpheme" },
    { "naturalClass": "<following-consonant-class-id>",
      "variables": [{ "variable": "alpha", "feature": "<place-id>", "polarity": "+" }] }
  ]
}
```

With underlying N + pa, N + ta and N + ka, expect mpa, nta and ŋka; npa, mta and the other wrong nasals have no analysis. Check each place and negative controls with a Trial before Apply. For a binary feature, Output polarity `-` and context polarity `+` express dissimilation instead. An empty `change` is allowed when alpha supplies the change by itself.

Motif refuses one variable naming different features, duplicate or contradictory polarities on one item, and a fixed and variable value for the same feature on one item. A referenced feature must be a declared closed feature with values in this project; it need not occur on any phoneme. Alpha references belong to feature natural classes, not literal phoneme or boundary items. They are not available in allomorph environment strings. FieldWorks' current loader cannot discover a variable used only inside optional or repeated items in multi-item contexts, so Motif explains this limit before staging such a rule. The same variable is discoverable when it also occurs on Input, Output, an ordinary context item, or a context containing only the repeated item.

## Read and edit

[Author a sound rule](cmd:compose-author-phonological-rule) and [Edit a sound rule](cmd:compose-edit-phonological-rule) accept these items through `--intent`. Their MCP tools stage the same intent in a Draft; a person Applies the Proposal.

Read `motif_grammar(kind="phonological_rules", detail="detailed")` before editing. Copy its `intent` into `expected`, and use its returned variable identifiers in changed parts to keep sharing with parts left in place. Read-back uses each stored feature constraint's identity as the variable name; author-supplied labels are local to authoring and are not stored by LibLCM. If every reference is in replaced Input, the constraint is recreated with a new identity while its sharing and polarity stay the same. Feature Output classes read back with their `naturalClass` identities and alpha references, preserving sharing with other users of the class. Multiple right-hand sides read back as an ordered `rightHandSides` sequence with per-case Output, contexts, rule features and input categories. Replace that complete sequence under `expected.rightHandSides` to add, remove or reorder cases; alpha scope and sharing span the whole rule. Only an unrepresentable context or applicability reference prevents editable read-back.

The default PanGloss engine supports feature changes and alpha agreement. Its FST engine may refuse alpha rules. Alpha on Input is representable and supported by the FieldWorks loader, but hc.dll parsing parity for that shape is unproven because the oracle hangs. A segment unspecified for a feature does not satisfy a fixed minus value in a synthesis rule or its environment. A multi-member Output segment-list class does not supply alternatives, while multiple right-hand sides are ordered cases: the first applicable case wins. Rule features restrict each case but do not make overlapping cases optional. Metathesis is a separate capability.

entries.title: Segmental nasal assimilation
entries.description: A linguist sees a nasal change its sound near another consonant, while the morpheme remains the same. When the evidence supports a sound rule, FieldWorks can encode the change as a phonological rule instead of listing a separate affix spelling for every context.
entries.helpPage:
# Segmental nasal assimilation

A linguist sees a nasal change its sound near another consonant, while the morpheme remains the same. When the evidence supports a sound rule, FieldWorks can encode the change as a phonological rule instead of listing a separate affix spelling for every context.

## Encode the pattern

- First establish the underlying nasal and the contexts in which its surface form changes.
- Use phonological features or natural classes to describe the nasal, the conditioning sounds and the change. Keep the context narrow enough to exclude unrelated nasals and consonants.
- Use a regular segmental rule for a sound change across forms. Record rule order and whether the pattern applies simultaneously or iteratively when that affects the evidence.
- Do not duplicate a whole affix for each place of articulation when one rule accounts for the alternation. Do not write a rule that changes every nasal merely because some nasals assimilate.
- Treat deletion, exceptional spellings or lexical restrictions as separate decisions when the data supports them; do not hide them in an over-broad assimilation rule.

## Motif support

`motif_grammar` can read phonemes, natural classes and phonological rules. `motif_add_phoneme`, `motif_add_natural_class` and `motif_add_phonological_rule` create the sound inventory, reusable sound classes and regular rules. A rule intent names existing phonemes or natural classes in its input, output and contexts. `motif_edit_phonological_rule` changes a rule in place, `motif_order_phonological_rules` reorders rules, `motif_set_phonological_rule_disabled` turns one off or on, and `motif_delete_phonological_rule` removes one. A context item may be optional or repeated. Input and Output each accept up to eight phoneme or natural-class items in order, and may have different lengths. A segment-list natural class in the Output does not choose a member; it applies only the features its members share, and the input keeps its own value for the rest. An aligned feature-class Output changes the named features on the matched segment and preserves the rest; see [Feature rules](guide:encoding/feature-rules). Read `motif_grammar(kind="phonological_rules", detail="detailed")` to get the rule's `intent` for an edit's `expected` guard. `motif_add_phonological_feature` and `motif_add_phonological_feature_value` define the phonological features and their values, `motif_edit_phoneme_features` sets them on phonemes, and `motif_edit_natural_class_features` changes the feature constraints of a natural class; a class by features can be created with `motif_add_natural_class` (`features`). A nasal that changes with its neighbour is often an archiphoneme, a phoneme only the underlying form carries (`motif_guide(topic="archiphonemes")`). `motif_add_affix_process` and `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph` express a substitution as pattern-based forms of one affix instead. `motif_guide(topic="conditioned-allomorphs")` describes the related case where the evidence instead supports stored conditioned variants.

## Order the rules

Rules apply one after another, and a later rule sees the output of the earlier ones. A chain such as a place rule (a class becomes a nasal after the archiphoneme) followed by a deletion rule (the archiphoneme drops before a nasal) and an elsewhere rule (the archiphoneme becomes the velar nasal) works only in that order. If the elsewhere rule comes first, the archiphoneme is gone before the others see it and the words get no analysis. Reorder instead of rewriting; test a word for each branch. A segment-list natural class can also be used without phonological features. Feature-class rules require the relevant features and represented counterpart phonemes.

## Check with a Trial

Include attested forms for each conditioning place, forms where the nasal should stay unchanged, and negative words that should not become valid. Check that each output matches the evidence and that rule ordering does not alter unrelated segments.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the forms do not decide whether the change is assimilation, a stored allomorph or a lexical exception. Build one contrast from actual project forms: “In `<attested form A>`, the nasal is before `<observed sound A>`; in `<attested form B>`, it is before `<observed sound B>`. Does the same morpheme occur before `<attested sound C>`, and what form do speakers use?” Replace bracketed items with evidence and distinguish observed forms from predictions.

## Common wrong choices

- Duplicating an affix for each place of articulation when one rule explains the alternation.
- An unconstrained affix process for a nasal change may require substantial parser work. Several processes kept as allomorphs of one Verb-only entry (the restriction comes from the entry's grammatical info; the composer has no category input), with `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`, stopped no words with compounding off.
- A rule that changes every nasal because only some assimilate.

When only some prefixes substitute, the change is conditioned by the morpheme, not by sound alone. Cebuano is an example: Wolff treats substitution at the paN-, maN-, naN- and hiN- boundary as systematic (p, b become m; t, d, s become n; k and glottal stop become ng; l becomes ngl or nl, both accepted), while ning- and ming- keep k (ningkubit, mingkuyánap). Put the substituting forms on one entry as process allomorphs with `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`, not in a phonological rule that would also apply to the prefixes that keep the consonant.

entries.title: A supported finding of no inflection
entries.description: A linguist may find that words keep the same form across grammatical contexts that another language marks with affixes. Motif should preserve that finding instead of inventing a prefix, suffix or template to match expectations from another language.
entries.helpPage:
# A supported finding of no inflection

A linguist may find that words keep the same form across grammatical contexts that another language marks with affixes. Motif should preserve that finding instead of inventing a prefix, suffix or template to match expectations from another language.

## Encode the pattern

- Compare the same lexemes across the grammatical contexts at issue. Check representative words and exceptions before deciding that there is no inflection.
- Leave out affix entries, slots and templates for a category when the evidence shows no inflectional form change there.
- Keep lexical meaning, part of speech and any grammatical features that the analysis actually needs. A language can have grammatical distinctions without marking them by affixes.
- Do not add a null affix or empty slot just to represent an assumed default. Do not conclude “no inflection” from one unchanged word or from missing data.

## Motif support

`motif_lexicon`, `motif_grammar` and `motif_word` can show the forms and analyses already recorded. `motif_add_lexeme_form` can edit an existing form, and `motif_add_feature_structure` can add an empty structure to an existing stem analysis; neither is needed to record the absence of an affix. No grammar composer is required to leave an unsupported affix out.

## Check with a Trial

Do not use a Trial as proof that an affix does not exist. If a Proposal changes nearby grammar, include representative unchanged forms and negative words in `motif_trial`; confirm they remain unchanged and do not gain analyses from the new rule. If there is no change to propose, report the evidence without creating an empty Proposal.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the project lacks enough comparable forms to separate no inflection from missing or unrecorded data. Use attested examples: “`<attested form A>` and `<attested form B>` have the same form in the contexts recorded here. Are these the same lexeme in contrasting `<grammatical contexts>`, and is there another form speakers use?” Replace bracketed items with observed project data; do not state the absence as settled until the comparison is supported.

## Common wrong choices

- Inventing an affix or template because another language marks the distinction.
- Approximating a missing composer with unrelated edits.

entries.title: Authoring and editing phonological rules
entries.description: A regular rewrite rule shares its Input, name and direction across one or more right-hand sides. Each right-hand side has its own Output, left and right environments, required and excluded rule features, and optional input categories. Input and Output each contain up to eight ordered phoneme or natural-class items. Empty Input means insertion; empty Output means deletion. Context items can be optional or repeated and can name word and morpheme boundaries.
entries.helpPage:
# Authoring and editing phonological rules

A regular rewrite rule shares its Input, name and direction across one or more right-hand sides. Each right-hand side has its own Output, left and right environments, required and excluded rule features, and optional input categories. Input and Output each contain up to eight ordered phoneme or natural-class items. Empty Input means insertion; empty Output means deletion. Context items can be optional or repeated and can name word and morpheme boundaries.

## One rule, several outcomes

Wolff section 5.15 gives *kabukiran* and *kabukilan* from *bukid*. A rule cannot offer both. A rule whose Output is a multi-member segment class does not choose a member. It applies only the features the members share, so the input segment keeps its own value for every feature the members differ on. An *l* stays *l* under {l,w}, and a [-lat] *d* becomes *r* under {r,l}. Only an input with no value for those features matches every member (fieldworks-parser-conformance#38). Author a free d → r/l (or l → w) alternation as an alternate form of the stem on the existing entry, one per source-attested stem, so no second entry or analysis is needed. Use a rule only for a change that is obligatory where it applies: a literal phoneme or a feature-class Output, with a required exception feature on the stems the source selects. Tag only the analyses supported by the source: *sayran* does not license *saylan*. Preserve any quantity or environment conditions supported by the source and check both forms and untagged controls in a Trial.

Multiple right-hand sides are ordered cases, rather than freely alternating branches. FieldWorks uses the first applicable case at a matching site. Two overlapping d → r and d → l cases therefore do not produce both alternatives; an Output class supplies that choice within one case. Features restrict which words a case affects. They do not make overlapping cases optional or silently introduce dialect/register scope. Use explicit lexical features only where the evidence supports that distinction.

## Intent and guarded edits

[Author a sound rule](cmd:compose-author-phonological-rule) accepts `rightHandSides`, an array of one or more such cases, instead of the single-outcome `output`, `left` and `right` shorthand. The number of cases has no authoring ceiling. Within each case, `requiredFeatures` names the exception features or inflection classes the word must carry, and `excludedFeatures` names those it must carry none of. Omitting either means an empty set for that case. Features restrict applicability; they do not make overlapping cases optional or introduce a dialect or register model. A dialect distinction can be represented by explicit features on the appropriate analyses when the linguistic evidence supports it.

[Edit a sound rule](cmd:compose-edit-phonological-rule) replaces the complete `rightHandSides` sequence under `expected.rightHandSides`. Copy the detailed rule read into `expected`, then add, remove or reorder outcome objects. An unrestricted single-outcome read uses the older `output`, `left` and `right` form; copying all three into `expected` also guards its conversion to several outcomes. Omitted fields within a replacement outcome become empty, so retain its contexts and rule features when they should stay. Input, direction and rule name remain shared. [Feature changes and alpha variables](cmd:compose-author-phonological-rule) work within each case, with alpha identities shared across the whole rule.

Each outcome requires `output`. Its omitted `left`, `right`, `requiredFeatures`, `excludedFeatures` and `inputCategories` are empty lists. Rule features name exception features or inflection classes, and `inputCategories` names part-of-speech identities (including their subcategories). A feature cannot be both required and excluded in the same outcome. Different outcomes may have different sets. Output `change` and `variables` use the feature-rules encoding contract; alpha identities are shared across the whole rule.

Read `motif_grammar(kind="phonological_rules", detail="detailed")` and retain the complete returned intent. A guarded sequence replacement creates fresh right-hand-side objects while keeping the rule's identity, position and disabled flag. Omitted fields inside replacement cases are cleared, so copy every restriction that should survive. A stale sequence, including a changed case order or applicability set, stages nothing. The older Output/context shorthand remains available for editing one outcome; on multiple outcomes use the complete sequence.

Example with distinct environments:

```json
{
  "name": "context-dependent nasal outcomes",
  "direction": "simultaneous",
  "input": [{ "phoneme": "<n-id>" }],
  "rightHandSides": [
    { "output": [{ "phoneme": "<m-id>" }], "right": [{ "phoneme": "<p-id>" }], "requiredFeatures": ["<tag-id>"] },
    { "output": [{ "phoneme": "<ng-id>" }], "right": [{ "phoneme": "<k-id>" }], "requiredFeatures": ["<tag-id>"] }
  ]
}
```

Before Apply, Dry Run and Trial words for every case, every lexical alternative and each negative control. Two sounds that trade places are a metathesis rule: use [Author a metathesis rule](cmd:compose-author-metathesis-rule).

entries.title: Prefix and suffix slots
entries.description: A linguist sees prefixes or suffixes recurring in the same grammatical order across words. FieldWorks represents each affix as a lexical entry and uses a template to say where it can occur.
entries.helpPage:
# Prefix and suffix slots

A linguist sees prefixes or suffixes recurring in the same grammatical order across words. FieldWorks represents each affix as a lexical entry and uses a template to say where it can occur.

## Encode the pattern

- Keep one affix entry for one morpheme, with its prefix or suffix morph type, form and grammatical analysis.
- Put inflectional affixes in slots owned by the part of speech they apply to. Put those slots in the template in the order speakers use them.
- Mark a slot optional only when that grammatical position may truly be absent. Use separate templates when forms have different required positions.
- Do not make a new affix entry for each stem that takes the same affix. Do not use one broad slot for affixes with different grammatical jobs.

## Motif support

`motif_grammar` can read categories, templates and slots. `motif_add_lexical_entry` creates one entry and one sense with a structured MSA: use an inflectional MSA for a slot-filling affix, or a derivational MSA with both its source and destination categories. `motif_add_affix_slot` creates a category-owned slot and can assign existing inflectional MSAs; `motif_add_affix_template` creates the ordered prefix and suffix slots. Use returned entity ids in later calls or batches after the creating call completes. Batch intents may reference only ids from earlier completed calls or batches; declare operation ordering and dependencies in the intent data, since array position alone does not establish them.

## Restricting which stems an affix attaches to

Where the restriction goes depends on the kind of affix, because FieldWorks' parser reads it from different places.

- Inflectional grammatical info: restrict the affix form to inflection classes. `motif_add_alternate_form` and `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph` take `inflectionClasses`, and `compose-edit-affix-inflection-classes` changes them later. FieldWorks reads the form's Inflection Classes for inflectional grammatical info only.
- Derivational grammatical info: use the `motif_edit_derivational_affix_restriction` MCP tool or `compose-edit-derivational-affix-restriction` CLI verb to set or clear its From Inflection Class and, optionally, set From Exception Features and To Exception Features (the features the derived stem receives); `alsoMsas` applies the same change to many affixes in one intent, and `compose-add-exception-features` adds features to many derivational affixes at once (`"side":"to"` for the To set). An affix process such as reduplication takes the same restriction, since the features sit on its grammatical info. FieldWorks reads those fields from the derivational grammatical info. Form inflection classes do not restrict a derivational analysis, so a mixed entry can use both paths for their corresponding analyses. If an entry has no inflectional grammatical info, Motif refuses form `inflectionClasses` and names the derivational restriction tool.

An unmarked stem does not take a derivational affix restricted to a class: only stems assigned that class do. Assign the class to the stems first, or the affix will stop applying to every stem you meant it for.

## Check with a Trial

Include words that should take each affix and words that should not. Check that the affixes appear in the intended order, that required slots are filled, and that unrelated words do not gain extra parses. A Trial checks the Proposal; it does not create grammar objects.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the forms do not show whether an affix is required, optional or ordered relative to another affix. Build one question from attested words: “I found `<attested form A>` with `<affix A>` and `<attested form B>` with `<affix B>`. In `<attested context C>`, should both affixes occur, and in what order?” Replace each bracketed item with evidence from this project.

## Common wrong choices

- An affix entry per stem, or one broad slot for affixes with different jobs.
- An unclassified affix when an inflectional or derivational analysis with a slot fits.
- An ad hoc prohibition for an order a template can express.
- Inflection classes on a form when the entry has no inflectional grammatical info; restrict its derivational grammatical info instead.

entries.title: Work through one grammar question
entries.description: Start by learning what the saved project and words already show. Make one small Proposal, try it against observed examples and counterexamples, and hand the measured result to the linguist.
entries.helpPage:
# Work through one grammar question

Start by learning what the saved project and words already show. Make one small Proposal, try it against observed examples and counterexamples, and hand the measured result to the linguist.

## Inspect

- Use `motif_list_projects`. If the intended project is not Known, ask for its exact existing `.fwdata` path if
  needed, call `motif_open` with that path, then pass it as `project` on later calls. Use the Known project name or
  recorded path for other calls.
- Read `motif_overview`, then `motif_grammar` and `motif_lexicon` for the relevant objects and forms.
- Use `motif_word` for the linguist's recorded analysis and `motif_try_word` to see how the current grammar handles a form.
- Read the guide for the phenomenon: `motif_guide` over MCP, or `motif help guide:encoding/<topic> --full` from the CLI (`motif help` lists the topics). Check whether Motif has a composer for every object the encoding needs.

## Draft one small Proposal

- State one linguistic claim and the project evidence for it.
- Use `motif_start_proposal` and the available semantic composers that fit the claim. New grammar objects include parts of speech, lexical entries with one sense and MSA, inflection features and classes, stem names, affix slots and templates, plus phonemes, natural classes, environments and phonological rules.
- Use `motif_compose_batch` to stage related intents together. Supply each as a `verb` and structured `intent` object, with an optional `citation`. Use entity ids returned by earlier completed calls or batches; an intent that needs a newly created entity's returned id belongs in a later call or batch.
- Keep the Proposal to one related change. If a required composer is missing, say which encoding cannot be made and why; do not approximate it with unrelated edits.

## A stem two obligatory rules both want

Phonological rules in FieldWorks are obligatory, and there is no optional rule and no per-stem rule order. When two rules each need their own exception feature and the first removes what the second needs (syncope bleeding a d-to-r rule), a stem tagged for both surfaces only the first outcome. This is Black's route, not an optional rule: exception features that gate rules (Black 2.1.6, and 6.1.2.2.2, "Rule applies only with certain properties"), tried before any ad hoc rule. Give the stem one analysis per outcome, each tagged for one rule only:

1. Tag the existing analysis for the first rule with `motif_edit_exception_features` (`compose-edit-exception-features`).
2. Add a second analysis tagged for the other rule with `motif_add_morphosyntax_analysis`, giving `msa.exceptionFeatures` and a `gloss` for its sense. The original sense stays on the original analysis and the gloss adds a second sense, so an entry with one sense ends with two; each analysis needs a sense of its own, because a sense points at exactly one analysis and FieldWorks removes an analysis no sense uses; one sense cannot serve both. Make the gloss say what the sense is for, in the form `<original gloss> (second analysis: <rule or form it carries>)`, for example `to open (second analysis: d-to-r form)`. FieldWorks shows this sense in the entry beside the original, and a person can merge or reword it there. Do not move the only sense with `senses`: the old analysis would be dropped and the split becomes a retag.
3. Run a Trial with both surface forms and a word neither rule should make. Split only stems whose second form is attested: each split costs one more parse path for that stem.

A form that may surface either way takes a third analysis with no tag. A whole-word variant listed as its own entry also works, but it misses the productive forms built on the stem.

## Name an object by its form, not its id

An id is a GUID, and an object a Proposal creates gets a new one every time that Proposal is composed, so a plan written against one project (a private copy, say) names ids that do not exist in another (the live project). Any string in an intent that starts with `lookup:` is read as a name and replaced by the id of the object in the project the Draft is composed against, including one an earlier step of the same Draft created: `lookup:entry:ika-` (an entry by lexeme form, with the affix hyphen to pick the affix; add `|gloss` to separate homographs), `lookup:sense:FORM|GLOSS`, `lookup:msa:FORM|GLOSS` (the sense's grammatical info), `lookup:phoneme:GRAPHEME`, `lookup:category:NAME`, `lookup:phonological-feature:NAME` and `lookup:phonological-feature-value:FEATURE|VALUE`. Phonological feature and value names or abbreviations match exactly in the default analysis writing system. A name that matches nothing, or more than one object, is refused with the ids of the objects it matched. Stored Drafts keep the resolved ids, so a Draft replays the same way afterwards.

## Try it, then ask or defer

- Run `motif_dry_run`, then `motif_trial` with attested positive forms, contrasting forms and words that should not parse.
- Read the Trial summary in order: negatives now parsing, positives lost, unfinished cases, other changes, counts.
- Use `motif_difference` with the stored Difference id and category to page through exact before and after analyses. Unfinished cases prove no absence.
- If evidence leaves competing analyses that change the Proposal, ask one question using attested forms. Defer when the linguist cannot yet answer it.
- Revise and repeat the Trial after a meaningful change. Do not describe an unmeasured change as a parser improvement.

## Hand off

- When the Dry Run and Trial support the change, call `motif_finalize_proposal` and tell the linguist what evidence was checked and what remains uncertain.
- The linguist reviews the Proposal in Motif and decides whether to apply it. Do not claim that it was applied.

## CLI equivalents

The guides name MCP tools. From the CLI, use the matching `motif` command; run `motif help <command> --full` for its flags.

| MCP tool | CLI command |
|---|---|
| `motif_list_projects`, `motif_open` | `motif open <fwdata>` |
| `motif_overview` | `motif overview` |
| `motif_grammar`, `motif_lexicon` | `motif grammar read --kind <kind>` (`lexical_entry` for the lexicon) |
| `motif_texts` | `motif texts list` |
| `motif_word` | `motif word-context --word <word>` |
| `motif_try_word` | `motif trace --word <word>` |
| `motif_start_proposal` | `motif new --draft <name>` |
| the add and edit tools, such as `motif_add_phonological_rule` or `motif_edit_allomorph_condition` | the `compose-author-*` and `compose-edit-*` commands, such as `motif compose-author-phonological-rule` |
| `motif_compose_batch` | `motif compose-batch` |
| `motif_finalize_proposal` | `motif finalize` |
| `motif_dry_run`, `motif_trial` | `motif dry-run`, `motif trial` (add `--wait` to read the result) |
| `motif_difference` | `motif difference produce` |
| `motif_guide` | `motif help guide:encoding/<topic> --full` |

## Composer notes

- **Exception features are set as a whole list.** `compose-edit-exception-features` replaces the exact list on a stem or an inflectional affix. To add a feature to an entry that already has some, read its current features first and send the merged list: the old ones plus the new one. Sending only the new one removes the rest. `compose-add-exception-features` adds without replacing, to stems, inflectional affixes and derivational affixes (From Exception Features by default, To with `"side":"to"`).
- **Bulk retype uses `compose-batch`.** One file with an intent per stem (`compose-set-stem-part-of-speech`) stages hundreds in one Draft and one Proposal. `grammar-check` lists the likely stems as `lexicon.stem-typed-as-content-word`, with duplicate entries and affixes whose hyphen is on the wrong side; the report changes nothing.
- **Reaching an object made earlier in the same batch.** Give the step an `as` label, then write `@label` as a whole value in a later step in place of the id the first step created. If the step created several objects, name the one you mean: `@label:msa`, `@label:senses`, `@label:codes`. Select a particular created phonological feature value with `@label:values:NAME`; a bare `:values` refuses if several values were created. Rule input, output and feature contexts resolve the same labels; a later step that needs the rule an earlier step created can name it with `@label:phonrules`.
- **There is no `@FEAT:` form.** A placeholder written `@FEAT:name` is not recognised: it stays as literal text and is then refused because it is not an id. A feature made in the same batch is reached by an `as` label on its `compose-author-exception-feature` step and `@label`. An existing feature has no placeholder at all: read its id from the project (`motif grammar read`) and write the id.
- **An allomorph shares its entry's analysis.** `compose-author-affix-process-allomorph` adds a form to the entry and does not create a second analysis, so one allomorph cannot carry a different tense or other label than the entry. To label two forms differently, make two entries, or add a second analysis with `compose-add-morphosyntax-analysis`.
- **Do not parse does not stop FieldWorks parsing.** Motif can mark an entry do-not-parse, but FieldWorks' HermitCrab, its XAmple transform and PanGloss all parse a flagged entry, so the flag is not a way to retire one. To stop a stem parsing, retype it with `compose-set-stem-part-of-speech` or delete it (see `compose-set-entry-do-not-parse`).

## Common wrong choices

- Reaching for an affix process, ad hoc prohibition or batch when a typed composer fits the claim.
- Making one large Proposal for several grammar questions.
- Describing an unmeasured change as an improvement.

entries.title: Choosing what to measure
entries.description: Motif measures words from the same texts and any added words each time, so its numbers can be compared from run to run. On a new project, Motif captures its first Baseline when you open the project, then opens setup. Setup takes four steps.
entries.helpPage:
# Choosing what to measure

Motif measures words from the same texts and any added words each time, so its numbers can be compared from run to run. On a new project, Motif captures its first Baseline when you open the project, then opens setup. Setup takes four steps.

On **What Should Motif Measure Every Time?**, choose one or more texts, or add words in the box labeled **Add Words:**. A long list of added words scrolls inside the box. Choose texts you have interlinearized: Motif compares its parses with the analyses you approved there. Words you add yourself are parsed too; if the saved project has an analysis for one, Motif can compare the parse with it. Choose at least one text or add at least one word to continue. On the Texts step and in **Analyze texts**, choose **Select All Texts** to check every text. On a long list, choose **Clear** to uncheck them all.

On **How Much Work Should Each Word Get?**, set the **Parser Work Limit per Word**. The default is 20,000,000 parser work. You can change the shared parsing limits later as the **Parser Work Limit per Word** in Analysis options or Settings. **No Parser Work Limit** lets every word run to the end, which can take a very long time; you can still **Cancel**.

This becomes the project's [Default Selection](term:default-selection), the words Motif measures every time. **Start First Run** saves your choice and starts parsing; the progress panel shows how far it has got and stays on a final stage while Motif reads PanGloss's statistics. **Skip for Now** closes first-time setup without saving these choices and does not offer it again until you choose **Configure…**. **Cancel**, or Escape, also closes setup without saving; setup is offered again the next time the project is opened or refreshed. See [Settings](guide:settings) for the saved parsing policy.

Choose **Back** or **Next: Texts**, **Next: Limits**, and **Next: First Run** to move through setup.

![Choosing texts and added words in first-time setup](shot:first-run-setup-parse/selection)

entries.helpPage:
# Installing Motif

Download the Windows x64 **Setup.exe** asset from the [Motif Releases page](https://github.com/sillsdev/motif/releases), choosing the beta version named in your invitation. Beta downloads are marked as prereleases. Run Setup and follow the installer. It installs Motif for your Windows user and creates a Start menu shortcut. Launch **Motif** from that shortcut, then choose **Select new…** and browse to your FieldWorks `.fwdata` file. Motif reads your project and changes nothing in it until you choose **Apply to FieldWorks project**. Motif is a tech demo. Keep a FieldWorks backup and try it on a copy of your project first.

The official Windows release includes the matching PanGloss parser. You do not need to download PanGloss separately.

Motif keeps workflow records in a file beside the FieldWorks project: for `Koro.fwdata`, the file is `Koro.motif.db`. It stores selections, pending changes, and measurement metadata; it is not a saved copy of the FieldWorks project. Motif does not currently support moving an existing project workspace: the database is bound to the `.fwdata` path and refers to files stored separately. Keep the project at its original path. The `.motif.db` alone is not a complete backup; include the `.fwdata`, `.motif.db`, and Motif worker root, which holds file-backed Baselines and parser artifacts. On Windows, the worker root defaults to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SIL\Motif`; `MOTIF_WORKER_ROOT` can select another location.

Motif stops the PanGloss parser if it uses more memory than a limit, so one runaway word cannot take the rest of your computer's memory from other programs. The limit is 75% of the memory available to Motif (the container or cgroup limit when one applies). To change it, set the `MOTIF_PARSER_MEMORY_LIMIT` environment variable to a number of bytes, to a number with a binary suffix such as `12GiB`, or to `none`. `none` removes the limit; that is your choice to make, and while it is set one parser run can slow or crash everything else on the machine. Any other value is refused with a message naming the setting. A run stopped for passing the limit says so in its result; measure with fewer parser threads or a per-word parser work limit, or raise the limit.

Beta Windows builds may be unsigned. An unsigned Setup can show **Windows protected your PC** and **Unknown publisher**. Confirm that the version and download came from the Motif GitHub Releases page and match your invitation. If you trust that source, Windows may offer **More info** and then **Run anyway**; your organization's policy may prevent continuing. A signed build can also show a SmartScreen warning while it is new. If you cannot verify the download or Windows blocks it, ask the person running the trial for help. See [Microsoft's explanation of SmartScreen reputation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/package-and-deploy/smartscreen-reputation).

The same release offers preview downloads for Linux x64 and macOS with Apple silicon. On Linux, make the AppImage executable and run it. On macOS, extract the portable ZIP and open the Motif app. These previews are not notarized macOS distributions or a promise of support for every Linux distribution. If your system blocks the preview, report the message to the person running the trial. An Intel Mac preview is not included.

Save in FieldWorks before **Refresh**; Motif reads the last saved project and can do that while FieldWorks remains open. Close FieldWorks before **Apply to FieldWorks project**. Motif refuses Apply if FieldWorks still owns the project.

Before 1.0, incompatible Motif stores are refused rather than upgraded. A confirmed **Delete Motif's store and reopen** recreates a refused project store and loses changes not applied yet. For damaged project or machine stores, follow [the recovery instructions](guide:when-something-goes-wrong); remove only the identified Motif file, never the FieldWorks project.

Motif keeps a local usage log of command names and argument shapes, not the supplied values. It has no usage-upload feature. Motif reads writing systems from the project's own files and the shared writing-system repository and makes no online language-tag lookups unless you set `MOTIF_SLDR_ONLINE=1`, so a machine without a network opens and checks projects; a language-tag cache already on the machine from the SIL Locale Data Repository may still be read. **Report a problem** lets you review a report that excludes project and language data by default; optional local details and AI Handoff files can contain private data, so review them before sharing.

Automatic updates are not enabled; download and install a newer release yourself. Uninstalling Motif removes its installation and command registration while leaving your FieldWorks project and Motif data in place.

entries.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
entries.description: Inside text inputs, Ctrl+C/X/V and Ctrl+Z/Y use the control's own copy, cut, paste, undo and redo. Elsewhere, Ctrl+C copies selected text or the focused word, Ctrl+V does nothing, Ctrl+Z undoes the last staging action, and Ctrl+Y redoes it; on macOS use ⌘, with ⌘+Shift+Z also redoing. Letter shortcuts work when focus is outside text entry. A, D and U stage an opinion for Review Changes; Apply there writes it to the FieldWorks project. In Analyze texts, Delete stages removing the word's FieldWorks analysis, S stages Incorrect spelling, P opens the PanGloss analyses to add, and Shift+F10 opens the word's opinion tiles. In Analyze texts, Up and Down focus the first word on the previous or next line, Page Up and Page Down move by a screen of visible lines, and Home and End focus the first or last line of the Text. For the available display choices, see Settings.
