entries.title: Affixes, slots, and templates
entries.description: An affix is a meaningful piece attached to a stem. A prefix comes before it, a suffix after it, and an infix inside it. As illustrative English examples, un-happy shows a prefix and kind-ness a suffix. The Turkish form evler (“houses”) illustrates a suffix attached to ev (“house”).
entries.helpPage:
# Affixes, slots, and templates

An affix is a meaningful piece attached to a stem. A **prefix** comes before it, a **suffix** after it, and an **infix** inside it. As illustrative English examples, *un-happy* shows a prefix and *kind-ness* a suffix. The Turkish form *evler* (“houses”) illustrates a suffix attached to *ev* (“house”).

Languages often restrict which affixes can combine and in what order. A **slot** is a position in that sequence. For example, an illustrative verb pattern might allow a person marker before a tense marker. Putting the same affixes in the reverse order could produce a form the language does not use.

In FieldWorks, affix templates organize slots for a part of speech. A noun template can describe noun patterns, while a verb template can describe verb patterns. Some slots are obligatory: a valid word using that template must fill them. Others are optional and may be skipped. These settings help the parser avoid treating every affix as freely combinable with every word.

When a trace reaches the right stem but stops before the expected ending, check the relevant template. Is the affix in the right slot? Is the order right? Is the slot required or optional as intended? Does the template apply to this part of speech? Keep one known word that should use the pattern and one similar word that should not; both help you check whether the template says what you mean.

The examples here are illustrative and simplified. Real languages can have several templates, and a slot can allow more than one affix.

entries.title: Allomorphs and environments
entries.description: One meaningful piece can have more than one form. Those forms are allomorphs. The conditions that choose between them are their environments: the sounds or features around a form that make it fit.
entries.helpPage:
# Allomorphs and environments

One meaningful piece can have more than one form. Those forms are **allomorphs**. The conditions that choose between them are their **environments**: the sounds or features around a form that make it fit.

Turkish vowel harmony is a useful real-language example. The plural suffix has the forms *-lar* and *-ler*. In the standard pattern, *-lar* follows a stem with a back last vowel, as in *okullar* (“schools”), and *-ler* follows a stem with a front last vowel, as in *evler* (“houses”). The forms belong to the same plural pattern; the stem’s vowel helps select which one fits.

A **natural class** groups sounds by a shared property, such as “front vowels” or “voiceless consonants.” Instead of writing a separate environment for every vowel, a grammar can use a natural class when the same condition applies to that group. This can make a rule clearer and easier to check.

When the parser builds the stem but cannot use the expected affix form, compare the allomorphs and their environments. Does the needed form exist? Does its environment mention the right sounds or features? Is the environment too narrow, so it misses a valid word, or too broad, so it allows the form where it does not belong?

The Turkish forms illustrate a common pattern; they are not a full account of Turkish. Real patterns may depend on additional features and exceptions.

entries.title: Help the parser work with your language
entries.description: You know the words and patterns of your language. A parser does not. It follows the lexicon and rules someone entered for it, one step at a time. An AI consultant may help you work out which parser setting to inspect; Motif gives both of you evidence about what happened.
entries.helpPage:
# Help the parser work with your language

You know the words and patterns of your language. A parser does not. It follows the lexicon and rules someone entered for it, one step at a time. An AI consultant may help you work out which parser setting to inspect; Motif gives both of you evidence about what happened.

The work is a loop:

1. **Measure.** Save your FieldWorks work, choose **Refresh**, then choose [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to measure words you care about. [Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) tells you how much of the chosen material parsed.
2. **Understand.** Try a difficult word in **Try a Word**. Read the parser’s furthest attempt, then follow its steps to see what it built and where it stopped. Use **Timing** when words take a long time.
3. **Fix.** Use your language knowledge to check the likely cause. Make any grammar or lexicon change in FieldWorks, save it, then choose **Refresh** and **Parse all words** to measure again.

Motif's synthetic samples are generated to demonstrate its tools and give us small, safe places to practise. They are synthetic-turkic (Turkish-style), synthetic-bantu (Swahili-style), and synthetic-philippine (Tagalog-style), each modelled loosely on the named language. Their data are invented: they are not real language data and must not be used as descriptions of Turkish, Swahili, Tagalog, or any language.

You do not need to become a parser engineer to take part. You can tell an AI consultant what a word should mean and how it is built. Ask it to connect that analysis to the trace, suggest one small change, and name other words that should test the idea. Then check the suggestion against your language knowledge and Motif’s evidence. The AI can help with the machinery; it cannot decide what is right in your language.

entries.title: Modelling grammar in FieldWorks
entries.description: Start with the patterns you want your grammar to describe. Write down what each part means, then compare that account with forms and contrasts in the language.
entries.helpPage:
# Modelling grammar in FieldWorks

Start with the patterns you want your grammar to describe. Write down what each part means, then compare that account with forms and contrasts in the language.

## Start from the language

Write down what each part of your grammar means before you enter it: "the plural is *-ler* after front vowels and *-lar* after back vowels." Use examples from the language to check whether that description fits, including forms that show where the pattern does and does not occur.

## Sounds and spellings

Spelling and sound do not always line up one to one. When a pattern depends on a sound contrast, describe that contrast in the language and consider how the writing system represents it.

## Environments

An environment such as `/ [V] _` describes where an allomorph occurs. Use examples to identify the sounds or features around it, including contexts where a different form occurs.

## Allomorph order

When several allomorphs of one morpheme could fit, the first eligible one wins and blocks the rest. Put the most specific allomorph first and the general one last.

## Slots and templates

An inflectional template describes an order of affix slots. Decide which sequences occur in the language and which positions are optional, then compare the template with forms that illustrate those patterns.

## Features and classes

Features, their values, and inflection classes link by reference, not by name: two things with the same name are not connected. A noun-class system can use both an inflection class and a feature value for each class, as the synthetic Bantu-style sample does, but test agreement on real words before you rely on it.

## When a grammar is slow

When a parse takes longer than expected, use [Timing](cmd:timing) after [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to inspect the time recorded on this computer. The Learn page **Why a grammar is slow** explains how to read Timing. Compare parser work when judging a grammar change.

## Change one thing at a time

After each change: save in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh**, then choose **Parse all words** before checking the words you expected to change, plus a few that shouldn't. One change per measurement tells you what each change did.

entries.title: Phonological rules
entries.description: When a sound alternation follows a regular pattern, a phonological rule can describe the change once instead of listing a separate form for every word. The choice depends on how the language works: some alternations are best represented with allomorphs, some with rules, and some with both.
entries.helpPage:
# Phonological rules

When a sound alternation follows a regular pattern, a phonological rule can describe the change once instead of listing a separate form for every word. The choice depends on how the language works: some alternations are best represented with allomorphs, some with rules, and some with both.

English plural endings give an illustrative example of a familiar sound pattern. The ending is usually pronounced with a voiceless [s] after a voiceless sound, as in *cats*, and with [z] after a voiced sound, as in *dogs*. After sibilant sounds, as in *buses*, an extra vowel is heard. These examples show how nearby sounds can affect the way an ending is pronounced; spelling alone does not show every sound detail.

A rule says what changes and in what environment. In plain words, one part of this pattern could be described as “make the ending voiced after a voiced sound.” A well-chosen rule covers the words that share that environment. A rule that is too broad can also change words you meant to leave alone, so check examples from both sides of the pattern.

Rule order matters when one rule changes something that another rule looks for. If Rule 1 creates the sound that Rule 2 needs to see, Rule 1 must apply first. If Rule 2 applies first, it cannot act on a sound that does not exist yet. When a trace shows an unexpected output, check both the rule’s environment and whether earlier rules have already changed the relevant sound.

You can change a rule after it exists: widen its environment, make an item in it optional or repeated, move it earlier or later, turn it off to see what the grammar does without it, or delete it. A rule's environment can name a word or morpheme boundary. Input and Output each hold up to eight phoneme or natural-class items in order; unequal lengths express shortening or lengthening, and an empty side means insertion or deletion.

## One rule, several outcomes

Wolff section 5.15 gives *kabukiran* and *kabukilan* from *bukid*: a lexically selected d alternates with r or l. A rule cannot express this free choice. A rule whose Output is a multi-member segment class does not choose a member. It applies only the features the members share, so the input segment keeps its own value for every feature the members differ on. An *l* stays *l* under {l,w}, and a [-lat] *d* becomes *r* under {r,l}. Only an input with no value for those features matches every member (fieldworks-parser-conformance#38). Give each attested variant as an alternate form of the stem on the same entry, so there are no duplicate lexical entries. Keep rules for obligatory changes, with a literal or feature-class Output and a required exception feature on the selected stem analysis. Tag only the analyses supported by the source; this does not license *saylan* merely because *sayran* exists. The same holds for *lalum/lawum*.

Several right-hand sides serve a different purpose: they are ordered cases within one rule. Each has its own Output, left and right contexts, required and excluded rule features, and optional input categories. The first applicable case wins at a matching site. Two identical environments with d → r first and d → l second do not give free variation: the first hides the second. For optional lexical alternatives in one environment, use an Output class with the intended members, then check both forms in a Trial.

[Author a sound rule](cmd:compose-author-phonological-rule) and [Edit a sound rule](cmd:compose-edit-phonological-rule) let you keep several ordered cases in one rule, with lexical applicability per case. Read `motif help guide:encoding/phonological-rules --full` for the intent shape, expected-current guards and lexical alternatives. Rule features restrict applicability; they do not create an implicit dialect or register model.

entries.title: Reading why a word fails
entries.description: Try a Word records the parser's search for one word. Enter it in Type any word..., choose Try it, and read the result. The word can be new; it does not have to occur in the project's texts or lexicon.
entries.helpPage:
# Reading why a word fails

**Try a Word** records the parser's search for one word. Enter it in **Type any word...**, choose **Try it**, and read the result. The word can be new; it does not have to occur in the project's texts or lexicon.

Start with the result and search status:

- **Parsed** means a completed search found an analysis.
- **No parse** with **Search complete** means the search finished without finding an analysis.
- **Search incomplete** means the search did not finish. Read its recorded stop reason; an unfinished search is not evidence that no analysis exists, even when the trace contains no analysis.
- **Nothing to parse** means the grammar's character table does not define a character in the word.

Read any **Analysis summaries** before the **Recorded trace**. Expand tree context to see the recorded events. Select an event to read its exact input, output, raw reason code and captured rejection operands. A rule that was **Tried** was not necessarily **Applied**. **Blocked** names the recorded event without identifying an unrecorded blocker or treating it as the whole word's failure.

**Reason not recorded** and **Rejection details not recorded** mark missing evidence. A raw reason code is separate from the actual features or environment the parser captured. Do not infer a responsible rule from a nearby rejection or assume that every failed path explains the word's result. One attempt may fail while another succeeds.

**Grammar source not recorded** means the page cannot establish the trace's source save. **FieldWorks word context unavailable** means its stored analyses and opinions are unavailable here; it does not mean FieldWorks has no analysis. Use **Analyze texts** on the result to read the word in its text. Use **Full derivation** for the complete recorded tree and filters. The diagnostic tools save the original trace independently of filters.

entries.title: Stems and the lexicon
entries.description: The lexicon is the grammar’s store of words and their linguistic information. A lexical entry may include a stem, a gloss that reminds you of its meaning, and a part of speech such as noun or verb. Those labels help the grammar decide which forms and patterns can apply.
entries.helpPage:
# Stems and the lexicon

The lexicon is the grammar’s store of words and their linguistic information. A lexical entry may include a stem, a gloss that reminds you of its meaning, and a part of speech such as noun or verb. Those labels help the grammar decide which forms and patterns can apply.

As an illustrative English example, *walk* is the stem, *to move on foot* is a possible gloss, and *verb* is its part of speech. The form *walked* can be built from that stem and a past-tense ending. A gloss is a short guide for people, not a complete definition or a promise that two languages divide meaning in the same way.

One of the most common causes of failure is a missing stem. If a grammar expects to start with *walk* but that stem is absent or entered under a different form, adding the ending rule will not give the parser a starting point. In a simplified, illustrative Turkish example, the stem *ev* (“house”) is needed before the grammar can analyse *evler* (“houses”) with the plural suffix.

When a word fails, compare the form you typed with the lexicon entry you expect. Check spelling and the relevant writing system, then check that the entry has the stem and part of speech your analysis requires. If the stem is there, move on to the affixes and rules that should build the rest of the word.

The examples here are illustrative; real entries and analyses depend on the language and the choices made in its FieldWorks project.

entries.title: What the parser knows
entries.description: A parser is literal. It sees the word you give it and searches using the lexicon, grammar, character information, and limits in the current Baseline. It does not know what you meant or guess a missing entry from the conversation.
entries.helpPage:
# What the parser knows

A parser is literal. It sees the word you give it and searches using the lexicon, grammar, character information, and limits in the current [Baseline](term:baseline). It does not know what you meant or guess a missing entry from the conversation.

A **parse** is an analysis the grammar can build for a word. As an illustrative English example, *cats* can be analysed as the stem *cat* plus the plural ending *-s*. The parser must find a matching stem and a permitted way to combine it with the ending. A word can have more than one possible analysis, and a completed search may find none.

“It doesn’t parse” describes the result for this word and saved grammar. To judge whether that grammar matches the language, compare the result with the forms and patterns speakers use.

First check whether the search completed. A completed search with **No parse** tells you the grammar did not produce a reading. **Search incomplete** means the parser stopped before finishing, so it cannot show that the grammar has no possible analysis. A search may stop at the work limit (its analysis-parser work limit or the derived work limit), at the time safety net or for another cause. If the record does not identify which it reached, Motif keeps that reason general. A word with a character missing from the grammar’s character table is a different case again.

The parser reports what its grammar allowed. You decide whether that grammar matches the language.

entries.title: Why a grammar is slow
entries.description: A grammar can find the right analysis and still make the parser do too much work. Optional slots, broad environments, duplicated affixes and empty affixes can each give it more paths to explore, but none of them is always costly: measure before you change anything.
entries.helpPage:
# Why a grammar is slow

A grammar can find the right analysis and still make the parser do too much work. Optional slots, broad environments, duplicated affixes and empty affixes can each give it more paths to explore, but none of them is always costly: measure before you change anything.

An optional slot lets the parser consider a form both with and without that slot. Broad environments let a rule apply in many places, creating more possible continuations. An empty affix adds no visible letters, so the parser can add it without consuming part of the word, though PanGloss often handles these cheaply: in the synthetic Bantu-style sample, 160 empty allomorphs added no measurable work. A duplicated real affix is different; there, copying one object marker into a second slot multiplied the work.

Use [Timing](cmd:timing) after [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to locate recorded parser work. **Timing** counts parser work first by kind of rule, then by rule, and then shows slow words. Start with **Slowest** or **All**, select a costly rule, and look at the words that use it. Timing reports where the work went; it does not record what caused it. Compare the words and grammar around a costly rule, then choose what to inspect.

Check that each optional slot is truly optional, each environment names the sounds it should, and each affix appears only once. Change one thing at a time and measure again. If a search stopped at the work limit, raise **Parser work limit** under **Re-run**; this also raises PanGloss's derived work limit. If it stopped at the time safety net, increase **Seconds per word** there. A timing result shows where work was spent, while your language knowledge helps decide whether the grammar can be made more specific.

entries.title: Working with an AI consultant
entries.description: You bring knowledge of the language. An AI consultant can help connect that knowledge to parser rules and FieldWorks settings. Motif adds evidence: AI Handoff writes a folder you can choose to share with a chat model. It contains selected project material and, when available, the results of Parse all words with a starter question. The folder can contain real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and sentences, so read the notice and share it only with a service you trust.
entries.helpPage:
# Working with an AI consultant

You bring knowledge of the language. An AI consultant can help connect that knowledge to parser rules and FieldWorks settings. Motif adds evidence: **AI Handoff** writes a folder you can choose to share with a chat model. It contains selected project material and, when available, the results of [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) with a starter question. The folder can contain real grammar rules, lexicon entries, and sentences, so read the notice and share it only with a service you trust.

Ask a focused question. For example: “This word should be stem plus plural. The trace stops at this affix. Which slot or environment would you check first? What evidence supports that, and what other words would distinguish your suggestion from an alternative?” Ask for one small proposed change and examples that should still fail. You can ask the AI to explain parser terminology, but check every claim about your language against what speakers say and use.

Treat the answer as a hypothesis, not an instruction. Check that it accounts for the failing word without breaking a known-good word. If you decide to change the grammar or lexicon, make the edit in FieldWorks, save, choose **Refresh**, then **Parse all words** before checking whether the expected words now parse.

**Review Changes** has a narrower role: it reviews pending analysis choices made in Motif. If the AI suggests choosing or changing an analysis for a word, make that choice through **Texts**, then open **Review Changes**. Inspect the word and action, choose **Check these changes** to measure their effect, and apply only if the changes still fit and the evidence is current. Review Changes does not import an AI answer or apply grammar edits; your judgement remains in charge.

entries.title: Opening a project
entries.description: Open the project menu and choose Select new… to browse for a FieldWorks .fwdata file. To return to another project Motif knows, choose Open recent and select it, or choose it from the list on the initial Choose a project page. The window opens on Overview and shows the results from the last run. Opening a project doesn't parse anything.
entries.helpPage:
# Opening a project

Open the project menu and choose **Select new…** to browse for a FieldWorks `.fwdata` file. To return to another project Motif knows, choose **Open recent** and select it, or choose it from the list on the initial **Choose a project** page. The window opens on **Overview** and shows the results from the last run. Opening a project doesn't parse anything.

On **Choose a project**, each recent row shows its recorded state and wordform count when those details are available. **Refresh needed** means the saved project is newer than those results. **Open folder** opens the folder containing the project without opening the project in Motif; you can reach the link with Tab and activate it with Enter.

You can also choose a FieldWorks backup, a `.fwbackup` file. Motif restores it into a new folder beside the backup, named after the project, and opens that copy, so the backup itself is never changed. If a folder of that name is already there, Motif uses the next free name, such as `Koro 2`, and leaves the earlier copy as it was.

If this project has no Baseline yet, Motif captures one when you open it and then opens setup. Later, press **Refresh** to read the project as FieldWorks last saved it. Save your latest edits in FieldWorks first if you want them included: unsaved edits in FieldWorks are not part of the file Motif reads. You do not have to close FieldWorks just to open a project. If another program is using the project, Refresh may say “the project 'Koro' is in use by another program” (using your project’s name); close the other program and try again.

On a new project, Motif captures the first Baseline and asks which words to measure. See [Choosing what to measure](guide:first-run-setup).

![A project open on the Overview](shot:open-project-overview/overview)

entries.title: Overview
entries.description: Overview is the first page you see. It shows the results of your last run: how many of your words parse, how many words with approved analyses were rebuilt exactly, which words are slow, and what the grammar check found. Opening it doesn't parse anything. Nothing here changes your FieldWorks project.
entries.helpPage:
# Overview

**Overview** is the first page you see. It shows the results of your last run: how many of your words parse, how many words with approved analyses were rebuilt exactly, which words are slow, and what the grammar check found. Opening it doesn't parse anything. Nothing here changes your FieldWorks project.

The figure strip shows the project's counts: words you chose to measure, places in your texts, wordforms, rules, and lexemes. **Look first** points to recorded words or timings worth inspecting, including the unparsed words you use most and entries with a stem not tagged with an inflection class. Up to seven table sections follow; a section appears when its measurements are available:

- **Speed**: how many words were measured, their total and median parser work, and the work recorded for each kind of grammar work.
- **Slowest Words**: the measured words with the most parser work, each with its parser work. **Stopped** marks a word explicitly recorded as hitting the work limit.
- **Text Coverage**: how many of your chosen words parse, and how many places in your texts they cover (each time a word occurs in a text). If no chosen words occur in the chosen Texts, it says there are no places to cover. A line beneath says how many places hold only digits or are written in other writing systems; those places are not in the share.
- **Text Coverage by Frequency Band**: the chosen words ranked by how often they occur, cut into ranks 1 to 100, 101 to 1,000, 1,001 to 10,000, and the rest. Each band says how many of its words parse and how many of its places are covered; the bands add up to the Text Coverage totals. A Selection that is not made of chosen Texts is titled **By Frequency Band**: its words are ranked by the counts in the word-list file it was saved from (see [Choose a Default Selection](cmd:selection%20set-default)), and a word the file gave no count ranks after the counted words and adds nothing to a band's occurrences. If some chosen words are not in the saved parse, a note says so.
- **Ambiguity**: the mean number of analyses per parsed word, how many parsed words have more than one analysis, and the ten with the most, each opening in Texts. Words that did not parse are not in it.
- **Approved Analyses Kept**: how many words with an approved analysis the grammar rebuilt exactly. When no analysis is approved yet, it says there is nothing to rebuild.
- **Grammar Warnings**: what the grammar check found, with errors counted separately.

The **Grammar Warnings** section gives the warning count and any nonzero error count. Its word line counts how many different chosen words exactly use an item named by a warning. Before parsing, it says **Parse to see which of your words they touch**. The table lists the three largest warning kinds. Where the evidence is complete, each kind shows the word count; matches based only on spelling are labelled separately. Open **Warnings →** to see each kind's subjects.

These are separate measures, not one overall score. The project's counts appear after you press **Refresh**, which also checks the grammar. **Speed**, **Text Coverage**, and **Approved Analyses Kept** show parse results after you choose **Parse all words**.

The project chip in the top bar says whether these numbers are current: a green, orange or red dot, the project name and, in a wide window, the status in words. Choose the chip to open the project card, which says what changed and when the words were last parsed. If you have saved in FieldWorks since the last Refresh, the card says when; the ⟳ beside the chip and the card's **Refresh** button read the saved project. Times use your local clock; a save from another day includes its weekday and date. Press **Refresh** to read the saved project, then **Parse all words** to measure your [chosen words](term:default-selection) again. If Motif cannot read the numbers, the page says so in one line, with **Try again** and **Report a problem**.

Choose a section's link, such as **Slowest Words →**, **Texts →**, **Matrix →**, or **Warnings →**, to see more on that page. The links stay visible. Each **Look first** row opens the words or timings it names; its word-count link stays visible. Choose a slow word to open it in Texts. The Overview Inspector shows recorded Lost words and shared morphemes; **Open in Matrix** opens those Approved words in the Matrix. Expand **Project history** to see recorded activity. For a closer explanation of each measure and how to read its breakdowns, see [Reading the Overview](guide:reading-the-overview).

![Overview showing the project's stored results](shot:open-project-overview/overview)

Words marked **can’t read** were sent to PanGloss, which declined them. They are separate from completed searches that found no analysis and from words with no recorded parse. Choose that segment to read those words and their recorded reasons.

entries.title: PanGloss
entries.description: On Analyze texts, PanGloss runs the project's grammar on selected texts and compares its analyses with what FieldWorks stores.
entries.helpPage:
# PanGloss

On Analyze texts, PanGloss runs the project's grammar on selected texts and compares its analyses with what FieldWorks stores.

PanGloss parses the project's grammar. Motif records parser warnings and refusals alongside the results.

For a FieldWorks Opinion, A means Approved, U means Unknown, and D means Disapproved. An empty dashed box in the FieldWorks Opinion position means no analysis is stored. In Analyze texts, ≠ with a solid underline marks a new or different PanGloss result; ∅ with a dashed underline means no parse, and ◖ with a dotted underline means a stopped search. These PanGloss cues are separate from the FieldWorks Opinion, and their glyphs and line styles carry meaning alongside color. Staged means a choice is waiting for Apply to FieldWorks project.

![The compact word strip for geldi](shot:explained-word-card/approved-agrees)

entries.title: Parsimony
entries.description: The Parsimony page lists grammar-tidiness findings from the latest stored check of the grammar. Each finding names what was counted and how strong the evidence is. The page reads what the check stored. Opening it, or coming back to it, never starts a check, and it writes nothing to the project.
entries.helpPage:
# Parsimony

The **Parsimony** page lists grammar-tidiness findings from the latest stored check of the grammar. Each finding names what was counted and how strong the evidence is. The page reads what the check stored. Opening it, or coming back to it, never starts a check, and it writes nothing to the project.

Without a stored check, ask an AI assistant with Motif tools to run every Parsimony measure for this project, or run `motif parsimony --project "<project.fwdata>" --measure all --wait` in the CLI after replacing `<project.fwdata>` with the project file path. [Run every Parsimony measure](cmd:parsimony%20--measure%20all%20--wait) describes the command. Then come back here. Opening or returning to this page never starts a check.

The page has two tabs. **Active** lists the findings still to review. **Suppressed** lists the findings you kept or deferred, each with its reason, or with "No reason given" when you gave none. Each tab shows its count.

Findings are grouped by check. Each group names its grammar side: **Restrictiveness**, **Parsimony**, or both. A line under the tabs says once what each side means, and the page gives no combined score. A finding you have decided shows "staged, not yet applied" beside its decision until Apply writes it.

Select a finding to read its evidence in the detail column: what was counted, the items it names, why it was reported, the strength of the evidence, whether a paired parser check has run, and the limits of the count. A finding is a suggestion to look at, not a verdict on the grammar.

## Deciding a finding

Select an active finding. Its detail column has **Keep**, **Defer** and **Ask** buttons, and a note about **Fix**:

- **Keep** records that the finding is intended. You may write a reason. A kept finding moves to Suppressed once Apply and Refresh have run.
- **Defer** records that you will come back to the finding later. Like Keep, it takes an optional reason and moves to Suppressed once applied.
- **Ask** records a question about the finding. It needs the question you write. It stays active, because a question is not a decision to suppress.
- **Fix** is not a button. A note under the buttons names the Guide page that describes the update Motif supports for the check, and says you make the fix itself in FieldWorks. It records nothing. Where a check has no supported update yet, the note says so, and you can ask or defer instead.

When there are several Notebook record types, choose the one the decision goes under. The page never picks one by its English name.

Each action is staged in pending changes. The Parsimony page links to [Review Changes](guide:review-changes), where you can inspect the staged decision and use Apply. Nothing is written to FieldWorks until Apply. A staged decision shows as staged, not as suppressed. Refresh after Apply to see the decision in Suppressed.

## Suppressed decisions

A Suppressed decision stays in its own tab with its reason, its judgment ID (such as `MJ-7K3Q-9XDF`) and the title of its Notebook record, so you can match the row to the record in FieldWorks. Select it to read its details; that only shows them. **Return to Active** stages the withdrawal of the decision, so the finding comes back to the Active tab once Apply and Refresh have run.

A decision returns to Active on its own when the evidence it was made on changes. It then shows "Changed since it was kept" or "Changed since it was deferred" with the reason you gave before, so you can decide again. A Motif update that changes how a check reads its evidence can bring a kept or deferred finding back once in the same way, even though nothing in the grammar changed; the release notes say when an update does this.

A decision that conflicts with another, or that no longer matches any finding, stays visible and is not hidden. A conflict stays in Active and says what conflicts. A stale decision in Suppressed says that no current finding matches it.

Edit the reason in FieldWorks, in the Description of the judgment's record after the first sentence. Leave the sentence, the ID and the field named "Motif data (do not edit)" alone. If the data field is edited, the page lists that record as "hash failed on this record entry", and its decision stops suppressing the finding until it is recorded again. A changed ID or sentence only produces a warning, and the decision still applies.

If the stored check could not measure some of its checks, the page names them under **Not measured** and explains why. Those checks' findings are not listed. If the check was made from an earlier [Baseline](term:baseline), the page says so. Measure the grammar again to see current findings.

entries.title: Prohibitions could state order
entries.description: A slot order can replace repeated prohibitions only when it preserves their intended effect. Some restrictions express limits that order cannot capture.
entries.helpPage:
# Prohibitions could state order

A slot order can replace repeated prohibitions only when it preserves their intended effect. Some restrictions express limits that order cannot capture.

## Analyse

Read the complete flat prohibitions, exact targets, loader state, applicable template placements, and contrary Approved sequences. This measure's report shows whether grouped provenance is complete, but does not show group names, members, or rationale; read those in FieldWorks before deciding.

## Disposition

Fix only a same-side order that is entailed across every applicable placement and has no contrary Approved sequence. Keep confirmed adjacency-only, Anywhere, multi-target, person-hierarchy, cross-side, and other contextual restrictions with their reason. Ask whether intervening affixes are allowed when a rule forbids adjacency. Defer a grouped change when `adhoc_groups` is incomplete, or when target, loader, hierarchy, or order evidence is incomplete.

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether one affix must precede another even with an intervening affix, or whether only immediate adjacency is forbidden. For a person-hierarchy or other contextual restriction, confirm that a single order applies throughout the relevant categories and templates.

## Update

Use `EditAffixTemplate` to change an existing order, or `AuthorAffixTemplate` to state a new one. If the order needs a new slot, use `AuthorAffixSlot` and `EditInflectionalAffix` to place the affixes. Then use `EditAdhocProhibition` to disable each exact concrete prohibition that the new order replaces. Keep adjacency-only, Anywhere, multi-target, hierarchy, and other nonordering rules enabled unless their linguist-approved intent is also represented.

## Verify

Finalize the changes not applied yet as one set and run its Dry Run. Compare parser runs from before and after the edit with the same parser and settings. Confirm every existing Approved reading remains, each reviewed negative and Disapproved swap stays unparsed, and held-out forms remain. Read back the authored order and exact disabled rule identities. Confirm retained rules remain enabled with their original targets. The group itself is not the edit target, and this measure's report does not surface its rationale.

## Grounding

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Technical documents index](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Describes ordered, conjunctive prohibition targets and grouping rationales.
- **[ryan-2010]** — Kevin M. Ryan. 2010. “Variable Affix Order: Grammar and Learning.” *Language* 86(4):758–791. DOI: 10.1353/lan.2010.0032. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1353/lan.2010.0032). Shows affix ordering can be variable, nontransitive, or context-sensitive.
- **[stump-1993]** — Gregory T. Stump. 1993. “Position Classes and Morphological Theory.” *Yearbook of Morphology 1992*, 129–180. DOI: 10.1007/978-94-017-3710-4_7. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-017-3710-4_7). Cautions that position classes and linear ordering need not be the same representation.
- **[bender-poulson-drellishak-evans-2007]** — Emily M. Bender, Laurie Poulson, Scott Drellishak, and Chris Evans. 2007. “Validation and Regression Testing for a Cross-linguistic Grammar Resource.” In *ACL 2007 Workshop on Deep Linguistic Processing*, 136–143. Association for Computational Linguistics. [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/W07-1218/). Supports paired regression checks when replacing grammar constraints.

Exact entailment and the pair-family trigger are engineering checks over loaded identities and templates; adjacency is stronger than precedence. The current report does not read group rationale, and a completed `adhoc_groups` section establishes availability only.

entries.title: A zero affix may add no value
entries.description: Remove a zero affix only when it adds no grammatical distinction and no Approved reading depends on its identity. Keep meaningful zero morphology and explain what it contributes.
entries.helpPage:
# A zero affix may add no value

Remove a zero affix only when it adds no grammatical distinction and no Approved reading depends on its identity. Keep meaningful zero morphology and explain what it contributes.

## Analyse

Read `null-optional`, the authored form and its compiler record, feature and class contributions, slot optionality, senses, and incoming references. Count a null marker only when PanGloss facts show a final ordinary morphology output for its MSA; an import record alone is not proof. An empty string or a dropped or compacted marker alone does not establish a loaded zero.

## Disposition

If the zero contributes a feature, class restriction, or Approved reading, record a `keep` disposition with a reason. Ask about an unclear grammatical distinction or default interpretation. Defer when the compiler did not record the authored marker as represented.

Do not stage a zero-retirement change for a meaningful or referenced zero.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the zero contributes a feature or distinct reading, or only permits an already optional slot to be empty. Show its feature chart and incoming reference count.

## Update

For an unreferenced, featureless zero in an optional slot, use `RetireRedundantZeroAffix`. The operation accepts one ordinary primary prefix or suffix with no alternate forms. It removes the whole entry graph, including its senses, MSA, allomorphs, and last primary form, as one operation; deleting every owned object together makes removal of that final form safe. The optional slot and any template that uses it remain.

## Verify

Run Dry Run, then compare parser results from the current and edited scratch copies. Every existing Approved reading and each absence word must keep the same result, and reviewed negative examples must still have no parser reading. Confirm that the optional slot remains and grammar health has no errors. The count for this measure must fall because the authored graph was removed, not because the loader dropped its marker.

## Grounding

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Technical documents index](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Distinguishes optional slots from null affixes, including cases where a zero expresses a feature.
- **[becker-2024]** — Laura Becker. 2024. “Zero Marking in Inflection: A Token-Based Approach.” *Journal of Language Modelling* 12(2):349–413. DOI: 10.15398/jlm.v12i2.361. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.15398/jlm.v12i2.361). Treats zero marking as an analytical issue in inflection.
- **[alekseeva-myachykov-shtyrov-2022]** — Maria Alekseeva, Andriy Myachykov, and Yury Shtyrov. 2022. “Inflectional zero morphology – Linguistic myth or neurocognitive reality?” *Frontiers in Psychology* 13:1015435. DOI: 10.3389/fpsyg.2022.1015435. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.1015435). Reviews the debate about zero morphology and supports caution about blanket deletion.

The zero-realization classifier and cleanup eligibility are engineering checks; verify feature effects, references, and analyses for each affix it lists.

entries.title: An affix has no position
entries.description: Attested sequences can suggest where an affix belongs, but the linguist chooses its position class. Distance from a root is evidence, not a slot identity.
entries.helpPage:
# An affix has no position

Attested sequences can suggest where an affix belongs, but the linguist chooses its position class. Distance from a root is evidence, not a slot identity.

## Analyse

Review category and membership facts, Approved sequences, position histograms, and any contradictory precedence witnesses.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Fix a supported missing position; keep an intentional partial rule; ask when orders conflict; defer uncertain roots or thin evidence.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the witnessed order is required and whether the affix shares a position with another affix. Show the cited forms.

## Update

For an existing, compatible position, use `EditInflectionalAffix` to assign the affix's existing analysis to that slot. If the linguist chooses a new position, use `AuthorAffixSlot` and then assign the analysis with `EditInflectionalAffix`. Use `AuthorAffixTemplate` to add an explicit order or `EditAffixTemplate` to change an existing order. Root distance suggests a position to ask about; it does not identify a slot. Change optionality with `EditAffixSlot` only when the evidence supports absence.

## Verify

Use Review Changes to inspect what the edit would write. Compare parser results from the current and edited project for the same words. Confirm the target reading's before and after presence and that the affected unslotted count is zero. Check exact Approved readings, including held-out readings, and look for reviewed swaps or double fills that become accepted. If a reading is lost, a new negative is accepted, parser results are incomplete, or `rooted-morph` is unavailable, name that gap and leave the repair unverified.

## Grounding

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Technical documents index](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Describes templates, slots, and position concepts used to analyze affix placement.
- **[stump-1993]** — Gregory T. Stump. 1993. “Position Classes and Morphological Theory.” *Yearbook of Morphology 1992*, 129–180. DOI: 10.1007/978-94-017-3710-4_7. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-017-3710-4_7). Shows that position classes have competing analyses and must be established from distribution and morphological structure.
- **[durrett-deniro-2013]** — Greg Durrett and John DeNero. 2013. “Supervised Learning of Complete Morphological Paradigms.” In *Proceedings of NAACL-HLT 2013*, 1185–1195. Association for Computational Linguistics. [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/N13-1138/). Shows how paradigm evidence can support recurring form relations.
- **[kibrik-2005]** — Andrej A. Kibrik. 2005. “Inflection versus Derivation and the Template for Athabaskan Verb Morphology.” In Suzanne Gessner (ed.), *Alaska Native Language Center Working Papers 5: Proceedings of the 2005 Athabaskan Languages Conference*, 67–94. Fairbanks: Alaska Native Language Center. [Author-hosted paper](https://iling-ran.ru/kibrik/Inflection_derivation_template_Athabaskan%40ANLC_2005.pdf). Examines position variation and mixed morphological behavior in Athabaskan template analyses.
- **[ahlberg-forsberg-hulden-2015]** — Malin Ahlberg, Markus Forsberg, and Mans Hulden. 2015. “Paradigm classification in supervised learning of morphology.” In *Proceedings of NAACL-HLT 2015*, 1024–1029. Association for Computational Linguistics. DOI: 10.3115/v1/N15-1107. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3115/v1/N15-1107). Supports organizing form evidence by recurring paradigm behavior.

Motif's support floor and root-distance statistic prioritize questions; the cited work does not prescribe those cutoffs or assign FieldWorks slots.

entries.title: Repeated ad hoc restrictions
entries.description: Several prohibitions may encode the same parser restriction. Keep one supported statement and verify that the bounded cleanup preserves readings.
entries.helpPage:
# Repeated ad hoc restrictions

Several prohibitions may encode the same parser restriction. Keep one supported statement and verify that the bounded cleanup preserves readings.

## Analyse

Compare the full ordered targets, active load facts, descriptions, and witness cases. Choose the retained identity explicitly.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Fix only when the active signatures are identical and useful rationale remains. Keep, ask, or defer when group loading or target expansion is incomplete.

## Ask the linguist

Ask which wording should remain and whether both statements carry different linguistic explanations.

## Update

Disable only the confirmed duplicate. Do not delete either object or rewrite its target list.

## Verify

Confirm the duplicate count falls, the retained rule remains loaded, and completed parse readings stay equal. If `grouped-adhoc-load` is unavailable, name it and defer.

## Grounding

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Technical documents index](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Supports treating ad hoc prohibitions as a fallback and preserving their ordered, conjunctive targets.
- **[bender-poulson-drellishak-evans-2007]** — Emily M. Bender, Laurie Poulson, Scott Drellishak, and Chris Evans. 2007. “Validation and Regression Testing for a Cross-linguistic Grammar Resource.” In *ACL 2007 Workshop on Deep Linguistic Processing*, 136–143. Association for Computational Linguistics. [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/W07-1218/). Supports checking grammar outcomes with regression examples after a proposed cleanup.

The exact-signature trigger is an engineering lint; it does not establish that two authored prohibitions have identical parser effects.

entries.title: Listed shapes share a rule
entries.description: Repeated listed shapes can point to one sound change when their segment identities, conditions, and grammatical categories agree. This static report gives a lead to review; it is not evidence that a sound change is productive.
entries.helpPage:
# Listed shapes share a rule

Repeated listed shapes can point to one sound change when their segment identities, conditions, and grammatical categories agree. This static report gives a lead to review; it is not evidence that a sound change is productive.

## Analyse

Read `alternation-families` for the segment alignments and feature changes, independent morphemes, normalized conditions, the compiler's allomorph gates, and nearby rule limitations. Read each member's allomorph context to inspect its listed forms. Text and parser counts are unavailable in this static measure.

The `feature-weighted` lane reports feature changes only when the needed feature vectors are complete. The `segment-identity` lane records an equal-length pair that differs at exactly one phoneme identity; it reports the exact phoneme identities without feature changes or a generalized target. A whole allomorph form of `^0`, `*0`, `&0`, or `∅` is treated as empty. The limitations include abstention counts by reason, including forms that cannot be tokenized from the project's phoneme inventory.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Fix a confirmed sound rule; keep morphology, suppletion, or free variation; ask about direction and ordering; defer unsupported patterns.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the change extends to held-out contexts and how the replacement maps each old identity. Include referenced forms.

## Update

For a confirmed, supported phonological route, use `RetireAllomorph` with its `motif-allomorph-retirement` intent to create the bounded rule, explicitly map and retarget referenced allomorphs, and retire the redundant shapes, together, as changes not applied yet. `AuthorPhonologicalRule` authors a rule on its own.

## Verify

After a supported rule and explicit allomorph mapping are authored as changes not applied yet, run a Trial to preserve mapped and unchanged Approved readings and test held-out forms in both directions. The static report cannot verify those outcomes; defer when direction, context, or rule interactions remain unresolved. If Motif cannot map a written form to this project's sound inventory, name that gap and defer.

## Grounding

- **[chomsky-halle-1968]** — Noam Chomsky and Morris Halle. 1968. *The Sound Pattern of English*. New York: Harper & Row. [MIT Press publisher record](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262530972/the-sound-pattern-of-english/). Offers a notation-specific grammar-economy metric; Rasin et al. identify its aim as grammar economy.
- **[albright-hayes-2003]** — Adam Albright and Bruce Hayes. 2003. “Rules vs. Analogy in English Past Tenses: A Computational/Experimental Study.” *Cognition* 90(2):119–161. DOI: 10.1016/S0010-0277(03)00146-X. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0010-0277(03)00146-X). Supports forming feature-sensitive possible phonological rules from alternations and checking their scope.
- **[ellison-1994]** — T. Mark Ellison. 1994. “Constraints, Exceptions and Representations.” In *Computational Phonology*, SIGMORPHON 1994, 25–32. Association for Computational Linguistics. [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/W94-0203/). Discusses recovering conditioned allomorphs from a shared representation while preserving correct variants.
- **[lan-rasin-katzir-2019]** — Nur Lan, Ezer Rasin, and Roni Katzir. 2019. “Learning Morpho-phonology Using a Genetic Algorithm.” In *Proceedings of the Genetic and Evolutionary Computation Conference (GECCO ’19)*, Prague, July 13–17. [Author-hosted paper](https://www.cs.tau.ac.il/~nurlan/files/Lan_Rasin_Katzir_Learning_Morpho-Phonology_Using_a_Genetic_Algorithm_2018_v1.pdf). Gives a morphophonology learner that trades grammar complexity against data fit.
- **[rasin-berger-lan-katzir-2018]** — Ezer Rasin, Iddo Berger, Nur Lan, and Roni Katzir. 2018. “Learning Rule-Based Morpho-Phonology.” Manuscript, MIT and Tel Aviv University, 19 June 2018. [Manuscript PDF](https://taucompling.github.io/papers/RasinBergerLanKatzir%202018%20Learning%20rule-based%20morpho-phonology.pdf). Contrasts grammar economy with data fit and shows that shorter grammars can overgenerate.

This recipe suggests possible rules; its alignment costs, family key, and recurrence trigger are Motif engineering choices, not one published learner's algorithm.

entries.title: Repeated allomorph forms
entries.description: This check finds non-abstract allomorphs of one entry with the same morph type, the same forms in every writing system, and the same environment list. Different environment lists are excluded from this finding.
entries.helpPage:
# Repeated allomorph forms

This check finds non-abstract allomorphs of one entry with the same morph type, the same forms in every writing system, and the same environment list. Different environment lists are excluded from this finding.

## Analyse

Read the entry, duplicate allomorph GUIDs, forms, morph type, and exact environment lists in `allomorph-context`. Confirm the matching fields; no similarity or language-wide generalization is inferred.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Classify the result as exact data duplication. Keep both records when each carries identity or history worth preserving; ask or defer when that distinction is unclear.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether both records are intentionally maintained despite having identical forms and conditions. Include the entry and every duplicate GUID.

## Update

Retire a duplicate only through an operation that preserves and retargets its Approved analyses. If that operation is unavailable, keep the records and defer the change.

## Verify

Confirm the exact duplicate group is gone and every retargeted Approved reading remains unchanged. Compare before and after evidence for the same Baseline scope.

## Grounding

Engineering check: exact redundancy in the authored grammar; no linguistic claim.

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Source](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Describes allomorph environments and ordered alternatives, without establishing that any duplicate is linguistically redundant.

entries.title: Subsumed allomorph forms
entries.description: This check finds an entry whose allomorphs repeat the same morph type and forms with different environment lists, where one copy's conditions are already covered by another: one copy has no environment, one list is a subset of the other, or both list the same environments in another order. Copies with disjoint or partly overlapping lists are not reported, because different environments for one form are a legitimate disjunction. Copies with identical environment lists belong to the repeated-forms check, and allomorphs without forms are skipped.
entries.helpPage:
# Subsumed allomorph forms

This check finds an entry whose allomorphs repeat the same morph type and forms with different environment lists, where one copy's conditions are already covered by another: one copy has no environment, one list is a subset of the other, or both list the same environments in another order. Copies with disjoint or partly overlapping lists are not reported, because different environments for one form are a legitimate disjunction. Copies with identical environment lists belong to the repeated-forms check, and allomorphs without forms are skipped.

## Analyse

Read the entry, the member allomorph GUIDs, their forms and their environment lists in `allomorph-context`. The finding says, per repeated form, which copy subsumes which. An unconditioned copy applies in every context, so a conditioned copy of the same form adds nothing the parser can use. An environment list that is a subset of another's is covered by it.

## Disposition

This finding has no closed Notebook subject, so it cannot be recorded with a disposition yet. Note the decision in the review conversation instead.

Classify the result as redundant conditioning, or as an intended restriction that the unconditioned copy has made moot.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the conditioned copy is meant to be the only one allowed in its context, in which case the unconditioned copy is too broad. Include the entry and every member GUID.

## Update

No typed action is available for this finding. If the conditioned copy is redundant, retire it by hand; if the unconditioned copy is too broad, give it the environment the conditioned copy was meant to carry.

## Verify

Re-run the check and confirm the entry is gone while every Approved reading that used either copy is unchanged.

## Grounding

Black 2018 describes allomorph environments as the conditions under which an allomorph applies, and an allomorph with none as applying wherever its morpheme does.

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Source](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Describes allomorph environments and ordered alternatives; the subsumption reading of repeated forms is this check's own.

entries.title: Duplicate or clone entries
entries.description: This check finds lexical entries that say the same thing twice. Entries are compared by their hyphen-trimmed form and morph type class. Two kinds of group are reported. A duplicate group holds entries whose gloss sets and MSA signatures (kind, categories with their from and to roles, and slots) are equal. A clone group is one clone entry listed first, followed by only the same-form homographs whose glosses it extends: every gloss of the clone is a gloss of that homograph plus a dotted suffix, or the capitalised form plus a dotted suffix, a clone made only to carry a feature. Each clone is its own group, so two clones of one entry give two findings. A clone whose glosses are all the capitalised form plus a dotted suffix names no homograph, so its group holds the clone alone. Entries whose lexeme form has no form text, such as a reduplication entered twice, are grouped by morph type class, glosses and MSA signature alone.
entries.helpPage:
# Duplicate or clone entries

This check finds lexical entries that say the same thing twice. Entries are compared by their hyphen-trimmed form and morph type class. Two kinds of group are reported. A duplicate group holds entries whose gloss sets and MSA signatures (kind, categories with their from and to roles, and slots) are equal. A clone group is one clone entry listed first, followed by only the same-form homographs whose glosses it extends: every gloss of the clone is a gloss of that homograph plus a dotted suffix, or the capitalised form plus a dotted suffix, a clone made only to carry a feature. Each clone is its own group, so two clones of one entry give two findings. A clone whose glosses are all the capitalised form plus a dotted suffix names no homograph, so its group holds the clone alone. Entries whose lexeme form has no form text, such as a reduplication entered twice, are grouped by morph type class, glosses and MSA signature alone.

## Analyse

Read each member's lexeme form in `allomorph-context` and compare the group's glosses and MSAs. A pair that differs only by a trailing hyphen, such as `xy` and `xy-`, is one entry typed twice when the morph type class is the same. Homographs with different glosses or categories, such as an inflectional and a derivational `-a`, are not reported. A dotted suffix on the gloss of a same-form homograph can also be a real distinction, such as a person or number label and its extension (`1` and `1.SG`), so check the member's MSA and the feature it carries before treating it as a copy.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

No disposition mapping exists for this finding yet, so it cannot be recorded with a Notebook disposition. Note the decision in the review instead.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the entries are one morpheme entered twice or two morphemes that happen to share a form. For a clone, ask which feature the clone carries and whether an exception feature or an inflection class on one entry would carry it instead. Include every member's identity.

## Update

No typed action is available for this finding. Merge the entries in FieldWorks, keeping one MSA per distinct reading, or retarget the clone's feature.

## Verify

Re-run the check and confirm that the group is gone and that no Approved reading changed.

## Grounding

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Source](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Advises against giving two morphemes the same gloss on purpose and treats one morpheme with several orthographic allomorphs as one entry; it does not decide any given pair, so the finding asks rather than concludes.

entries.title: Duplicate environments
entries.description: This check finds sets of two or more environments whose left sides match and whose right sides match, token for token. Spacing and class names do not matter, so /   l and /  l are the same environment. Each finding names every environment in the set and every allomorph that uses each copy.
entries.helpPage:
# Duplicate environments

This check finds sets of two or more environments whose left sides match and whose right sides match, token for token. Spacing and class names do not matter, so `/  _ l` and `/ _ l` are the same environment. Each finding names every environment in the set and every allomorph that uses each copy.

## Analyse

Read `statement-usage` for each environment in the set and `allomorph-context` for each allomorph that names one. An allomorph uses an environment as a phone environment or as an infix Position; both count. Environments that did not parse as valid are left out of the comparison and the finding says how many. Equal keys show the copies mean the same thing to the parser; they do not show the copies were meant to be one.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

This finding has no closed Notebook subject mapping yet, so it cannot be recorded with a disposition. Read it as a review prompt.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the copies are kept apart on purpose, for example because different people maintain them. Include each environment, its text and the allomorphs that use it.

## Update

No typed action merges environments yet. Relink the allomorphs of each extra copy to one environment in FieldWorks, then retire the unused copies. An environment that an allomorph uses only as an infix Position still needs relinking.

## Verify

Re-run the check and confirm the set is gone while every allomorph keeps an environment with the same sides.

## Grounding

Engineering check: exact redundancy in the authored grammar; no linguistic claim.

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Source](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Describes how environments condition allomorphs, without establishing that any duplicate is linguistically redundant.

entries.title: Literal host contexts
entries.description: This check finds an environment side or a phonological rule context made only of literal segments: no natural class, variable, repetition or option. A side is flagged when it spells three or more segments, or two or more segments next to a word anchor, a morpheme boundary or an affix hyphen. / # w o r d  is the shape: it limits an allomorph to one host word, which is a lexical listing written as phonology. Each finding names the environment or rule and every allomorph that uses the environment.
entries.helpPage:
# Literal host contexts

This check finds an environment side or a phonological rule context made only of literal segments: no natural class, variable, repetition or option. A side is flagged when it spells three or more segments, or two or more segments next to a word anchor, a morpheme boundary or an affix hyphen. `/ # w o r d _` is the shape: it limits an allomorph to one host word, which is a lexical listing written as phonology. Each finding names the environment or rule and every allomorph that uses the environment.

## Analyse

Read `statement-usage` for the environment and `allomorph-context` for each allomorph that names it. A rule context has no view; the finding names the rule, its right-hand side and the segments. Boundaries are not counted as segments: a word anchor, a morpheme boundary and a segment spelled without a letter or digit, such as the hyphen of an affix, all count as boundaries. Sides with a class, a variable or a repetition are never flagged, nor are one-segment sides.

entries.title: Features with few carriers
entries.description: This check finds exception features that fewer than four entries carry on stem MSAs, yet that an affix MSA requires or a phonological rule uses. An exception feature restricts an affix or rule to the stems that carry it. When only one to three stems carry it, the restriction lists words instead of describing a productive pattern. A feature with no carrier at all, and no affix or rule that uses it, is left to unused-statement reporting.
entries.helpPage:
# Features with few carriers

This check finds exception features that fewer than four entries carry on stem MSAs, yet that an affix MSA requires or a phonological rule uses. An exception feature restricts an affix or rule to the stems that carry it. When only one to three stems carry it, the restriction lists words instead of describing a productive pattern. A feature with no carrier at all, and no affix or rule that uses it, is left to unused-statement reporting.

## Analyse

Read the finding: it names the carrier entries, the affix MSAs that require the feature, and the rules that require or exclude it. Open each requiring MSA with `affix-context`. A rule that uses a feature with exactly one carrier is a rule that applies to a single word. The finding also states how many of PanGloss's 64 feature slots the grammar uses (inflection classes including subclasses, exception features and entry inflection types), so a reader sees the headroom before adding another feature. The count is approximate where PanGloss dedupes differently.

## Disposition

This finding has no closed Notebook subject, so it cannot be recorded with a disposition yet. Note the decision in the review conversation instead.

Classify the result as a listed word, a genuine rare restriction, or a feature still being filled in. A feature with no carrier cannot restrict anything yet.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the affix is attested on only these stems and is not productive. Name the feature, its carriers, and every affix or rule that requires it.

## Update

No typed action is available for this finding. If the affix is not productive, the honest model is one lexical entry per attested word, each a complex form of its base, and the feature and its requirers go away. If it is productive, record a `defer` and fill in the carriers.

## Verify

Re-run the check and confirm the feature is gone or carried by four or more entries, and that every Approved reading that used the affix is unchanged.

## Grounding

Black 2018 describes exception features as a way to mark the stems on which an affix is wrong or right when no phonological or categorial property separates them; the listed alternative is a separate entry per word.

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Source](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Describes exception ("produce restriction") features on stems and affixes; the four-carrier threshold is this check's own.

entries.title: Gloss that echoes the form
entries.description: This check finds senses whose gloss is only the entry's form written in capitals: XYZ on xyz-, or the capitals followed by a dotted suffix (XYZ.V). Hyphens and = are ignored, and any allomorph form of the entry counts. A gloss that adds only a dotted suffix is the mark of a clone entry made to carry a feature. A gloss written in the same case as the form, such as a proper name or a loanword (radar on radar), is not reported, because it can be a real gloss.
entries.helpPage:
# Gloss that echoes the form

This check finds senses whose gloss is only the entry's form written in capitals: `XYZ` on `xyz-`, or the capitals followed by a dotted suffix (`XYZ.V`). Hyphens and `=` are ignored, and any allomorph form of the entry counts. A gloss that adds only a dotted suffix is the mark of a clone entry made to carry a feature. A gloss written in the same case as the form, such as a proper name or a loanword (`radar` on `radar`), is not reported, because it can be a real gloss.

## Analyse

entries.title: Stem with no part of speech
entries.description: This check finds stem MSAs that name no part of speech. A stem with no category takes no affix that is restricted to a category, so a linguist meets it as an unexplained gap. Each finding names the entry and says whether its senses have glosses: an entry with no glosses is usually a stub, and one with glosses is usually missing its category.
entries.helpPage:
# Stem with no part of speech

This check finds stem MSAs that name no part of speech. A stem with no category takes no affix that is restricted to a category, so a linguist meets it as an unexplained gap. Each finding names the entry and says whether its senses have glosses: an entry with no glosses is usually a stub, and one with glosses is usually missing its category.

## Analyse

Read the MSA in `affix-context` to confirm that it has no category. Then read the entry's senses: if none has a gloss, the entry is a stub left from an import or a first pass; if some do, the entry was analysed but never given a part of speech. Count only stem MSAs; inflectional and derivational MSAs name their categories in other roles and are not read here.

## Disposition

entries.title: Unused grammar statements
entries.description: This check finds environments and natural classes that the parser never applies. A statement is used when some grammar object applies it: an affix process, a rule context, an infix position, or an allomorph environment. A statement that no reference the parser applies is reported as unused, and its finding names the referrers that do not apply it.
entries.helpPage:
# Unused grammar statements

This check finds environments and natural classes that the parser never applies. A statement is used when some grammar object applies it: an affix process, a rule context, an infix position, or an allomorph environment. A statement that no reference the parser applies is reported as unused, and its finding names the referrers that do not apply it.

## Analyse

Read `statement-usage` for each statement's references and their parser effect. Every reference in the grammar facts counts, so a reference from an affix process, a rule context or an infix position is seen the same way as one from an allomorph environment. A statement is used for parsing when one reference is `applied`. A statement whose references are all not applied, such as `ignored`, `unresolved` or `owner_not_loaded`, is unused for parsing. A statement with no reference at all is unused. The finding names each referrer that does not apply it.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

A statement with an applied reference is used for parsing and is never reported here. An unused statement that only references the parser does not apply may have a broken reference rather than an unused statement, so check those references before deciding.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether an unused statement is reserved for planned work or can be retired. Include its identity, its referrers, and their parser effects.

## Update

No typed retirement action is available for this finding. After confirming that a statement is unused, record a `defer` with the referrer evidence until a semantic removal action can name the supported deletion scope. A statement that a reference the parser does not apply still names needs that reference fixed first, not removal.

## Verify

Re-run the view and confirm the retired statement is absent while every applied reference and Approved reading remains intact.

## Grounding

Engineering check: exact redundancy in the authored grammar; no linguistic claim.

Bender, Laurie Poulson, Scott Drellishak, and Chris Evans. 2007. “Validation and Regression Testing for a Cross-linguistic Grammar Resource.” In *ACL 2007 Workshop on Deep Linguistic Processing*, 136–143. Association for Computational Linguistics. [Source](https://aclanthology.org/W07-1218/). Grounds the use of regression checks when changing grammar resources.

entries.description: This check finds a tag that at least half of a rule's candidate hosts carry. The tag is then the default, and the rule is better stated as applying everywhere with the minority tagged instead. It is computed from per-rule host counts that PanGloss already holds, in one pass over the tag and rule facts.
entries.helpPage:
# Tag on most candidate hosts

This check finds a tag that at least half of a rule's candidate hosts carry. The tag is then the default, and the rule is better stated as applying everywhere with the minority tagged instead. It is computed from per-rule host counts that PanGloss already holds, in one pass over the tag and rule facts.

This check is partial. It counts candidate hosts by the rule's category scope and does not see its phonological context, so a rule chosen by the form of the stem is not detected. No finding does not mean the tags are fine.

## Analyse

Read how many stems satisfy the rule context and how many of them carry the tag. A majority means the polarity is inverted: the exception is the stems that lack the tag.
