entries.title: A broad variant competes
entries.description: An unconditioned allomorph may be an intentional final fallback. Its selection order and other grammatical restrictions determine what to change.
entries.helpPage:
# A broad variant competes

An unconditioned allomorph may be an intentional final fallback. Its selection order and other grammatical restrictions determine what to change.

## Analyse

Read effective selection order, sibling conditions, load facts, and the contexts in which each variant is chosen.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Use `EditAllomorphCondition` to attach a confirmed condition to the exact broad variant. Use `OrderAllomorphs` when a confirmed broad variant should follow its conditioned siblings as the final fallback. Keep a confirmed fallback or free variant with a recorded reason and no grammar repair among the changes not applied yet; ask about morphological gates; defer invalid conditions to grammar health.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the broad form is a final fallback or should be limited to particular contexts. Include any unwanted-reading witness.

## Update

Stage a change with `EditAllomorphCondition` for a confirmed restriction or `OrderAllomorphs` for a confirmed fallback order. Both actions retain the existing allomorph identities; condition edits leave other allomorph users alone.

## Verify

Use Review Changes to inspect what the edit would write, then compare parser results from the current and edited scratch copies for the same words. Check the exact Approved readings, the attributed unwanted reading and reviewed negatives, held-out positives, and any elsewhere fallback cases. If `effective-allomorph-order` is unavailable, name it and defer.

## Grounding

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Technical documents index](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Describes allomorph environments, ordered alternatives, and default or elsewhere behavior.
- **[bender-poulson-drellishak-evans-2007]** — Emily M. Bender, Laurie Poulson, Scott Drellishak, and Chris Evans. 2007. “Validation and Regression Testing for a Cross-linguistic Grammar Resource.” In *ACL 2007 Workshop on Deep Linguistic Processing*, 136–143. Association for Computational Linguistics. [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/W07-1218/). Supports checking intended and unwanted parser outcomes with regression examples.

This is an engineering check grounded in FieldWorks practice; no general linguistic rule makes a final fallback harmful.

entries.title: Environment may be too broad
entries.description: Unobserved contexts are not bad forms. The first check covers one neighboring phoneme or an explicit boundary on one side; unsupported shapes and ambiguous alignments abstain.
entries.helpPage:
# Environment may be too broad

Unobserved contexts are not bad forms. The first check covers one neighboring phoneme or an explicit boundary on one side; unsupported shapes and ambiguous alignments abstain.

## Analyse

Read `environment-excess` for the effective contexts after compiled sibling order, OR alternatives, observed triggers, extra contexts, and missed triggers. Reading the whole view, each list shows its first 30 names; reading one object (`--object-id`, which a finding's evidence links use) lists every name. The row's `totals` give the full count of every list and of the loaded context universe. A limit line in the Report names the first dozen contexts and counts the rest. Filter by an environment identity to inspect the other measured users. `approved-morph-sequences` carries the aligned word evidence. Ambiguous alignment or a condition outside the one-neighbor capability is reported as inconclusive.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Ask by default when the only evidence is that a context has not appeared in the Texts. An extra licensed context is not evidence that the context is wrong. A finding needs an extra context and at least three Approved word types across two stems; that support floor ranks a question but does not decide it. Keep a productive extension and defer unsupported context shapes.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether a contrasting form in the extra licensed context is possible. Offer valid, invalid, or unknown as the response.

## Update

Only after a linguist confirms a wrong-context example, stage changes with `AuthorEnvironment` and `EditAllomorphCondition`, declaring the environment creation as a dependency of the relink. Relink only the intended allomorph user; leave shared users attached to their current environment. Do not narrow globally to the observed segments by default. Use the named word-boundary context for a word edge; do not infer a word edge from a displayed `#` marker.

## Verify

Use Review Changes to inspect what the edit would write, then compare parser results from the current and edited scratch copies for the same words. Check every exact Approved reading, held-out positive forms, and reviewed wrong-context negatives; confirm the shared users remain unchanged. The view reports extra and missed trigger sets; a missed trigger prevents an excess score. Show context counts, not a correctness rate. If the context universe, compiler order, or unique alignment is unavailable, name it and defer.

## Grounding

- **[prince-tesar-2004]** — Alan Prince and Bruce Tesar. 2004. “Learning Phonotactic Distributions.” In *Constraints in Phonological Acquisition*, 245–291. Cambridge University Press. DOI: 10.1017/CBO9780511486418.009. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511486418.009). Shows that positive evidence can leave different grammars making different predictions about unseen forms.
- **[tenenbaum-griffiths-2001]** — Joshua B. Tenenbaum and Thomas L. Griffiths. 2001. “Generalization, Similarity, and Bayesian Inference.” *Behavioral and Brain Sciences* 24(4):629–640. DOI: 10.1017/S0140525X01000061. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X01000061). Derives a preference for smaller extensions under a specified strong-sampling model and explains how priors affect it.
- **[gold-1967]** — E. Mark Gold. 1967. “Language Identification in the Limit.” *Information and Control* 10(5):447–474. DOI: 10.1016/S0019-9958(67)91165-5. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(67)91165-5). Shows that positive-only learning depends on the hypothesis class and the form of the evidence.
- **[wexler-1993]** — Kenneth Wexler. 1993. “The Subset Principle is an Intensional Principle.” In Eric Reuland and Werner Abraham (eds.), *Knowledge and Language: Volume I, From Orwell’s Problem to Plato’s Problem*, 217–239. Dordrecht: Springer. DOI: 10.1007/978-94-011-1840-8_10. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-011-1840-8_10). States a smallest-language choice for a nested hypothesis space under its learning assumptions.
- **[wexler-manzini-1987]** — Kenneth Wexler and M. Rita Manzini. 1987. “Parameters and Learnability in Binding Theory.” In Thomas Roeper and Edwin Williams (eds.), *Parameter Setting*, 41–76. Dordrecht: D. Reidel. DOI: 10.1007/978-94-009-3727-7_3. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-3727-7_3). Identifies a distinct parameter-setting and learnability chapter in binding theory; it is background, not evidence about Motif's environment detector.

The finite context universe and support floor are engineering choices, not a learned probability model or linguistic law.

entries.description: Extra natural-class members may be productive. Review every usage site, its Approved triggers, the feature intersection, and unknown membership before changing the class. A feature intersection is a deterministic set calculation, not a probability; it cannot show that an unobserved member is wrong.

Extra natural-class members may be productive. Review every usage site, its Approved triggers, the feature intersection, and unknown membership before changing the class. A feature intersection is a deterministic set calculation, not a probability; it cannot show that an unobserved member is wrong.

## Analyse

Read `natural-class-excess` for each measured usage site, the current effective extension, observed triggers, missed triggers, feature-intersection extension, and unknown members. Reading the whole view, each list shows its first 30 names; reading one object (`--object-id`, which a finding's evidence links use) lists every name. The row's `totals` give the full count of every list and of the loaded context universe. A limit line in the Report names the first dozen members and counts the rest. `approved-morph-sequences` contains aligned Approved words. The shared feature assignments determine the set of possible class members from the loaded chart; this calculation has no sampling model and is not a probability. Missing feature values remain unknown, and a class may intentionally generalize beyond its current observations.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Fix only an independently reviewed leak; keep a productive extension with a reason; ask for contrasts; defer incomplete feature or context attribution. The measure reports definite extras at a uniquely attributed site, including sparse support, and makes no automatic change. A p-only observation with held-out b and m positives supports keeping B={p,b,m} when those members remain productive.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the process applies to the additional segments and request independent examples, not endorsement of the smallest observed set.

## Update

Use `EditNaturalClass` to change the segment members of one explicitly scoped class. Its review lists every environment, rewrite rule, and morphological insertion that uses the class. When users have different meanings, use `AuthorNaturalClass` to create a separate class and `RelinkNaturalClass` to move only the confirmed typed environment or rule contexts. The other users stay on the original class. Neither route changes a feature chart.

## Verify

Use Review Changes to inspect what the edit would write, then compare parser results from the current and edited scratch copies for the same words. A confirmed correction must make the reviewed wrong form complete with no accepted reading, preserve every Approved reading, and retain valid held-out positives such as b and m. For a relink, verify the intended user changes and the other users still parse through the original class. A Keep records its reason against the finding evidence and makes no grammar edit. The view reports the definite feature-intersection extension and unknown members; when membership is unknown, do not claim an exact excess rate or a tightest class. If class extension or unique context attribution is unavailable, name it and defer.

## Grounding

- **[chomsky-halle-1968]** — Noam Chomsky and Morris Halle. 1968. *The Sound Pattern of English*. New York: Harper & Row. [MIT Press publisher record](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262530972/the-sound-pattern-of-english/). Its notation-specific evaluation metric illustrates one proposal for comparing grammar economy.
- **[albright-hayes-2003]** — Adam Albright and Bruce Hayes. 2003. “Rules vs. Analogy in English Past Tenses: A Computational/Experimental Study.” *Cognition* 90(2):119–161. DOI: 10.1016/S0010-0277(03)00146-X. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0010-0277(03)00146-X). Uses segmental features to generalize conditioning environments from paradigm examples.
- **[gold-1967]** — E. Mark Gold. 1967. “Language Identification in the Limit.” *Information and Control* 10(5):447–474. DOI: 10.1016/S0019-9958(67)91165-5. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(67)91165-5). Supports keeping an unobserved class member distinct from a disconfirmed one.

Feature intersection is a deterministic way to describe a possible class from the loaded chart. It is not a probability, and an unobserved segment is not thereby shown to be wrong.

entries.title: A required slot blocks a form
entries.description: This Text-tier finding shows an Approved form that fits no applicable template with all obligatory slots filled. A template accepts the reading when it embeds the sequence in order and all its obligatory slots are filled; one accepting template prevents a finding. The measure does not run a parser counterfactual and does not establish that the parser blocked the form.
entries.helpPage:
# A required slot blocks a form

This Text-tier finding shows an Approved form that fits no applicable template with all obligatory slots filled. A template accepts the reading when it embeds the sequence in order and all its obligatory slots are filled; one accepting template prevents a finding. The measure does not run a parser counterfactual and does not establish that the parser blocked the form.

## Analyse

Read each Approved sequence against every applicable template that embeds it in order. Inspect the obligatory slots left unfilled in each failed template; alternative templates can leave different slots as joint or ambiguous causes. Read every slot user and any possible feature-bearing zeroes. The slot-context evidence must include every template and category that shares the slot, including subcategories, because optionality changes all of those users.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Ask whether the pattern calls for an optional slot, a separate template, or a null affix. Keep an obligatory marker when it carries a grammatical distinction; defer when the evidence does not distinguish the choices.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether these forms use an optional slot, a separate template, or a null affix. Show every compatible template, its unfilled obligatory slots, every template that shares each slot, and the Approved morph sequences.

## Update

For a one-slot comparison, make a change whose only edit is `EditAffixSlot` setting the implicated slot optional. A separate template through `AuthorAffixTemplate`, or a meaningful null affix through the appropriate lexical action, is a different change and needs its own evidence. The optionality change affects every template and subcategory that uses the shared slot.

## Verify

Use Review Changes to inspect what the edit would write. Compare parser results from the current and edited scratch copies for the same words. Check before and after production of the exact Approved target reading, every previously produced Approved reading, and each reviewed negative. Recommend making the slot optional only when the target is newly produced, no Approved reading is lost, and no reviewed negative becomes accepted. If parser results are incomplete, the target remains missing, an Approved reading is lost, or a reviewed negative becomes accepted, name that reason and leave the change unrecommended.

## Grounding

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Technical documents index](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Explains obligatory and optional slots, null affixes, and alternative templates.
- **[bender-poulson-drellishak-evans-2007]** — Emily M. Bender, Laurie Poulson, Scott Drellishak, and Chris Evans. 2007. “Validation and Regression Testing for a Cross-linguistic Grammar Resource.” In *ACL 2007 Workshop on Deep Linguistic Processing*, 136–143. Association for Computational Linguistics. [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/W07-1218/). Supports paired positive and negative regression checks after a grammar change.

The one-slot counterfactual and zero-loss, no-new-negative requirements are engineering safeguards, not a linguistic frequency rule.

entries.title: Order excludes a valid form
entries.description: An Approved reading may conflict with the order declared by a template. Alternative templates and ambiguous placements must remain visible.
entries.helpPage:
# Order excludes a valid form

An Approved reading may conflict with the order declared by a template. Alternative templates and ambiguous placements must remain visible.

## Analyse

Read complete slot placements, category inheritance, all alternative templates, and both attested directions. A certain contradiction requires complete assignment enumeration and no order-compatible applicable template; pair-order variability is descriptive evidence on its own.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Fix an incorrect order; keep a real alternative with an accurate representation; ask about dialect differences; defer uncertain attribution.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the template should reverse its slots or whether the forms belong to a separate template. Show both directions when attested.

## Update

Use `EditAffixTemplate` to reorder an existing template when the linguist confirms one order. When both directions are Approved, preserve the existing order and use `AuthorAffixTemplate` to add an explicit alternative with its own slot membership. Do not infer a derivation that chains multiple templates.

## Verify

Use Review Changes to inspect what the edit would write. Compare parser results from the current and edited project for the same words. Check the exact Approved readings in both directions: the intended reading must be produced and every previously produced Approved reading must remain. Look for reviewed mixed-branch combinations, slot swaps, and double fills that become accepted. If one is newly accepted or an Approved reading is lost, do not apply the change. If none of those combinations has a reviewed label, report structural improvement only. Incomplete parser results or unavailable `template-embeddings` leave the order claim unverified; name the gap and defer it.

## Grounding

- **[black-2018]** — H. Andrew Black. 2018. “Introduction to Parsing.” SIL FieldWorks technical document, 12 April 2018. [Technical documents index](https://software.sil.org/fieldworks/help/technical-documents/). Distinguishes slot order, optionality, and alternative templates.
- **[hyman-2003]** — Larry M. Hyman. 2003. “Suffix Ordering in Bantu: A Morphocentric Approach.” In *Yearbook of Morphology 2002*, 245–281. DOI: 10.1007/0-306-48223-1_8. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/0-306-48223-1_8). Presents a default Bantu suffix template alongside language-specific ordering constraints.
- **[hyman-mchombo-1992]** — Larry M. Hyman and Sam Mchombo. 1992. “Morphotactic Constraints in the Chichewa Verb Stem.” In *Proceedings of the Eighteenth Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society: General Session and Parasession on The Place of Morphology in a Grammar*, 350–364. DOI: 10.3765/bls.v18i1.1579. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3765/bls.v18i1.1579). Provides a language-specific analysis of constraints on Chichewa verb-stem morphology.
- **[stump-1993]** — Gregory T. Stump. 1993. “Position Classes and Morphological Theory.” *Yearbook of Morphology 1992*, 129–180. DOI: 10.1007/978-94-017-3710-4_7. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-017-3710-4_7). Discusses alternative position-class representations and limits of simple linear ordering.
- **[ryan-2010]** — Kevin M. Ryan. 2010. “Variable Affix Order: Grammar and Learning.” *Language* 86(4):758–791. DOI: 10.1353/lan.2010.0032. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1353/lan.2010.0032). Shows that affix order may be variable and that position-class formalisms can undergenerate some systems.

The embedding search, cap, and certain-contradiction rule are Motif engineering choices; preserve attested alternatives instead of averaging away variable order.

entries.title: A Disapproved reading parses
entries.description: A word can have both an Approved reading and a Disapproved one. Narrow only the condition that licenses the unwanted morphology.
entries.helpPage:
# A Disapproved reading parses

A word can have both an Approved reading and a Disapproved one. Narrow only the condition that licenses the unwanted morphology.

This measure reads a saved parser run bound to the exact Baseline or proposed source. Without one, the result is `not-run`.

## Analyse

Compare the ordered Form, MSA, and inflection-type identities under ADR 0027. The finding says that PanGloss produced the same morphology as a Disapproved analysis; it does not declare the whole word impossible. Approved and Unknown readings stay separate.

Inspect its retained parser case with `parsimony view` (parser cases) and the finding's exact case key. Incomplete searches and surfaces that cannot be joined to one writing-system wordform do not count as completed evidence.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Fix an identified condition; keep when rejection concerns sense rather than morphology; ask about missing conditions; defer unknown attribution.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the Disapproved reading has a distinct grammatical condition. Include all Approved readings on the same word.

## Update

Change only the confirmed allomorph condition, preserving identity, feature requirements, and selection order.

## Verify

Check that the exact Disapproved morphology disappears and every Approved morphology remains. If `parser-signatures` is unavailable, name it and defer.

## Grounding

- **[bender-poulson-drellishak-evans-2007]** — Emily M. Bender, Laurie Poulson, Scott Drellishak, and Chris Evans. 2007. “Validation and Regression Testing for a Cross-linguistic Grammar Resource.” In *ACL 2007 Workshop on Deep Linguistic Processing*, 136–143. Association for Computational Linguistics. [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/W07-1218/). Supports comparing parser outcomes against labeled positive and negative examples.
- **[kol-nir-wintner-2014]** — Sheli Kol, Bracha Nir, and Shuly Wintner. 2014. “Computational Evaluation of the Traceback Method.” *Journal of Child Language* 41(1):176–199. DOI: 10.1017/S0305000912000694. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000912000694). Reports computational evaluation exposing flaws in predicted analyses.

The exact morphology identity and Opinion meaning used here follow Motif's project contract; these sources support outcome testing, not that local identity rule.

entries.title: A reviewed negative parses
entries.description: A reviewed negative that parses is direct evidence of a possible restriction problem. The repair must target the witnessed structure and preserve valid readings.
entries.helpPage:
# A reviewed negative parses

A reviewed negative that parses is direct evidence of a possible restriction problem. The repair must target the witnessed structure and preserve valid readings.

## Analyse

Read the negative judgment, its provenance, the parser's returned morphs, and the current slot order. Check positive forms and alternate readings.

## Disposition

An applied keep or defer is tied to this finding's exact evidence. See [Disposition](term:disposition) for how it appears in Active and Suppressed lists and returns after relevant evidence changes.

Fix a confirmed order error; correct mistaken evidence separately; ask about register or reading differences; defer an unsupported cause.

## Ask the linguist

Ask whether the reversed order is impossible in this category or valid in another use. Show the actual analyses and a matching positive.

## Update

Edit the existing template order for the confirmed category. Keep the reviewed-negative judgment unchanged.

## Verify

Require a completed search with no target reading, preserved Approved readings, and stable held-out controls. If `reviewed-negative-expectations` is unavailable, name it and defer.

## Grounding

- **[gold-1967]** — E. Mark Gold. 1967. “Language Identification in the Limit.” *Information and Control* 10(5):447–474. DOI: 10.1016/S0019-9958(67)91165-5. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(67)91165-5). Distinguishes positive-only text from an informant that labels membership and nonmembership.
- **[bender-poulson-drellishak-evans-2007]** — Emily M. Bender, Laurie Poulson, Scott Drellishak, and Chris Evans. 2007. “Validation and Regression Testing for a Cross-linguistic Grammar Resource.” In *ACL 2007 Workshop on Deep Linguistic Processing*, 136–143. Association for Computational Linguistics. [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/W07-1218/). Supports keeping positive recovery and negative rejection as separate regression outcomes.
- **[prince-tesar-2004]** — Alan Prince and Bruce Tesar. 2004. “Learning Phonotactic Distributions.” In *Constraints in Phonological Acquisition*, 245–291. Cambridge University Press. DOI: 10.1017/CBO9780511486418.009. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511486418.009). Explains that grammars consistent with positive data can differ on unseen forms, while negative judgments are distinct evidence.

An absent word or an accepted parser probe alone is not a negative judgment.

entries.title: Pending changes
entries.description: Pending changes are the analysis choices you have collected in Motif but have not yet written to FieldWorks. They can come from Texts and are listed together on Review Changes. The window labels them as “changes not applied yet.”
entries.helpPage:
# Pending changes

[Pending changes](term:proposal) are the analysis choices you have collected in Motif but have not yet written to FieldWorks. They can come from **Texts** and are listed together on **Review Changes**. The window labels them as “changes not applied yet.”

Use **Undo** on **Review Changes** to withdraw a choice, or return to **Texts** to make a different choice for the same word and analysis. The list belongs to its project and remains available if you close Motif and open that project again.

Nothing is written to FieldWorks while you are collecting or reading these changes. Before applying, use **Check these changes** to measure the touched words, confirm that the evidence is current and complete, and make sure every choice still fits. Then choose **Apply to FieldWorks project**.

The list on **Review Changes** is the same list a Proposal has: you can walk it with **Previous** and **Next**, as described in [Review a Proposal](guide:review-a-proposal).

entries.title: Proposals
entries.description: Proposals lists every set of changes you can review: the Proposals an AI assistant put together, and the changes you collected yourself that are not applied yet. Its table shows who built each one, its status and, when it has a Trial, four measures from before and after.
entries.helpPage:
# Proposals

**Proposals** lists every set of changes you can review: the Proposals an AI assistant put together, and the changes you collected yourself that are not applied yet. Its table shows who built each one, its status and, when it has a Trial, four measures from before and after.

Use the filters to see three groups:

- **Your changes not applied yet** are the changes you collected on **Texts**; they are also listed on **Review Changes**.
- **Waiting for you** includes Proposals with a current Trial, Proposals that need another try, and Proposals that have not been tried. Choose **Try it** or **Try again** to measure one on a copy of the project; nothing re-runs until you ask.
- **Closed** lists Proposals that were applied, declined, superseded or withdrawn. Select **Closed** to see those Proposals. When closed Proposals exist, **Show closed** includes them with the other groups and clears the current filter; **Hide closed** hides them and clears the filter.

At wide widths, each row shows the Proposal's name and number of changes. At narrow widths, the table keeps the name, status and actions; choose **Details** from the row's **⋯** menu to read its counts and other facts in the Inspector. Its measures are approved words kept, Text Coverage, warnings and **Work**, the amount of parser work, with today's value beside the value from the last try. **Work** is blank when the Trial cannot be compared with today's parse, for example when a search was stopped; a blank number says why in its tooltip. A number that moved is shown in bold. When there is no Trial, the table says **Not tried yet**. A chip can say that approved words were lost, that a change no longer fits, or that another Proposal also changes some of the same words. A Proposal that only approves or removes analyses measures only the words it touches; every other word keeps today's value, so its totals still compare with today's.

Select a row to choose the Proposal's details. When the Inspector is collapsed, choose **Details** from the row's **⋯** menu to reveal them. The Inspector shows its status, who built it, a summary of its changes and the numbers from its last try. Choose **Open in Review Changes** there to review the Proposal. Choose **Open** on a row to open the Proposal: a bar across the window names it and has **Leave Proposal**, which returns every page to today; **Esc** does the same when nothing else is using it, so in a text box, with a menu open or inside a dialog it does that job first and the Proposal stays open.

Once the Proposal has been tried, the bar also says when, and on which saved state of the FieldWorks project, such as "Tried Fri 9 Oct, 08:00 on Baseline of Tue 22 Sep, 06:00", and then whether that try is still current. A Proposal that was never tried has no such sentence.

The bar's **Today**, **Today → Proposal** and **Proposal** buttons choose what **Overview** shows; they appear only while **Overview**, **Texts**, **Warnings** or **Timing** is the page you are on, and the choice is kept while you move between pages until you leave the Proposal.

On **Overview**, the four headline numbers (Text Coverage, Approved Analyses Kept, Speed and Grammar Warnings) show, by that choice, today's value, today's value and then the Proposal's, such as 7 → 8 of 9 words parse, or the Proposal's value alone. Under **Proposal** each headline stands alone, and the rows and captions that describe today's parse give way to a line saying that today's breakdown is in the **Today** view; the rest of the page is today's, and the note under the page title says which of these you are reading. A headline the Proposal has no value for says so, and never shows today's number in its place; under **Today → Proposal** it shows today's alone, as the note says. When today has no parse but the Proposal has one, **Today → Proposal** and **Proposal** show the tiles, with today's side reading as none, and **Today** keeps the page that asks you to parse; when neither has a parse the note says so. When the Proposal has not been tried, or its try did not finish, **Overview** says so.

**Warnings** pairs today's grammar findings with the Proposal's own check: each count reads today's and then the Proposal's, findings only today has are struck through, marked **Gone** and listed under **Gone with This Proposal**, and findings only the Proposal has are marked **New** and listed under **New with This Proposal**. The marks are words in the row, and the row's **Details** and **⋯** buttons carry them in their names, so they do not depend on colour or the strikethrough. Findings are matched by their kind, so one finding of a kind today and a different finding of the same kind in the Proposal are neither gone nor new; the counts can then read the same on both sides. **Touch your words** counts the words of the rows shown in that view, and changing the view keeps the selected finding, the sort and the filters. **Timing** pairs the total word time, the median and the number of words stopped at the work limit, and the work by kind, in parser work, but only when both sides were read for the same words, as the note says. When the two sides cover different words, for example the slowest words or the words that stopped, nothing is paired and the page shows today's numbers and says so. When two tries cannot be compared in parser work, **Timing** pairs only the words stopped at the work limit and keeps today's totals; under **Proposal** the total word time, the median and the work by kind then read none, and the stopped words stay the Proposal's. The rule-work comparison lists percentage changes against the Trial’s retained Baseline for the selected words; new, missing and unattributed work are identified, and unavailable comparisons are never treated as zero. The bar and the original rule table stay today's, and a kind only one side has reads as none on the other side. Each page reads the Proposal's side only while it is shown, once for the Proposal, its try and the words chosen, and says it is reading until that read lands; it never shows an earlier Proposal's number in its place. On both pages a number the Proposal lacks says so and never shows today's in its place. On **Texts** the same choice applies to the matrix on the Matrix tab: under **Today → Proposal** each cell, each row total and each column total reads today's count and then the Proposal's, such as 12 → 9, and a cell whose count moved is outlined; under **Proposal** the cells and totals show the Proposal's counts alone. The places under a cell follow the same choice: today's places then the Proposal's, such as 5 → 3 places, or the Proposal's alone, taken from the words the Proposal puts in that cell; where its try measured words that today's matrix has no places for, the cell's places are blank under **Proposal**, and its tooltip and spoken name say the places are not counted with this Proposal, and it keeps today's places alone under **Today → Proposal**, rather than a number that would read as complete. The words listed under the matrix follow the same choice. Under **Today** they are today's. Under **Today → Proposal** each word gains a **With This Proposal** column that says where the Proposal put it, such as **Same** or **No parse**, or **Not measured with this Proposal** when its try did not measure that word; when the Proposal measured the same words as today's matrix, a word is listed if either side puts it in a chosen cell, so a cell that reads 0 → 5 lists those five words, and when it measured different words the list stays today's. Under **Proposal** the list shows the Proposal's own words in the cells you chose, with the **With This Proposal** column and the Proposal's time in parser work, and sorting by the slowest orders by those steps; the chips, the fix-first list and the buttons that parse or propose again give way, because they act on today's words, the shared morphemes give way whenever the list holds the Proposal's words, and the list says nothing until the Proposal's counts have been read. A word only the Proposal's try measured, which today's matrix does not have, is counted in its cell but cannot be listed, so the heading after the list's words says how many are counted but not listed, and the other numbers stay true. Counts are paired only when the Proposal's try measured the same words as today's matrix, as the note says; when it measured different words nothing is paired and the cells show today's counts. A pair compares counts, so a cell that reads the same on both sides can still hold different words, and a cell that reads 0 → 5 is not drawn faint. While the Proposal's counts are being read the note says so and the cells show today's counts. If the keyboard focus was in the chips or the fix-first list when you switched to **Proposal**, it moves to a cell of the matrix. A Proposal with no try shows its cells as none, never as zero. The Proposal's counts are read once for the Proposal and its try, only while **Texts** is shown, and the page says it is reading until they land; if they cannot be read the note says so and they are read again the next time you show **Texts** or the evidence is published. Changing the view keeps the chosen cells, the sort and the filters.

On **Lists** the same choice applies to each list: under **Today → Proposal** a list's chip and header read today's words and then the Proposal's, such as 5 → 3 words · 8 → 6 places, and under **Proposal** they read the Proposal's alone, and a list with no words in the number drawn drops its chip unless it is the list you are reading. Where the Proposal's try measured words that today's matrix has no places for, the header says the places are not counted with this Proposal and never reads them as zero. The chosen list shows the words the choice lists for its cells, a line under its header says which, the **With This Proposal** column says where the Proposal puts each word, and **AI Handoff for This List** sends the words shown. A chip's name says which number is today's and which is with this Proposal. Under **Today → Proposal** and **Proposal**, the **Moved By This Proposal** chip beside the sort on **Matrix** and **Lists** narrows the words to those the Proposal puts in a different cell than today does, over the words both sides have; its number counts them in the chosen cells, it hides when there are none unless it is chosen, a word only one side has is never counted, and under **Today** every word is listed again while the choice waits for you to return. **AI Handoff** sends the words listed, and leaving or switching the Proposal drops the choice.

**What Changed** under **Today → Proposal** lists the words that went from one cell today to another with the Proposal: each move reads today's cell and then the Proposal's, with how many words moved, and choosing a move lists its words, each with today's parse and the cell the Proposal puts it in. Only words that today's matrix and the Proposal's try both have are compared; the words only one side has are counted under the summary and never listed as moved. Under **Today** the tab keeps comparing the last two runs; under **Today → Proposal** and under **Proposal** it lists the same moves, since a move is a word's cell today and its cell with the Proposal. The moves are found once for the Proposal and today's words, only while **What Changed** is shown beside the Proposal, and are let go when you leave the Proposal; a flip between the two views reads nothing. The note is not shown when there is no matrix; the word cards show the Proposal's block as before.

Every other page shows today's numbers while a Proposal is open. If the bar is too narrow for one row it wraps to two, so **Try Again** and **Leave Proposal** stay in the window. The copy used for a Trial is thrown away; your FieldWorks project is not changed.

Below those numbers the Inspector shows a **Difference** section for every Proposal you select that is not a draft. A Difference compares what the Proposal's last try built with the Approved analyses saved in FieldWorks, for one Text. It is advice only: it never changes the project and never applies anything. Choose a Text, then choose **Make Difference**. It is never made for you after a try, because it can take a while. A bar shows how many words are compared, and **Cancel** stops it; a cancelled run saves nothing. When it is ready the section shows how many words to check and how many improved, with chips that list those words and, for one word, where it occurs in the Text. A Proposal keeps one Difference for each Text and each set of decisions it was compared with, so several sit side by side: making one for another Text replaces nothing. When there is more than one, a **Saved Differences** list switches between them, and every Difference says which Text it compares and whether it was read against the Approved analyses people saved in FieldWorks or against a program's decisions. **Make Difference** always compares with people's decisions, and the same button reads **Make Difference Again** when the Proposal already has one for the chosen Text; it replaces only that one. A Proposal that was never tried shows a note asking you to try it first, with no button. Once a Proposal is decided, only the Difference's summary is kept, the section says so, and a new one cannot be made. A deferred Proposal also keeps only the summary, and its words are not shown; the section says so and **Make Difference Again** brings the words back until the Proposal's status next changes.

Below the buttons the Inspector shows a **Parsimony** section for every Proposal you select that is not a draft. Parsimony is advice about the grammar, and it never changes the project, **Readiness** or **Apply**. A Trial that finishes queues it by itself; nothing in this window starts it or a parse. The section says where the advice stands: **Not Set Up**, **Not Yet Run**, **Queued**, **Running**, **Ready**, **Out of Date** (with what changed) or **Did Not Finish** (with why). It updates while the job runs, and keeps checking more slowly if the job takes a long time, until the state is final or you select another Proposal; a busy project does not stop it. Advice that did not finish is only advice that did not finish: the Trial, **Readiness** and **Apply** are not affected. The **Grammar Group** shows its own state and, under **Counts by Measure**, how many findings each measure found new, resolved, unchanged or with changed evidence; counts are per measure and are not added together. The **Text Group** does not run on its own, so it says it is not set up or not yet run. **Ready** advice does not check a changed human judgment or Parsimony Selection, so it can be behind on those. The section shows no start time or duration.

The status column says **Draft** for your changes and **Ready**, **Deferred**, **Applied**, **Declined**, **Superseded** or **Withdrawn** for other rows. A declined or withdrawn Proposal offers **Reopen**, which makes it a Draft again with its history kept. A declined, superseded or withdrawn Proposal offers **Delete**, which removes it and its tries. An applied Proposal cannot be deleted; it and its record of what was applied are kept. The **⋯** menu repeats each row's available actions.

The number beside **Proposals** in the sidebar counts Proposals whose Trial is current. While a Proposal is open, **Texts**, **Warnings** and **Timing** also show a purple badge: Texts counts the net change in the words in Same (the Proposal's Same words less today's), Warnings the findings the Proposal gains or loses, and Timing the percentage change in parser work over the same words, each as "+" or "−" from today's. A page shows its badge once it has read the Proposal's side, and none when nothing changed or the two sides cover different words. Its tooltip and a screen reader say what the badge counts and that it is the Proposal's number.

entries.title: Reading the Overview
entries.description: The Overview brings together saved results and project counts. Text Coverage tells you how many of your chosen words parse and how often they occur in your selected texts. Approved Analyses Kept counts words with an Approved analysis that the grammar rebuilt exactly. Its detail line counts words whose forms and glosses match but whose recorded entries differ when entry evidence is available, as well as Lost, Stopped, and Not parsed outcomes when those results are recorded. A high Text coverage number with a lower Approved analyses kept number means many chosen words parse, but fewer approved analyses were rebuilt exactly; open Texts and inspect the words because the tables measure different things. A slow word is a place to investigate, not an answer about what to change. Broad slots or environments may be worth checking, but timing does not identify a fix. Grammar Warnings lists what the grammar check found; read each finding before deciding whether to change the grammar.
entries.helpPage:
# Reading the Overview

The [Overview](term:overview) brings together saved results and project counts. **Text Coverage** tells you how many of your chosen words parse and how often they occur in your selected texts. **Approved Analyses Kept** counts words with an Approved analysis that the grammar rebuilt exactly. Its detail line counts words whose forms and glosses match but whose recorded entries differ when entry evidence is available, as well as **Lost**, **Stopped**, and **Not parsed** outcomes when those results are recorded. A high Text coverage number with a lower Approved analyses kept number means many chosen words parse, but fewer approved analyses were rebuilt exactly; open **Texts** and inspect the words because the tables measure different things. A slow word is a place to investigate, not an answer about what to change. Broad slots or environments may be worth checking, but timing does not identify a fix. **Grammar Warnings** lists what the grammar check found; read each finding before deciding whether to change the grammar.

**Speed** counts parser work in parser work, because parser work do not change with how busy this computer is; compare them when judging a grammar change. The total, the median and 95th percentile per word, each slowest word, and each kind's share all use parser work. A word the parser tried without a count says **parser work not recorded**. The one time on the tile is how long the whole run took on this computer, which machine load changes; the **Slowest Words** are the words with the most parser work, so they do not depend on how busy this computer was. A very large run keeps work by kind and rule as totals for the whole run, so its shares stay. A run stored before Motif kept those totals says its work by kind was not kept; choose **Parse all words** again to keep it. **Look first** opens the saved words or timings behind a measured group. It calls out Approved words whose forms and glosses match but whose recorded entries differ when entry evidence is available, as well as words Lost and searches that stopped. In a word row, Motif marks the differing PanGloss morpheme; when both entry names are recorded, its tooltip names them. When a word has Unknown and Disapproved analyses, its Matrix row summarizes FieldWorks status while each analysis keeps its approval status. In **Unknown × Different**, the cell says **Have a look** when PanGloss matched an analysis marked Disapproved and shows the recorded comparison detail. A stopped search does not establish which analyses were not built.

For the full page tour—including freshness, timing, warnings and the links beside each table—see [Overview](guide:overview). Opening the page shows stored results; it does not start a parse. After saving in FieldWorks, press **Refresh**, then **Parse all words** to measure your current [Default Selection](term:default-selection) against the saved project. See [Parse all words](guide:assessment).

![Overview results after Parse all words](shot:review-apply-refresh-parse/parsed)


The **Look first** row for unparsed words lists the ten chosen words with no completed parse that occur most often, with their counts, and the total. Under it, the words are grouped only by what the parser stored: a refusal code, the work limit or time limit that stopped the search, or no analysis. Motif does not guess a cause. Words that FieldWorks marks as an incorrect spelling are counted apart and not listed. When the Selection has no counts of places in Texts, the first ten words by spelling are listed instead, and the row says so. When the Selection comes from a word list with counts, a word the list gives no count has no number beside it and ranks after the counted words, and the row says how many words have no count, so the total may be too low. The link opens those words in the Matrix.

A **Look first** row can say that some entries have a stem **not tagged with an inflection class**. It counts the stems whose category, and every category above it, has no default inflection class, where an affix of that category is restricted by inflection class. The parser gives such a stem no class, so the stem cannot take those affixes. The row lists the ten entries with the most such affixes, each with its category, and its link opens the first in the inspector. This is advice that ranks a place to look. It never stops an Apply, a Draft or an edit, and it does not look at inflection features. It is read from the saved project when the Baseline is captured, so it never runs the parser.

**Ambiguity** counts the analyses PanGloss built for the words that parsed. A word the parser refused, stopped, or built nothing for has no analysis to count, so it is left out; so is a parsed word whose analyses could not all be read, and the tile says how many it counted. A mean above 1 means some words have several analyses; whether that matters depends on your grammar, and Motif does not grade it. If some chosen words are not in the saved parse, a note says so.

In the frequency bands, a high share in the first band and a low share in the last usually means the common words parse and the long tail does not. Read the bands as parts of one Selection: the words and places in all bands add up to the Text Coverage totals. A band is a count, not a verdict on the grammar.

entries.title: Refresh the project
entries.description: Use Refresh after saving changes in FieldWorks when you want Motif to read that saved state. Refresh captures a new Baseline and checks the grammar for Warnings. It does not parse words. Choose Parse all words after Refresh to measure the current Default Selection.
entries.helpPage:
# Refresh the project

Use **Refresh** after saving changes in FieldWorks when you want Motif to read that saved state. Refresh captures a new [Baseline](term:baseline) and checks the grammar for **Warnings**. It does not parse words. Choose [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) after Refresh to measure the current [Default Selection](term:default-selection).

1. Save your work in FieldWorks.
2. In Motif, choose **Refresh** (the ⟳ beside the project name in the top bar) and let it finish.
3. If setup opens after the first Baseline, choose what to measure and press **Start First Run**. Otherwise, open the project card (choose the project name in the top bar) and choose **Parse all words**.
4. Check **Overview**. Refresh updates the project counts and checks the grammar; parsing updates the parse results.

If you cancel **Parse all words** or the parser refuses it, Refresh's new Baseline remains; parse results do not describe it until a parse completes. Opening Motif again does not refresh a project that already has a Baseline.

![Refresh captures a Baseline before a separate parse updates the numbers](shot:review-apply-refresh-parse/refreshed)

entries.title: Changing a pending change
entries.description: You can change your mind before Apply. To replace a pending opinion, return to Texts, open the same word form, choose the reading or action you want instead, and collect that change. A new choice for the same word and analysis slot replaces the earlier pending choice.
entries.helpPage:
# Changing a pending change

You can change your mind before Apply. To replace a pending opinion, return to **Texts**, open the same word form, choose the reading or action you want instead, and collect that change. A new choice for the same word and analysis slot replaces the earlier pending choice.

To remove a change without replacing it:

1. Open **Review Changes**.
2. Find the word and action you want to withdraw.
3. Choose **Undo** beside it.

The remaining pending changes stay in the list. Use **Back to Analyze texts** (or **Back to Try a Word**) to return to the page where the first pending change was collected. Changes belong to the project and remain available if you close Motif and open that project again.

![A staged choice before you replace or undo it](shot:explained-word-card/unknown-staged)

entries.title: Review a Proposal
entries.description: When a Proposal is open, Review Changes names it in the heading, such as “Sound change · 4 changes”, and lists every change in it in one order: the Grammar changes first, a change that others depend on before the ones that depend on it, then changes to words, grouped as they are for your own changes. You can read that list without applying anything.
entries.helpPage:
# Review a Proposal

When a Proposal is open, **Review Changes** names it in the heading, such as “Sound change · 4 changes”, and lists every change in it in one order: the **Grammar changes** first, a change that others depend on before the ones that depend on it, then changes to words, grouped as they are for your own changes. You can read that list without applying anything.

1. Choose **Next** to move down the list. Choosing **Next** marks the change you leave as looked at; **Previous** moves back and marks nothing. **Keep** marks the current change and moves on, and **Keep all** in the toolbar's **⋯** menu, which shows how many it marks, marks every change. Every change, grammar or word, has its own **Keep** and **Undo** at the end of its row, and shows a **✓** mark once it has been looked at.
2. Read the count in the navigator, such as “2 of 4 looked at”. Looking at a change is attention, not approval. Apply never waits for it, and it never changes the Proposal.
3. Choose **Undo** beside a change you do not want. If other changes depend on it, Motif names them first, such as “Undoing “Voicing rule before vowels” also undoes “Retarget the restriction to the new rule”.” Choose **Undo both** (or **Undo these 3** when there are more), or **Cancel** to leave everything as it was.
4. After an Undo, the Proposal needs another try, because what it was tried against has changed. Choose **Try again**. Nothing re-runs on its own.
5. Choose **Apply to FieldWorks project** when Apply is no longer blocked. The Apply area lists what Apply checks, each with ✓ or ✗: whether the Proposal was tried as it is now, whether every change still fits, and whether it is ready to apply.

Choose **Decline** if you do not want the Proposal at all. It is kept with its tries as a record, the window leaves it, and its card moves to **Closed** on **Proposals**, where **Reopen** opens it again.

A change stops counting as looked at when the change itself changes, or when the Proposal is tried again. An undone change leaves the count. Keyboard shortcuts for this list are in [Keyboard shortcuts](guide:keyboard-shortcuts).

![Review Changes listing the changes of a Proposal](shot:proposal-review-keep-undo/review-list)

entries.title: Review Changes
entries.description: Review Changes gathers changes to words, grammar and the lexicon, grouped by what they do. For each word, it shows its analysis, the staged change, and whether the change still fits the current FieldWorks project. Select a change to read its full details in the Inspector. If the Inspector is closed, choose Details from the change's ⋯ menu. Keep marks a change looked at; Apply writes every eligible remaining change. Reading this page does not apply anything. In the Inspector, choose Inspect beside a pending morpheme when that action is available to open its object. The form and gloss remain copyable.
entries.helpPage:
# Review Changes

**Review Changes** gathers changes to words, grammar and the lexicon, grouped by what they do. For each word, it shows its analysis, the staged change, and whether the change still fits the current FieldWorks project. Select a change to read its full details in the Inspector. If the Inspector is closed, choose **Details** from the change's **⋯** menu. Keep marks a change looked at; Apply writes every eligible remaining change. Reading this page does not apply anything. In the Inspector, choose **Inspect** beside a pending morpheme when that action is available to open its object. The form and gloss remain copyable.

1. Check each listed word and change. Choose **Undo** beside a change you no longer want, or **Undo all** to take back a whole group. **Undo all** in the toolbar's **⋯** menu takes out every change at once; the window's Undo puts them back.
2. Choose **Check these changes** to measure the words you touched. The Apply area shows how many changed words keep their approved analyses. If the check is still running, you can choose **Cancel**.
3. Read what blocks Apply. The page title counts the changes that block Apply; the Apply area shows why Apply is unavailable. Use **Check these changes** in the Apply area, **Undo** beside a change, **Undo all** beside a group or in the toolbar's **⋯** menu, and **Refresh** in the top bar as needed. Apply only when the changes still fit, the numbers are current, the evidence is complete, FieldWorks is not holding the project open, and no approved analysis would be lost.
4. Choose **Apply to FieldWorks project**. After a successful Apply, the page shows a receipt. There is no extra confirmation step.

To go through a Proposal's changes one at a time with **Previous**, **Next**, **Keep** and **Undo**, see [Review a Proposal](guide:review-a-proposal).

If a change is in the **No longer fits** group, Apply stays blocked. Remove that change or refresh the project and check it again. A change that no longer fits cannot be forced. See **When a change no longer fits** for steps to recheck it.

If a change is in the **Needs another look** group, its sentence changed in FieldWorks after you made it. Select that change to read the refreshed sentence in the Inspector. Choose **Check again** there to keep the change, or **Undo** to take it back.

If Motif could not confirm an Apply, the page says that FieldWorks may already have these changes. Choose **Refresh** to check what the project holds now. Apply stays blocked until you do.

![Review Changes after measuring a pending analysis change](shot:review-apply-refresh-parse/measured)

entries.title: Settings
entries.description: Open Settings from the bottom of the left navigation rail to change how Motif looks and to find its keyboard shortcuts, project parsing limits, grammar-check defaults, problem reports, and version information. Help beside it opens guidance for the current page. Display choices are remembered for this user on this computer; a project's parsing limits are saved with that project's Default Selection.
entries.helpPage:
# Settings

Open **Settings** from the bottom of the left navigation rail to change how Motif looks and to find its keyboard shortcuts, project parsing limits, grammar-check defaults, problem reports, and version information. **Help** beside it opens guidance for the current page. Display choices are remembered for this user on this computer; a project's parsing limits are saved with that project's [Default Selection](term:default-selection).

Settings opens as a page. **Back** returns to the page you were using; Escape does the same after handling any field edit. The section navigator is the page's side panel and collapses in a narrow window. Select **Settings** again to open it, then choose a section or collapse the side bar to use the page's full width. [The Motif window](guide:the-window) describes how the panels fold away and return.

## Display

Zoom changes the Motif window's layout and text together. At higher zoom the usable page area is smaller, so scroll within a page to reach its content. Display shows the available zoom choices; [Keyboard shortcuts](guide:keyboard-shortcuts) lists their keys.

**Reset to 100%** is always visible and is disabled when zoom is already 100%.

Theme can follow the operating system or use Light or Dark. The change applies while Settings is open.

## Parsing

The Parsing group edits the current project's Default Selection. Setup, Settings, and **Analysis options** edit that same saved limit policy; the next parse uses it, while earlier results keep the limits from their own run. See [Default Selection](guide:default-selection) and [first-run setup](guide:first-run-setup) for choosing what to parse.

**Texts to Parse** shows the selected Text count; **Use All Texts** saves every project Text in the Default Selection while keeping its added words and parsing limits.

When the parser work limit is finite, the time limit can follow Motif's estimate or use an explicit value. An explicit value remains in force when the parser work limit changes until you choose the estimate again. When it follows the estimate, a parse gives each word ten times the estimated time as a safety net, so a slow computer reaches the parser work limit first; Setup, Settings and the command line all work this way. With no parser work limit there is no time limit, and an explicit override is cleared. Enter commits a number; leaving the field also commits it. If Motif refuses the value because it is not a positive whole number or the time is out of range, it says why beside the field and keeps what you typed there; nothing is saved and the Selection a run uses stays as it was. Escape, leaving the Parsing group, or leaving Settings puts the last saved value back in the field. If the value is fine but Motif cannot save it, for example because the Selection was changed elsewhere first, Motif restores the saved limits and says why.

## Default Proposal Checks

Default Proposal Checks sets how thorough Motif's grammar check is when it runs by itself, from Warnings, or for a Proposal. **Compare Stored Analyses** checks that each word's saved analyses still parse, which is the one part of a grammar check that slows down as a project grows. Choose one:

- **Within a work budget (recommended)** compares words until a fixed amount of work is spent, then says how many were left. It gives the same result on every computer.
- **Every word** compares all of them. A large project can take half a minute or more.
- **Off** skips the comparison; the other grammar checks still run.

The choice is remembered for this user on this computer and applies to the next grammar check. Results already shown keep the choice they were checked with. The command line's [Check a grammar](cmd:grammar%20check) accepts `--stored-analyses` to override it for one run.

## Writing Systems

For the project's writing-system settings and how to change them in FieldWorks, see [Writing systems in the window](guide:writing-systems).

## Texts

**Use All Texts** saves every Text in the current project as its Default Selection. Parsing limits and added words keep their saved values.

## Help and reports

Settings lets you preview a problem report. Read [When something goes wrong](guide:when-something-goes-wrong) for what a report includes and how local details are handled.

## About and data folders

About shows Motif, PanGloss, and operating-system versions and can copy those lines. Its folder button opens the managed data root, which holds Motif's paired project data and parser artifacts; FieldWorks projects remain in their own folders. See [When something goes wrong](guide:when-something-goes-wrong) for report contents and privacy choices.

entries.title: Switching projects
entries.description: Use the project menu at the top of the Motif window to move between FieldWorks projects.
entries.helpPage:
# Switching projects

Use the project menu at the top of the Motif window to move between FieldWorks projects.

1. Choose **Select new…** to browse for a `.fwdata` file, or choose **Open recent** and select a project Motif already knows.
2. Wait for the project’s Baseline, Selection, and stored results to load.
3. Check the project name on **Overview** before taking an action.

Each project has its own Motif workflow information. Switching away does not move its pending changes into another project; when you open it again, its changes are shown with that project. If Parse all words or AI Handoff is running, switching projects cancels that work before Motif loads the new project.

Choose **Configure…** from the project menu to reopen the project’s saved Selection and parsing limits. Use **Refresh** to read the saved project and capture a new Baseline, then choose **Parse all words** to measure the saved Selection; opening the project alone only reads stored results.

![The Overview after selecting a project](shot:open-project-overview/overview)

entries.title: Text Coverage
entries.description: Text Coverage shows what share of the Default Selection’s words, and their places in the chosen Texts, parsed in the last saved parse. The Overview reports both selected words and their places, so the two numbers may differ: one word form can appear many times in a Text.
entries.helpPage:
# Text Coverage

[Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) shows what share of the Default Selection’s words, and their places in the chosen Texts, parsed in the last saved parse. The Overview reports both selected words and their places, so the two numbers may differ: one word form can appear many times in a Text.

Use the breakdown to see parsed words alongside words with no parse, incomplete searches, or other recorded outcomes. Digit-only places and places in other writing systems are counted apart in a line beneath the share, from the Text summaries saved with the Baseline. A word the parser refuses as an invalid shape stays in the share. A word that stopped at the work limit or the time safety net did not complete its search, so read that outcome separately from a completed search with no parse.

**Text Coverage by Frequency Band** splits the same share by how often each word occurs, so you can see whether the words you use most parse. Words that occur equally often are ranked by spelling, so the bands are the same every time. A Selection with fewer words than a band has only the bands it fills. A Selection saved from a word-list file with counts is ranked by those counts instead, is titled **By Frequency Band**, and is never called Text Coverage, because the counts are the file's and not places in a Text. Text Coverage is about the selected Texts and words. It is not the same as **Accuracy**, which compares parser readings with approved analyses, or grammar coverage over an outside Corpus. Choose **Texts** to inspect words and places; read [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to understand which run the Overview is showing.

entries.title: Texts
entries.description: Texts is where you choose material to measure and compare word analyses. Its tabs are Matrix, Analyze texts, Lists, and What changed. In Analyze texts, use Read text to follow words in context or Word list to inspect words directly. Choose texts or added words there, then use Parse all words to record results for that Selection. If the Baseline has no Texts, Analyze texts says so and does not offer a Choose texts action. The text picker sits in the side panel beside the page. On narrow windows it folds away; choose the active Texts icon again to open or close it. The Inspector has its own labelled edge strip to reopen it. When the window cannot fit the page beside it, the Inspector uses the working area; Back to page returns to the same work. Crossing a panel’s width threshold restores the automatic layout.
entries.helpPage:
# Texts

**Texts** is where you choose material to measure and compare word analyses. Its tabs are **Matrix**, **Analyze texts**, **Lists**, and **What changed**. In **Analyze texts**, use **Read text** to follow words in context or **Word list** to inspect words directly. Choose texts or added words there, then use **Parse all words** to record results for that Selection. If the Baseline has no Texts, Analyze texts says so and does not offer a Choose texts action. The text picker sits in the side panel beside the page. On narrow windows it folds away; choose the active Texts icon again to open or close it. The Inspector has its own labelled edge strip to reopen it. When the window cannot fit the page beside it, the Inspector uses the working area; **Back to page** returns to the same work. Crossing a panel’s width threshold restores the automatic layout.

The **Read text** view creates line rows as they are needed while you scroll through a long Text, instead of building them all in advance. This keeps the reader responsive on long Texts.

The Matrix groups words by what FieldWorks holds, down the side, and what PanGloss found, across the top: **Same**, **Different**, **No parse**, **Stopped** or **Not parsed**. Each cell says in a few words what happened, such as **Kept**, **Lost** or **Built anyway**. Each cell shows its word count in larger type and its place count beneath it, including zero counts. A chosen cell's list says both counts, such as **1 word · 1 place**. The outcome legend names each outcome with its sign and word, and each entry opens those words in the Matrix. The chips above the Matrix, such as **Lost** or **New: PanGloss proposes**, choose those cells for you.

Every word row uses the meaning named by its Matrix cell, including in **Lists** and **Analyze texts**. A card may show recorded comparison detail beneath that shared meaning. For example, a word with Unknown and Disapproved analyses can appear in **Unknown × Different** when PanGloss matched an analysis FieldWorks marked Disapproved; the row keeps the cell's **Have a look** meaning and shows recorded comparison detail beneath it. When Approved and Disapproved analyses share a morphology, both opinions remain visible; that match does not establish which other analyses PanGloss matched.

An **Analyze texts** card can also show which FieldWorks item a grammar warning names in that word. **Other words that use -a** lists words with the same named item. Membership and spelling matches stay labelled as possible matches. This evidence records a connection to the warning; it does not say the warning caused the word's result. Open the warning to read PanGloss's full description.

A stopped search does not establish that an analysis was not built, even if it found some readings. Those words stay in **Stopped**, with **No result**; a word that was not parsed has no new comparison evidence. Matrix, the shared word lists and **Analyze texts** use the same per-word comparison.

**Word list** counts words by their FieldWorks opinion, with a separate filter for Approved, Unknown, Disapproved and Not in FieldWorks. These counts describe words, while each analysis in a word card keeps its own opinion. The shared row also shows the meaning, places and time. Identical forms and glosses can still name different entries; the differing PanGloss morpheme is marked. When both entry names are recorded, its tooltip names them.

Select a cell to list its words below the Matrix. The list's heading names the cell and says in one line what it means. When two or more of its words use the same morpheme, **What these words share:** shows each such morpheme and how many of the words use it. Morphemes are matched by their identity in FieldWorks, never by spelling. Choose a morpheme to open it in the Inspector; its FieldWorks link appears when you point at or focus it. Choose **Open in text** to see a word in **Analyze texts** when the Baseline has Texts; otherwise, **Open word** shows its result without a Text. For ticked words, the Matrix offers **Add as Unknown** and **Incorrect spelling**. On a **Word list** or **Lists** row, press **A**, **D** or **U** to stage Approve, Disapprove or Make Unknown for a word with one stored analysis. If it has several analyses, choose one in **Analyze texts**. Each action applies to the word form everywhere in the project, not only the occurrence currently shown, and remains pending until you apply it.

**Lists** holds the Matrix's named shortcuts, such as **Lost** or **Built something else**, with the same words, and opens on the first list that has words. One line names the list, counts its words and places, and says what it holds. Open a word to see the same FieldWorks and PanGloss card used in the Matrix; its morphemes open in the Inspector, and FieldWorks links appear when you point at or focus a morpheme. Tick words to send just those: the button says **AI Handoff for this word** or names the number of words. **AI Handoff for this list** sends every word in the selected list. With no words ticked, **AI Handoff** is disabled and explains **Tick words first.** A list of stopped or unparsed words also offers **Parse again**. A refused word stays under **No parse**, with the badge **PanGloss can’t read it** and its recorded reason on the row and card. Refused words are excluded from **Parse again**. If the reason names this project’s phonemes, inspect the phoneme inventory before starting another parse. On a **Word list** or **Lists** row, press **A**, **D** or **U** to stage Approve, Disapprove or Make Unknown for a word with one stored analysis. If it has several analyses, choose one in **Analyze texts**. Each action applies to the word form everywhere in the project and remains pending until you apply it.

In **What changed**, a move between two problem outcomes begins **Still a problem:** and names the old and new outcomes. The outcome changed, while the word remains a problem.

Use the keyboard to move through a Text, the Word list and Lists, and stage an opinion on one stored analysis at a time. [Keyboard shortcuts](guide:keyboard-shortcuts) lists the keys for Analyze texts, the Word list, Lists and Matrix.

Changes you collect remain pending until you review and apply them. The page’s **Review Changes** link opens that list; it does not write anything to FieldWorks. [Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) appears on the Overview after a measurement.

![Texts after Parse all words records the current comparison](shot:open-project-overview/texts)

A compact row shows one analysis and states the total when PanGloss returned several analyses. Open the word card to see every analysis and its grammatical category, even when the analyses have the same spelling.

entries.title: The Motif window
entries.description: The Motif window is a fixed frame with the same parts on every page. Nothing in it is saved or needs resetting: the frame arranges itself from the window's width each time you open Motif.
entries.helpPage:
# The Motif window

The Motif window is a fixed frame with the same parts on every page. Nothing in it is saved or needs resetting: the frame arranges itself from the window's width each time you open Motif.

- **The rail** is the narrow strip down the left edge. It lists the pages, such as **Overview**, **Texts** and **Review Changes**; choose one to open it. **Help** and **Settings** sit at the bottom of the rail.
- **The side panel** sits beside the page and holds that page's own controls, such as the text picker on **Texts**. Not every page has one.
- **The page** is where you do the work. A notice line above it shows project notices and the tech-demo notice. The tech-demo notice is one line with **Got It** beside its text; **Report a Problem** is in the **Help** menu and the status bar. A page's action buttons sit at the bottom of the page, or at the bottom of the Inspector while it is open. On **Review Changes** the buttons (**Check these changes** when it is offered, **Apply to FieldWorks project**, **Back** and **Decline** when they apply) stay in view; above them a **Details** area holds, in order, why Apply is unavailable, any refusal, the receipt after an Apply, the project name and count, what Apply checks, and the backup reminder. Choose Details and use the arrow keys to scroll it. In a short window the page keeps a few rows of its own and Details shrinks to its first line, so scroll it to read the rest.
- **The Inspector** shows the facts about the word, rule, morpheme or change you selected on the page. Until you select something it says "Select an item to inspect."
- **The status bar** runs along the bottom. It says that Motif writes nothing until you press Apply, offers **Report a problem**, summarises your selection, and shows buttons for changes not applied yet, warnings and parse progress when there are any.

## Narrow windows

The side panel and the Inspector fold away when the window gets narrow. The side panel folds below 1200 wide and the Inspector below 1000 wide, measured after zoom, so a higher zoom folds them sooner. Each folded panel leaves a way back:

- For the side panel, choose the button at the top left of the page that shows the panel's name and **›**, or choose the active page's icon in the rail again. **‹** at the top of the panel folds it away.
- For the Inspector, choose the labelled **INSPECTOR** strip at the right edge. **›** at the top of the Inspector folds it away.
- When the window is too narrow to show the Inspector beside the page, the Inspector fills the working area. Choose **Back to page** at its top to return to the same work.

Opening one panel can fold the other when both would not fit. Whatever you open or fold stays that way until the window crosses a panel's width, and then the automatic arrangement returns.

## Settings in the frame

[Settings](guide:settings) opens as a page in the frame, with **Back** to return to the page you were using. Its section list is the page's side panel, so it folds away and returns the same way.

## Sort orders

The word lists and tables that can sort remember their order for each project: the **Timing** statistics table, the word list under the **Texts** matrix and on **Lists**, and the **Warnings** table. Sort, go to another page and come back, or close the project and open it later, and the order is as you left it. Which row is selected is not remembered.

For keyboard routes into these parts, see [Keyboard shortcuts](guide:keyboard-shortcuts).

entries.title: Timing
entries.description: Timing counts parser work in parser work, which do not change with how busy this computer is; compare them when judging a grammar change. Timing opens on All and shows recorded parser work for the current Selection. It reads timing saved by Parse all words; opening the page does not start a parse. If there is no timing for those words, choose Parse again. If Stopped or Slowest has no words, choose Show all words to return to the full Selection.
entries.helpPage:
# Timing

Timing counts parser work in parser work, which do not change with how busy this computer is; compare them when judging a grammar change. **Timing** opens on **All** and shows recorded parser work for the current Selection. It reads timing saved by [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words); opening the page does not start a parse. If there is no timing for those words, choose **Parse again**. If **Stopped** or **Slowest** has no words, choose **Show all words** to return to the full Selection.

The **Words** row shows **All**, **Stopped**, and **Slowest** with their word counts. Choose **A Matrix cell** or **A list** to pick words from Texts; open **More** for words checked in Texts or words you enter by hand. **AI Handoff for these words** uses the current word group. **Re-run** opens the per-word time and parser work limits and the run controls. Its parser work limit starts at 20,000,000, and reaching it stops a word at the parser work limit. Shares use whole percentages; a positive share below one percent says **<1%**. **Parser** is the parser's own work that belongs to no single rule or lookup. **Not attributed** appears once in the kind legend for work the parser did not assign to a rule, a lookup or its own work; the kinds and **Not attributed** always add up to the total.
